oophoridium.c: Oophoridium ‖O`o*pho*rid"i*um (?), n.; pl. L. Oophorida (#), E. Oophoridiums (#). [NL., dim. fr. Gr.?. See Oophore.] (Bot.) The macrosporangium or case for the larger kind of spores in heterosporous flowerless plants.

oophoritis.c: Oophoritis ‖O`o*pho*ri"tis (?), n. [NL., fr. Gr. w,'o`n egg + fe`rein to bear + -itis.] (Med.) Ovaritis.

oophyte.c: Oophyte O"o*phyte (?), n. [Gr. w,'o`n an egg + fyto`n a plant.] (Bot.) Any plant of a proposed class or grand division (collectively termed oophytes or Oophyta), which have their sexual reproduction accomplished by motile antherozoids acting on oospheres, either while included in their oogonia or after exclusion.

oophytic.c: Oophytic O`o*phyt"ic (ō`o*fĭt"ĭk), a. (Bot.) Of or pertaining to an oophyte.

oorial.c: Oorial O*o"ri*al (?), n. (Zool.) A wild, bearded sheep inhabiting the Ladakh mountains. It is reddish brown, with a dark beard from the chin to the chest.

oosperm.c: Oosperm O"o*sperm (ō"o*spẽrm), n. [Gr. w,'o`n an egg + E. sperm.] (Biol.) The ovum, after fusion with the spermatozoon in impregnation. Balfour.

oosphere.c: Oosphere O"o*sphere (ō"o*sfēr), n. [Gr. w,'o`n an egg + E. sphere.]

oosporangium.c: Oosporangium ‖O`o*spo*ran"gi*um (?), n.; pl. L. Oosporangia (#), E. Oosporangiums (#). [NL., fr. Gr. w,'o`n an egg +? vessel.] (Bot.) An oogonium; also, a case containing oval or rounded spores of some other kind than oospores.

oospore.c: Oospore O"o*spore (?), n. [Gr. w,'o`n an egg +? a seed.] (Bot.) (a) A special kind of spore resulting from the fertilization of an oosphere by antherozoids. (b) A fertilized oosphere in the ovule of a flowering plant.

oosporic.c: Oosporic O`o*spor"ic (?), a. (Bot.) Of or pertaining to an oospore.

oostegite.c: Oostegite O*os"te*gite (?), n. [Gr.? +? a roof.] (Zool.) One of the plates which in some Crustacea inclose a cavity wherein the eggs are hatched.

ootheca.c: Ootheca ‖O`o*the"ca (?), n.; pl. Oothecae (#). [NL., fr. Gr. w,'o`n an egg +? a case.] (Zool.) An egg case, especially those of many kinds of mollusks, and of some insects, as the cockroach. Cf. Ooecium.

ootocoid.c: Ootocoid Ooticoid { O*ot"i*coid (?), O*ot"o*coid (?), } n. [Gr.? laying eggs (? egg +? a bearing, ti`ktein to bear) + -oid.] (Zool.) A half oviparous, or an oviparous, mammal; a marsupial or monotreme.

ootype.c: Ootype O"o*type (?), n. [Gr.? + -type.] (Zool.) The part of the oviduct of certain trematode worms in which the ova are completed and furnished with a shell.

ooze.c: Ooze Ooze (?), n. [OE. wose, AS. wase dirt, mire, mud, akin to w?s juice, ooze, Icel. vās wetness, OHG. waso turf, sod, G. wasen.] 1. Soft mud or slime; earth so wet as to flow gently, or easily yield to pressure. “My son i' the ooze is bedded.” Shak.

Ooze Ooze, v. i. [imp. & p. p. Oozed (?); p. pr. & vb. n. Oozing.] [Prov. Eng. weeze, wooz. See Ooze, n.] 1. To flow gently; to percolate, as a liquid through the pores of a substance or through small openings.
Ooze Ooze, v. t. To cause to ooze. Alex. Smith.

Ooze leather Ooze leather. Leather made from sheep and calf skins by mechanically forcing ooze through them; esp., such leather with a soft, finely granulated finish (called sometimes velvet finish) put on the flesh side for special purposes. Ordinary ooze leather is used for shoe uppers, in bookbinding, etc. Hence Ooze calf, Ooze finish, etc.

oozoa.c: Oozoa ‖O`ö*zo"a (?), n. pl. [NL., fr. Gr. w,'o`n an egg + zw^,on an animal.] (Zool.) Same as Acrita.

oozy.c: Oozy Ooz"y (?), a. Miry; containing soft mud; resembling ooze; as, the oozy bed of a river. Pope.

opacate.c: Opacate O*pa"cate (?), v. t. [L. opacatus, p. p. of opacare.] To darken; to cloud. [Obs.] Boyle.

opacity.c: Opacity O*pac"i*ty (?), n. [L. opacitas: cf. F. opacité.] 1. The state of being opaque; the quality of a body which renders it impervious to the rays of light; want of transparency; opaqueness.

opacous.c: Opacous O*pa"cous (?), a. [L. opacus. See Opaque.] Opaque. [R.] Milton. -- O*pa"cous*ness, n. [R.]

opah.c: Opah O"pah (?), n. (Zool.) A large oceanic fish (Lampris guttatus), inhabiting the Atlantic Ocean. It is remarkable for its brilliant colors, which are red, green, and blue, with tints of purple and gold, covered with round silvery spots. Called also king of the herrings.

opal.c: Opal O"pal (?), n. [L. opalus: cf. Gr.?, Skr. upala a rock, stone, precious stone: cf. F. opale.] (Min.) A mineral consisting, like quartz, of silica, but inferior to quartz in hardness and specific gravity.

opalesce.c: Opalesce O`pal*esce" (?), v. i. [imp. & p. p. Opalesced (?); p. pr. & vb. n. Opalescing (?).] To give forth a play of colors, like the opal.

opalescence.c: Opalescence O`pal*es"cence (?), n. (Min.) A reflection of a milky or pearly light from the interior of a mineral, as in the moonstone; the state or quality of being opalescent.

opalescent.c: Opalescent O`pal*es"cent (?), a. Reflecting a milky or pearly light from the interior; having an opaline play of colors.

opaline.c: Opaline O"pal*ine (?), a. [Cf. F. opalin.] Of, pertaining to, or like, opal in appearance; having changeable colors like those of the opal.
Opaline O"pal*ine (?), n. 1. An opaline variety of yellow chalcedony.

opalize.c: Opalize O"pal*ize (?), v. t. [imp. & p. p. Opalized (?); p. pr. & vb. n. Opalizing.] [Cf. F. opaliser.] To convert into opal, or a substance like opal. Lyell.

opalotype.c: Opalotype O*pal"o*type (?), n. [Opal + -type.] (Photog.) A picture taken on “milky” glass.

opaque.c: Opaque O*paque" (?), a. [F., fr. L. opacus. Cf. Opacous.]
Opaque O*paque", n. That which is opaque; opacity. Young.

opaqueness.c: Opaqueness O*paque"ness, n. The state or quality of being impervious to light; opacity. Dr. H. More.

ope.c: Ope Ope, v. t. & i. To open. [Poetic]

opeidoscope.c: Opeidoscope O*pei"do*scope (?), n. [Gr.?,?, voice + e'i^dos form + -scope.] (Physics) An instrument, consisting of a tube having one end open and the other end covered with a thin flexible membrance to the center of which is attached a small mirror. It is used for exhibiting upon a screen, by means of rays reflected from the mirror, the vibratory motions caused by sounds produced at the open end of the tube, as by speaking or singing into it. A. E. Dolbear.

opelet.c: Opelet Ope"let (?), n. (Zool.) A bright-colored European actinian (Anemonia sulcata, syn. Anthea sulcata); -- so called because it does not retract its tentacles.

open.c: Open O"pen (?), a. [AS. open; akin to D. open, OS. opan, G. offan, Icel. opinn, Sw. öppen, Dan. aaben, and perh. to E. up. Cf. Up, and Ope.] 1. Free of access; not shut up; not closed; affording unobstructed ingress or egress; not impeding or preventing passage; not locked up or covered over; -- applied to passageways; as, an open door, window, road, etc.; also, to inclosed structures or objects; as, open houses, boxes, baskets, bottles, etc.; also, to means of communication or approach by water or land; as, an open harbor or roadstead.
Open O"pen (?), n. Open or unobstructed space; clear land, without trees or obstructions; open ocean; open water. “To sail into the open.” Jowett (Thucyd.).

Open O"pen v. t. [imp. & p. p. Opened (?); p. pr. & vb. n. Opening.] [AS. openian. See Open,a.] 1. To make or set open; to render free of access; to unclose; to unbar; to unlock; to remove any fastening or covering from; as, to open a door; to open a box; to open a room; to open a letter.
Open O"pen, v. i. 1. To unclose; to form a hole, breach, or gap; to be unclosed; to be parted.
Open door O"pen door. (a) Open or free admission to all; hospitable welcome; free opportunity.
Open sea Open sea. (Internat. Law) A sea open to all nations. See Mare clausum.

Open verdict Open verdict. (Law) A verdict on a preliminary investigation, finding the fact of a crime but not stating the criminal, or finding the fact of a violent death without disclosing the cause.

openair.c: Open-air O"pen-air` (?), a. Taking place in the open air; outdoor; as, an open-air game or meeting.

openbill.c: Openbill O"pen*bill` (?), n. (Zool.) A bird of the genus Anastomus, allied to the stork; -- so called because the two parts of the bill touch only at the base and tip. One species inhabits India, another Africa. Called also open-beak. See Illust. (m), under Beak.

opener.c: Opener O"pen*er (?), n. 1. One who, or that which, opens. “True opener of my eyes.” Milton.

openeyed.c: Open-eyed O"pen-eyed` (?), a. With eyes widely open; alert to possible danger; watchful; vigilant. Shak.

openhanded.c: Open-handed O"pen-hand`ed (?), a. Generous; liberal; munificent. -- O"pen-hand`ed*ness, n. J. S. Mill.

openhearted.c: Open-hearted O"pen-heart`ed (?), a. Candid; frank; generous. Dryden. -- O"pen-heart`ed*ly, adv. -- O"pen-heart`ed*ness, n. Walton.

openhearth.c: Open-hearth steel Open-hearth steel. See under Open.

opening.c: Opening O"pen*ing, n. 1. The act or process of opening; a beginning; commencement; first appearance; as, the opening of a speech.

openly.c: Openly O"pen*ly, adv. [AS. openlice.] 1. In an open manner; publicly; not in private; without secrecy.

openmouthed.c: Open-mouthed O"pen-mouthed` (?), a. Having the mouth open; gaping; hence, greedy; clamorous. L'Estrange.

openness.c: Openness O"pen*ness, n. The quality or state of being open.

openwork.c: Openwork O"pen*work` (?), n. 1. Anything so constructed or manufactured (in needlework, carpentry, metal work, etc.) as to show openings through its substance; work that is perforated or pierced.

opera.c: Opera Op"er*a (ŏp"ẽr*ȧ), n. [It., fr. opera work, composition, opposed to an improvisation, fr. L. opera pains, work, fr. opus, operis, work, labor: cf. F. opéra. See Operate.] 1. A drama, either tragic or comic, of which music forms an essential part; a drama wholly or mostly sung, consisting of recitative, arias, choruses, duets, trios, etc., with orchestral accompaniment, preludes, and interludes, together with appropriate costumes, scenery, and action; a lyric drama.

operameter.c: Operameter Op`er*am"e*ter (?), n. [L. opus, operis, pl. opera work + -meter.] An instrument or machine for measuring work done, especially for ascertaining the number of rotations made by a machine or wheel in manufacturing cloth; a counter. Ure.

operancy.c: Operancy Operance { Op"er*ance (?), Op"er*an*cy (?), } n. The act of operating or working; operation. [R.]

operand.c: Operand Op"er*and (?), n. [From neuter of L. operandus, gerundive of operari. See Operate.] (Math.) The symbol, quantity, or thing upon which a mathematical operation is performed; -- called also faciend.

operant.c: Operant Op"er*ant (?), a. [L. operans, p. pr. of operari. See Operate.] Operative. [R.] Shak. -- n. An operative person or thing. [R.] Coleridge.

operate.c: Operate Op"er*ate (?), v. i. [imp. & p. p. Operated (?); p. pr. & vb. n. Operating.] [L. operatus, p. p. of operari to work, fr. opus, operis, work, labor; akin to Skr. apas, and also to G. üben to exercise, OHG. uoben, Icel. æfa. Cf. Inure, Maneuver, Ure.] 1. To perform a work or labor; to exert power or strength, physical or mechanical; to act.
Operate Op"er*ate, v. t. 1. To produce, as an effect; to cause.

operatical.c: Operatical Operatic { Op`er*at"ic (?), Op`er*at"ic*al (?), } a. Of or pertaining to the opera or to operas; characteristic of, suitable for, or resembling, the opera; as, an operatic voice.

operation.c: Operation Op`er*a"tion (?), n. [L. operatio: cf. F. opération.] 1. The act or process of operating; agency; the exertion of power, physical, mechanical, or moral.

operative.c: Operative Op"er*a*tive (?), a. [Cf.L. operativus, F. opératif.] 1. Having the power of acting; hence, exerting force, physical or moral; active in the production of effects; as, an operative motive; operative laws.
Operative Op"er*a*tive, n. 1. A skilled worker; an artisan; esp., one who operates a machine in a mill or manufactory.

operatively.c: Operatively Op"er*a*tive*ly, adv. In an operative manner.

operator.c: Operator Op"er*a`tor (?), n. [L.] 1. One who, or that which, operates or produces an effect.

opercle.c: Opercle O"per*cle (?), n. [Cf. F. opercule. See Operculum.] 1. (Anat.) Any one of the bony plates which support the gill covers of fishes; an opercular bone.

opercular.c: Opercular O*per"cu*lar (?), a. Of, pertaining to, or like, an operculum.
Opercular O*per"cu*lar, n. (Anat.) The principal opercular bone or operculum of fishes.

operculated.c: Operculated Operculate { O*per"cu*late (?), O*per"cu*la`ted (?), } a. [L. operculatus, p. p. of operculare to furnish with a lid, fr. operculum lid.] 1. (Bot.) Closed by a lid or cover, as the capsules of the mosses.

operculiform.c: Operculiform O*per"cu*li*form (?), a. [L. operculum a cover + -form: cf. F. operculiforme.] Having the form of a lid or cover.

operculigenous.c: Operculigenous O*per`cu*lig`e*nous (?), a. [Operculum + -genous.] (Zool.) Producing an operculum; -- said of the foot, or part of the foot, of certain mollusks.

operculum.c: Operculum O*per"cu*lum (?), n.; pl. L. Opercula (#), E. Operculums (#). [L., a cover or lid, fr. operire to cover.] 1. (Bot.) (a) The lid of a pitcherform leaf. (b) The lid of the urnlike capsule of mosses.

operetta.c: Operetta Op`er*et"ta (?), n. [It., dim. of opera.] (Mus.) A short, light, musical drama.

operose.c: Operose Op"er*ose` (?). a. [L. operosus, fr. opera pains, labor, opus, operis, work, labor.] Wrought with labor; requiring labor; hence, tedious; wearisome. “Operose proceeding.” Burke. “A very operose calculation.” De Quincey. -- Op"er*ose`ly, adv. -- Op"er*ose`ness, n.

operosity.c: Operosity Op`er*os"i*ty (?), n. [L. operositas.] Laboriousness. [R.] Bp. Hall.

operous.c: Operous Op"er*ous (?), a. Operose. [Obs.] Holder. -- Op"er*ous*ly, adv. [Obs.]

opertaneous.c: Opertaneous Op`er*ta"ne*ous (?), a. [L. opertaneus; operire to hide.] Concealed; private. [R.]

opetide.c: Opetide Ope"tide` (?), n. [Ope + tide.] Open time; -- applied to different things: (a) The early spring, or the time when flowers begin opening. [Archaic] Nares. (b) The time between Epiphany and Ash Wednesday wherein marriages were formerly solemnized publicly in churches. [Eng.] (c) The time after harvest when the common fields are open to all kinds of stock. [Prov. Eng.] Halliwell. [Written also opentide.]

ophelic.c: Ophelic O*phel"ic (?), a. (Chem.) Of, pertaining to, or designating, a substance (called ophelic acid) extracted from a plant (Ophelia) of the Gentian family as a bitter yellowish sirup, used in India as a febrifuge and tonic.

ophicleide.c: Ophicleide Oph"i*cleide (?), n. [F. ophicléide, fr. Gr. 'o`fis a serpent +?, gen.?, a key. So named because it was in effect the serpent, an old musical instrument, with keys added.] (Mus.) A large brass wind instrument, formerly used in the orchestra and in military bands, having a loud tone, deep pitch, and a compass of three octaves; -- now generally supplanted by bass and contrabass tubas. It developed from the older wooden instrument called the serpent. Moore (Encyc. of Music).

ophidia.c: Ophidia ‖O*phid"i*a (?), prop. n. pl. [NL., fr. Gr.?, dim. of 'o`fis a snake.] (Zool.) The suborder of reptiles which includes the serpents; called also Serpentes.

ophidian.c: Ophidian O*phid"i*an (?), n. [Cf. F. ophidien.] (Zool.) One of the Ophidia; a snake or serpent.
Ophidian O*phid"i*an, a. [Cf. F. ophidien.] (Zool.) Of or pertaining to the Ophidia; belonging to serpents.

ophidioid.c: Ophidioid O*phid"i*oid (?), a. [Ophidion + -oid.] (Zool.) Of or pertaining to the Ophidiidae, a family of fishes which includes many slender species. -- n. One of the Ophidiidae.

ophidion.c: Ophidion ‖O*phid"i*on (?), n.; pl. Ophidia (#). [L., fr. Gr.? little snake, fr. 'o`fis a serpent.] (Zool.) The typical genus of ophidioid fishes. [Written also Ophidium.] See Illust. under Ophidioid.

ophiolatry.c: Ophiolatry O`phi*ol"a*try (ō`fĭ*ŏl"ȧ*try̆), n. [Gr. 'o`fis serpent + latrei`a worship.] The worship of serpents.

ophiological.c: Ophiological Ophiologic { O`phi*o*log"ic (?), O`phi*o*log"ic*al (?), } a. Of or pertaining to ophiology.

ophiologist.c: Ophiologist O`phi*ol"o*gist (?), n. One versed in the natural history of serpents.

ophiology.c: Ophiology O`phi*ol"o*gy (?), n. [Gr.? a serpent + -logy: cf. F. ophioloqie.] That part of natural history which treats of the ophidians, or serpents.

ophiomancy.c: Ophiomancy O"phi*o*man`cy (?), n. [Gr. 'o`fis a serpent + -mancy: cf. F. ophiomantie.] Divination by serpents, as by their manner of eating, or by their coils.

ophiomorpha.c: Ophiomorpha ‖O`phi*o*mor"pha (?), n. pl. [NL. See Ophiomorphous.] (Zool.) An order of tailless amphibians having a slender, wormlike body with regular annulations, and usually with minute scales imbedded in the skin. The limbs are rudimentary or lacking. It includes the caecilians. Called also Gymnophiona and Ophidobatrachia.

ophiomorphite.c: Ophiomorphite O`phi*o*mor"phite (?), n. [Gr. 'o`fis a serpent + morfh` form.] (Paleon.) An ammonite.

ophiomorphous.c: Ophiomorphous O`phi*o*mor"phous (?), a. [Gr. 'o`fis a serpent + -morphous.] Having the form of a serpent.

ophiophagous.c: Ophiophagous O`phi*oph"a*gous (?), a. [Gr. 'o`fis a serpent +? to eat: cf. F. ophiophage.] (Zool.) Feeding on serpents; -- said of certain birds and reptiles.

ophiophagus.c: Ophiophagus ‖O`phi*oph"a*gus, n. [NL. See Ophiophagous.] (Zool.) A genus of venomous East Indian snakes, which feed on other snakes. Ophiophagus elaps is said to be the largest and most deadly of poisonous snakes.

ophism.c: Ophism Oph"ism (?), n. 1. Doctrines and rites of the Ophites.

ophite.c: Ophite O"phite (?), a. [Gr. 'ofi`ths, fr. 'o`fis a serpent.] Of or pertaining to a serpent. [Obs.]

Ophite O"phite, n. [L. ophites, Gr. 'ofi`ths (sc.?), a kind of marble spotted like a serpent: cf. F. ophite.] (Min.) A greenish spotted porphyry, being a diabase whose pyroxene has been altered to uralite; -- first found in the Pyreness. So called from the colored spots which give it a mottled appearance. -- O*phi"ic (#), a.
Ophite O"phite, n. [L. Ophitae, pl. See Ophite, a.] (Eccl. Hist.) A mamber of a Gnostic serpent-worshiping sect of the second century.

ophiuchus.c: Ophiuchus ‖O`phi*u"chus (?), n. [L., fr. Gr.?, lit., holding a serpent; 'o`fis a serpent +? to hold.] (Astron.) A constellation in the Northern Hemisphere, delineated as a man holding a serpent in his hands; -- called also Serpentarius.

ophiura.c: Ophiura ‖O`phi*u"ra (?), n. [NL., from Gr. 'o`fis snake + 'oyra` a tail.] (Zool.) A genus of ophiurioid starfishes.

ophiuran.c: Ophiuran O`phi*u"ran (?), a. (Zool.) Of or pertaining to the Ophiurioidea. -- n. One of the Ophiurioidea.

ophiurioid.c: Ophiurioid O`phi*u"ri*oid (?), a. (Zool.) Of or pertaining to the Ophiurioidea. -- n. One of the Ophiurioidea. [Written also ophiuroid.]

ophiuroidea.c: Ophiuroidea Ophiurioidea { ‖O`phi*u`ri*oi"de*a (?), ‖O`phi*u*roi"de*a (?), } n. pl. [NL., fr. Gr. 'o`fis serpent + 'oyra` tail + e'i^dos form.] (Zool.) A class of star-shaped echinoderms having a disklike body, with slender, articulated arms, which are not grooved beneath and are often very fragile; -- called also Ophiuroida and Ophiuridea. See Illust. under Brittle star.

ophryon.c: Ophryon ‖Oph"ry*on (?), n. [NL., fr. Gr.?,?, the brow.] (Anat.) The supraorbital point.

ophthalmia.c: Ophthalmia Oph*thal"mi*a (ŏf*thăl"mĭ*ȧ), n. [F. ophthalmie, L. ophthalmia, fr. Gr. 'ofqalmi`a, fr. 'ofqalmo`s the eye, akin to E. optic. See Optic.] (Med.) An inflammation of the membranes or coats of the eye or of the eyeball.

ophthalmic.c: Ophthalmic Oph*thal"mic (ŏf*thăl"mĭk; 277), a. [Gr. 'ofqalmiko`s: cf. F. ophthalmique. See Ophthalmia.] (Anat.) Of, pertaining to, or in the region of, the eye; ocular; as the ophthalmic, or orbitonasal, nerve, a division of the trigeminal, which gives branches to the lachrymal gland, eyelids, nose, and forehead.

ophthalmite.c: Ophthalmite Oph*thal"mite (?), n. [Gr. 'ofqalmo`s the eye.] (Zool.) An eyestalk; the organ which bears the compound eyes of decapod Crustacea.

ophthalmological.c: Ophthalmological Oph*thal`mo*log"ic*al (?), a. Of or pertaining to ophthalmology.

ophthalmologist.c: Ophthalmologist Oph`thal*mol"o*gist (?), n. One skilled in ophthalmology; an oculist.

ophthalmology.c: Ophthalmology Oph`thal*mol"o*gy (?), n. [Gr. 'ofqalmo`s the eye + -logy: cf. F. ophthalmologie.] The science which treats of the structure, functions, and diseases of the eye.

ophthalmometer.c: Ophthalmometer Oph`thal*mom"e*ter, n. [Gr. 'ofqalmo`s eye + -meter.] (Physiol.) An instrument devised by Helmholtz for measuring the size of a reflected image on the convex surface of the cornea and lens of the eye, by which their curvature can be ascertained.

ophthalmoscope.c: Ophthalmoscope Oph*thal"mo*scope (?), n. [From Gr. 'ofqalmo`s the eye + -scope.] (Physiol.) An instrument for viewing the interior of the eye, particularly the retina. Light is thrown into the eye by a mirror (usually concave) and the interior is then examined with or without the aid of a lens. -- Oph*thal`mo*scop"ic (#), a.

ophthalmoscopy.c: Ophthalmoscopy Oph`thal*mos"co*py (?), n. [Cf. F. ophthalmoscopie.] 1. A branch of physiognomy which deduces the knowledge of a person's temper and character from the appearance of the eyes.

opianic.c: Opianic O`pi*an"ic (?), a. [From Opium.] (Chem.) Of, pertaining to, or designating, an organic acid obtained by the oxidation of narcotine.

opianine.c: opianine o"pi*a*nine (?), n. (Chem.) An alkaloid (C22H23NO7) found in small quantity in opium. It is identical with narcotine. It is present in amounts up to 11% in Papaver somniferum, and is used clinically as an antitussive. MI11

opiate.c: Opiate O"pi*ate (?), n. [From Opium: cf. F. opiat.] 1. Originally, a medicine of a thicker consistency than sirup, prepared with opium. Parr.
Opiate O"pi*ate, a. [See Opium.] Inducing sleep; somniferous; narcotic; hence, anodyne; causing rest, dullness, or inaction; as, the opiate rod of Hermes. Milton.
Opiate O"pi*ate (?), v. t. To subject to the influence of an opiate; to put to sleep. [R.] Fenton.

opiferous.c: Opiferous O*pif"er*ous (?), a. [L. opifer; ops, opis, help + ferre to bear.] Bringing help. [R.]

opifice.c: Opifice Op"i*fice (?), n. [L. opificium, fr. opifex workman. See Office.] Workmanship. [Obs.] Bailey.

opificer.c: Opificer O*pif"i*cer (?), n. An artificer; a workman. [Obs.] “The almighty opificer.” Bentley.

opinable.c: Opinable O*pin"a*ble (?), a. [L. opinabilis.] Capable of being opined or thought. Holland.

opination.c: Opination Op`i*na"tion (?), n. [L. opinatio. See Opine,] The act of thinking; a supposition. [Obs.]

opinative.c: Opinative O*pin"a*tive (?), a. Obstinate in holding opinions; opinionated. [Obs.] -- O*pin"a*tive*ly, adv. [Obs.] Burton. Sir T. More.

opinator.c: Opinator Op"i*na`tor (?), n. [L.] One fond of his own opinions; one who holds an opinion. [Obs.] Glanvill.

opine.c: Opine O*pine" (?), v. t. & i. [imp. & p. p. Opined (?); p. pr. & vb. n. Opining.] [L. opinari, p. p. opinatus; akin to opinus (in comp.) thinking, and perh. to E. apt: cf. F. opiner.] To have an opinion; to judge; to think; to suppose. South.

opiner.c: Opiner O*pin"er (?), n. One who opines. Jer. Taylor.

opiniatre.c: Opiniatre Opiniaster { O`pin*ias"ter (?), O`pin*ia"tre (?), } a. [OF. opiniastre, F. opiniâtre. See Opinion.] Opinionated. [Obs.] Sir W. Raleigh.
Opiniatre Opiniator { O`pin*ia"tor, O`pin*ia"tre } (?), n. One who is opinionated. [Obs.] South. Barrow.

opiniate.c: Opiniate O*pin"iate (?), v. t. To hold or maintain persistently. [Obs.] Barrow.

opiniative.c: Opiniative O*pin"ia*tive (?), a. Opinionative. Glanvill. -- O*pin"ia*tive*ly, adv. -- O*pin"ia*tive*ness, n.

opiniatrety.c: Opiniatrety O`pin*iat"re*ty (?), n. [Cf. F. opiniâtreté.] Obstinacy in opinions. [Written also opiniatry.] [Obs.]

opinicus.c: Opinicus O*pin"i*cus (?), n. (Her.) An imaginary animal borne as a charge, having wings, an eagle's head, and a short tail; -- sometimes represented without wings.

opinion.c: Opinion O*pin"ion (?), n. [F., from L. opinio. See Opine.] 1. That which is opined; a notion or conviction founded on probable evidence; belief stronger than impression, less strong than positive knowledge; settled judgment in regard to any point of knowledge or action.

opinionable.c: Opinionable O*pin"ion*a*ble (?), a. Being, or capable of being, a matter of opinion; that can be thought; not positively settled; as, an opinionable doctrine. C. J. Ellicott.

opinionated.c: Opinionated O*pin"ion*a`ted (?), a. Stiff in opinion; firmly or unduly adhering to one's own opinion or to preconceived notions; obstinate in opinion. Sir W. Scott.

opinionative.c: Opinionative O*pin"ion*a*tive, a. 1. Unduly attached to one's own opinions; opinionated. Milton.

opinionator.c: Opinionator O*pin"ion*a`tor (?), n. An opinionated person; one given to conjecture. [Obs.] South.

opinionist.c: Opinionist O*pin"ion*ist (?), n. [Cf. F. opinioniste.] One fond of his own notions, or unduly attached to his own opinions. Glanvill.

opiparous.c: Opiparous O*pip"a*rous (?), a. [L. opiparus, fr. ops, opis, riches + parare to provide.] Sumptuous. [Obs.] -- O*pip"a*rous*ly, adv. [Obs.] E. Waterhouse.

opisometer.c: Opisometer Op`i*som"e*ter (?), n. [Gr.? backwards + -meter.] An instrument with a revolving wheel for measuring a curved line, as on a map.

opisthion.c: Opisthion ‖O*pis"thi*on (?), n. [NL., fr. Gr.? hinder.] (Anat.) The middle of the posterior, or dorsal, margin of the great foramen of the skull.

opisthobranchiata.c: Opisthobranchiata Opisthobranchia { ‖O*pis`tho*bran"chi*a (?), O*pis`tho*bran`chi*a"ta (?), } n. pl. [NL., from Gr. 'o`pisqen behind +? gills.] (Zool.) A division of gastropod Mollusca, in which the breathing organs are usually situated behind the heart. It includes the tectibranchs and nudibranchs.

opisthobranchiate.c: Opisthobranchiate O*pis`tho*bran"chi*ate (?), a. (Zool.) Of or pertaining to the Opisthobranchiata. -- n. One of the Opisthobranchiata.

opisthocoelous.c: Opisthocoelous Opisthocoelian { O*pis`tho*coe"li*an (?), O*pis`tho*coe"lous (?), } a. [Gr. 'o`pisqen behind + koi^los hollow,] (Anat.) Concave behind; -- applied especially to vertebrae in which the anterior end of the centrum is convex and the posterior concave.

opisthodome.c: Opisthodome O*pis"tho*dome (?), n. [L. opisthodomus, Gr.?; 'o`pisqen behind + do`mos house: cf. F. opisthodome.] (Arch.) A back chamber; especially, that part of the naos, or cella, farthest from the main entrance, sometimes having an entrance of its own, and often used as a treasury.

opisthoglypha.c: Opisthoglypha ‖O*pis`tho*glyph"a (?), n. pl. [NL., from Gr. 'o`pisqen behind +? to carve.] (Zool.) A division of serpents which have some of the posterior maxillary teeth grooved for fangs.

opisthography.c: Opisthography Op`is*thog"ra*phy (?), n. [Gr. 'o`pisqen behind + -graphy.] A writing upon the back of anything, as upon the back of a leaf or sheet already written upon on one side. [R.] Scudamore.

opisthomi.c: Opisthomi ‖Op`is*tho"mi (?), n. pl. [NL., fr. Gr. 'o`pisqen behind +? the shoulder.] (Zool.) An order of eellike fishes having the scapular arch attached to the vertebrae, but not connected with the skull.

opisthopulmonate.c: Opisthopulmonate O*pis`tho*pul"mo*nate (?), a.[Gr. 'o`pisqen behind + E. pulmonate.] (Zool.) Having the pulmonary sac situated posteriorly; -- said of certain air-breathing Mollusca.

opisthotic.c: Opisthotic Op`is*thot"ic (?), n. [Gr. 'o`pisqen behind +?,?, ear.] (Anat.) The inferior and posterior of the three elements forming the periotic bone.

opisthotonos.c: Opisthotonos ‖Op`is*thot"o*nos (?), n. [NL., from Gr.? backwards +? a stretching.] (Med.) A tetanic spasm in which the body is bent backwards and stiffened.

opitulation.c: Opitulation O*pit`u*la"tion (?), n. [L. opitulatio, fr. opitulari to bring help.] The act of helping or aiding; help. [Obs.] Bailey.

opium.c: Opium O"pi*um (?), n. [L., fr. Gr.? poppy juice, dim. of? vegetable juice.] (Chem.) The inspissated juice of the Papaver somniferum, or white poppy.

ople.c: Ople tree O"ple tree` (?). [L. opulus a kind of maple tree.] The witch-hazel. [Obs.] Ainsworth.

opobalsamum.c: Opobalsamum Opobalsam { Op`o*bal"sam (?), ‖Op`o*bal"sa*mum (?), } n. [L. opobalsamum, Gr.?;? vegetable juice +? balsam.] (Med.) The old name of the aromatic resinous juice of the Balsamodendron opobalsamum, now commonly called balm of Gilead. See under Balm.

opodeldoc.c: Opodeldoc Op`o*del"doc (?), n. [So called by Paracelsus. The first syllable may be fr. Gr.? vegetable juice.] 1. A kind of plaster, said to have been invented by Mindererus, -- used for external injuries. [Obs.]

opolchenie.c: Opolchenie ‖Op`ol*che"ni*e (?), n. [Russ., fr. opolchit' to make an army, polk army. Cf. Folk.] (Russia) See Army organization, above.

opopanax.c: Opopanax O*pop"a*nax (?), n. [L., fr. Gr.?;? vegetable juice + pa`nax, pa`nakes, a kind of plant: cf. F. opopanax.] The inspissated juice of an umbelliferous plant (the Opoponax Chironum), brought from Turkey and the East Indies in loose granules, or sometimes in larger masses, of a reddish yellow color, with specks of white. It has a strong smell and acrid taste, and was formerly used in medicine as an emmenagogue and antispasmodic. Dunglison.

opossum.c: Opossum O*pos"sum (?), n. [Of N. American Indian origin.] (Zool.) Any American marsupial of the genera Didelphys and Chironectes; called also possum. The common species of the United States is Didelphys Virginiana.

oppidan.c: Oppidan Op"pi*dan (?), a. [L. oppidanus, fr. oppidum town.] Of or pertaining to a town. Howell.
Oppidan Op"pi*dan, n. 1. An inhabitant of a town.

oppignerate.c: Oppignerate Op*pig"ner*ate (?), v. i. [L. oppigneratus, p. p. of oppignerare to pawn. See Ob-, and Pignerate.] To pledge; to pawn. [Obs.] Bacon.

oppilate.c: Oppilate Op"pi*late (?), v. t. [imp. & p. p. Oppilated (?); p. pr. & vb. n. Oppilating (?).] [L. oppilatus, p. p. of oppilare to stop up; ob (see Ob-) + pilare to ram down, to thrust.] To crowd together; to fill with obstructions; to block up. [Obs.] Cockeram.

oppilation.c: Oppilation Op`pi*la"tion (?), n. [L. oppilatio: cf. F. opilation.] The act of filling or crowding together; a stopping by redundant matter; obstruction, particularly in the lower intestines. Jer. Taylor.

oppilative.c: Oppilative Op`pi*la*tive (?), a. [Cf. F. opilatif. See Oppilate.] Obstructive. [Obs.] Sherwood.

oppleted.c: Oppleted Opplete { Op*plete" (?), Op*plet"ed (?), } a. [L. oppletus, p. p. of opplere to fill up; ob (see Ob-) + plere to fill.] Filled; crowded. [Obs.] Johnson.

oppletion.c: Oppletion Op*ple"tion (?), n. The act of filling up, or the state of being filled up; fullness. [Obs.]

oppone.c: Oppone Op*pone" (?), v. t. [L. opponere. See Opponent.] To oppose. [Obs.] B. Jonson.

opponency.c: Opponency Op*po"nen*cy (?), n. The act of opening an academical disputation; the proposition of objections to a tenet, as an exercise for a degree. [Eng.] Todd.

opponent.c: Opponent Op*po"nent (?), a. [L. opponens, -entis, p. pr. of opponere to set or place against, to oppose; ob (see Ob-) + ponere to place. See Position.] Situated in front; opposite; hence, opposing; adverse; antagonistic. Pope.
Opponent Op*po"nent, n. 1. One who opposes; an adversary; an antagonist; a foe. Macaulay.

opportune.c: Opportune Op`por*tune" (?), a. [F. opporiun, L. opportunus, lit., at or before the port; ob (see Ob-) + a derivative of portus port, harbor. See Port harbor.] Convenient; ready; hence, seasonable; timely. Milton.
Opportune Op`por*tune", v. t. To suit. [Obs.] Dr. Clerke(1637).

opportunism.c: Opportunism Op`por*tun"ism (?), n. [Cf. F. opportunisme.] The art or practice of taking advantage of opportunities or circumstances, or of seeking immediate advantage with little regard for ultimate consequences. [Recent]

opportunist.c: Opportunist Op`por*tun"ist, n. [Cf. F. opportuniste.] One who advocates or practices opportunism. [Recent]

opportunity.c: Opportunity Op`por*tu"ni*ty (?), n.; pl. Opportunities (#). [F. opportunité, L. opportunitas. See Opportune.] 1. Fit or convenient time or situation; a time or place permitting or favorable for the execution of a purpose; a suitable combination of conditions; suitable occasion; chance.

opposability.c: Opposability Op*pos`a*bil"i*ty (?), n. The condition or quality of being opposable.

opposable.c: Opposable Op*pos"a*ble (?), a. 1. Capable of being opposed or resisted.

opposal.c: Opposal Op*pos"al (?), n. Opposition. [R.] Sir T. Herbert.

oppose.c: Oppose Op*pose" (?), v. t. [imp. & p. p. Opposed (?); p. pr. & vb. n. Opposing.] [F. opposer. See Ob-, Pose, and cf.2d Appose, Puzzle, n. Cf.L. opponere, oppositum.] 1. To place in front of, or over against; to set opposite; to exhibit.
Oppose Op*pose" (ŏp*pōz"), v. i. 1. To be set opposite. Shak.

opposeless.c: Opposeless Op*pose"less, a. Not to be effectually opposed; irresistible. [Obs.] “Your great opposeless wills.” Shak.

opposer.c: opposer op*pos"er (ŏp*pōz"ẽr), n. One who opposes; an opponent; an antagonist; an adversary.

opposite.c: opposite op"po*site (ŏp"po*zĭt or ŏp"po*sĭt), a. [F., fr. L. oppositus, p. p. of opponere. See Opponent.] 1. Placed over against; standing or situated over against or in front; facing; -- often with to; as, a house opposite to the Exchange; the concert hall and the state theater stood opposite each other on the plaza.
Opposite Op"po*site, n. 1. One who opposes; an opponent; an antagonist. [Obs.]

oppositely.c: Oppositely Op"po*site*ly, adv. In a situation to face each other; in an opposite manner or direction; adversely.

oppositeness.c: Oppositeness Op"po*site*ness, n. The quality or state of being opposite.

oppositifolious.c: Oppositifolious Op*pos`i*ti*fo"li*ous (?), a. [See Opposite, Folious.] (Bot.) Placed at the same node with a leaf, but separated from it by the whole diameter of the stem; as, an oppositifolious peduncle.

opposition.c: Opposition Op`po*si"tion (?), n. [F., fr. L. oppositio. See Opposite.] 1. The act of opposing; an attempt to check, restrain, or defeat; resistance.

oppositionist.c: Oppositionist Op`po*si"tion*ist, n. One who belongs to the opposition party. Praed.

oppositipetalous.c: Oppositipetalous Op*pos`i*ti*pet"al*ous (?), a. [See Opposite, and Petal.] (Bot.) Placed in front of a petal.

oppositisepalous.c: Oppositisepalous Op*pos`i*ti*sep"al*ous (?), a. [See Opposite, and Sepal.] (Bot.) Placed in front of a sepal.

oppositive.c: Oppositive Op*pos`i*tive (?), a. [Cf. F. oppositif. See Opposite.] Capable of being put in opposition. Bp. Hall.

oppress.c: Oppress Op*press" (?), v. t. [imp. & p. p. Oppressed (?); p. pr. & vb. n. Oppressing.] [F. oppresser, LL. oppressare, fr. L. oppressus, p. p. of opprimere; ob (see Ob-) + premere to press. See Press.] 1. To impose excessive burdens upon; to overload; hence, to treat with unjust rigor or with cruelty. Wyclif.

oppression.c: Oppression Op*pres"sion (?), n. [F., fr. L. oppressio.] 1. The act of oppressing, or state of being oppressed.

oppressive.c: Oppressive Op*press"ive (?), a. [Cf. F. oppressif.] 1. Unreasonably burdensome; unjustly severe, rigorous, or harsh; as, oppressive taxes; oppressive exactions of service; an oppressive game law. Macaulay.

oppressor.c: Oppressor Op*press"or (?), n. [L.] One who oppresses; one who imposes unjust burdens on others; one who harasses others with unjust laws or unreasonable severity.

opprobrious.c: Opprobrious Op*pro"bri*ous (?), a. [L. opprobriosus, fr. opprobrium. See Opprobrium.] 1. Expressive of opprobrium; attaching disgrace; reproachful; scurrilous; as, opprobrious language.

opprobrium.c: Opprobrium Op*pro"bri*um (?), n. [L., fr. ob (see Ob-) + probrum reproach, disgrace.] A state of disgrace; infamy; reproach mingled with contempt; odium{3}.

oppugn.c: Oppugn Op*pugn" (?), v. t. [imp. & p. p. Oppugned (?); p. pr. & vb. n. Oppugning.] [OF. oppugner, L. oppugnare; ob (see Ob-) + pugnare to fight. See Impugn.] To fight against; to attack; to be in conflict with; to oppose; to resist.

oppugnancy.c: Oppugnancy Op*pug"nan*cy (?), n. [See Oppugnant.] The act of oppugning; opposition; resistance. Shak.

oppugnant.c: Oppugnant Op*pug"nant (?), a. [L. oppugnans, p. pr. of oppugnare. See Oppugn.] Tending to awaken hostility; hostile; opposing; warring. “Oppugnant forces.” I. Taylor. -- n. An opponent. [R.] Coleridge.

oppugnation.c: Oppugnation Op`pug*na"tion (?), n. [L. oppugnatio: cf. OF. oppugnation.] Opposition. [R.] Bp. Hall.

oppugner.c: Oppugner Op*pugn"er (?), n. One who opposes or attacks; that which opposes. Selden.

opsimathy.c: Opsimathy Op*sim"a*thy (?), n. [Gr.?.] Education late in life. [R.] Hales.

opsiometer.c: Opsiometer Op`si*om"e*ter (?), n. [Gr.? sight + -meter: cf. F. opsiomètre.] An instrument for measuring the limits of distinct vision in different individuals, and thus determiming the proper focal length of a lens for correcting imperfect sight. Brande & C.

opsonation.c: Opsonation Op`so*na"tion (?), n. [L. opsonatio.] A catering; a buying of provisions. [Obs.] Bailey.

optable.c: Optable Op"ta*ble (?), a. [L. optabilis.] That may be chosen; desirable. [Obs.] Cockeram.

optate.c: Optate Op"tate (?), v. i. [L. optatus, p. p. of optare.] To choose; to wish for; to desire. [Obs.] Cotgrave.

optation.c: Optation Op*ta"tion (?), n. [L. optatio. See Option.] The act of optating; a wish. [Obs.] Sir T. Browne.

optative.c: Optative Op"ta*tive (?), a. [L. optativus: cf. F. optatif.] Expressing desire or wish. Fuller.
Optative Op"ta*tive, n. [Cf. F. optatif.] 1. Something to be desired. [R.] Bacon.

optatively.c: Optatively Op"ta*tive*ly, adv. In an optative manner; with the expression of desire. [R.]

optic.c: Optic Op"tic (ŏp"tĭk), n. [From Optic, a.] 1. The organ of sight; an eye.

optical.c: Optical Optic { Op"tic (ŏp"tĭk), Op"tic*al (ŏp"tĭ*kail), } a. [F. optique, Gr. 'optiko`s; akin to 'o`psis sight, 'o`pwpa I have seen, 'o`psomai I shall see, and to 'o`sse the two eyes, 'o`ps face, L. oculus eye. See Ocular, Eye, and cf. Canopy, Ophthalmia.] 1. Of, pertaining to, or using vision or sight; as, optical illusions. [wns=2]

optically.c: Optically Op"tic*al*ly, adv. 1. By optics or sight.

optician.c: Optician Op*ti"cian (?), n. [Cf. F. opticien. See Optic, a.] 1. One skilled in optics. [R.] A. Smith.

optics.c: Optics Op"tics (?), n. [Cf. F. optique, L. optice, Gr.? (sc.?). See Optic.] That branch of physical science which treats of the nature and properties of light, the laws of its modification by opaque and transparent bodies, and the phenomena of vision.

optigraph.c: Optigraph Op"ti*graph (?), n. [Optic + -graph: cf. F. opticographe. See Optic, a. ] A telescope with a diagonal eyepiece, suspended vertically in gimbals by the object end beneath a fixed diagonal plane mirror. It is used for delineating landscapes, by means of a pencil at the eye end which leaves the delineation on paper.

optimacy.c: Optimacy Op"ti*ma*cy (?), n. [Cf. F. optimatie. See Optimate.] 1. Government by the nobility. [R.] Howell.

optimate.c: Optimate Op"ti*mate (?), a. [L. optimas, -atis, adj., optimates, n. pl., the adherents of the best men, the aristocrats, fr. optimus the best.] Of or pertaining to the nobility or aristocracy. [R.] -- n. A nobleman or aristocrat; a chief man in a state or city. [R.] Chapman.

optimates.c: Optimates ‖Op`ti*ma"tes (?), n. pl. [L. See Optimate.] The nobility or aristocracy of ancient Rome, as opposed to the populares.

optime.c: Optime Op"ti*me (?), n. [L., adv. fr. optimus the best.] One of those who stand in the second rank of honors, immediately after the wranglers, in the University of Cambridge, England. They are divided into senior and junior optimes.

optimism.c: Optimism Op"ti*mism (?), n. [L. optimus the best; akin to optio choice: cf. F. optimisme. See Option.]

optimistic.c: Optimistic Op`ti*mis"tic (?), a. 1. (Metaph.) Of or pertaining to optimism; tending, or conforming, to the opinion that all events are ordered for the best.

optimity.c: Optimity Op*tim"i*ty (?), n. [L. optimitas, fr. optimus the best.] The state of being best. [R.] Bailey.

option.c: Option Op"tion (?), n. [L. optio; akin to optare to choose, wish, optimus best, and perh. to E. apt: cf. F. option.] 1. The power of choosing; the right of choice or election; an alternative.

optional.c: Optional Op"tion*al (?), a. Involving an option; depending on the exercise of an option; left to one's discretion or choice; allowed but not compulsory; as, optional studies; it is optional with you to go or stay. -- n. See Elective, n.

optionally.c: Optionally Op"tion*al*ly, adv. In an optional manner.

optocoelia.c: Optocoelia Optocoele { Op"to*coele (?), ‖Op`to*coe"li*a (?), } n. [NL. optocoelia, fr. Gr.? optic + koi^los a hollow.] (Anat.) The cavity of one of the optic lobes of the brain in many animals. B. G. Wilder.

optogram.c: Optogram Op"to*gram (?), n. [Optic + -gram: cf. F. optogramme.] (Physiol.) An image of external objects fixed on the retina by the photochemical action of light on the visual purple. See Optography.

optography.c: Optography Op*tog"ra*phy (?), n. [Optic + -graphy.] (Physiol.) The production of an optogram on the retina by the photochemical action of light on the visual purple; the fixation of an image in the eye. The object so photographed shows white on a purple or red background. See Visual purple, under Visual.

optometer.c: Optometer Op*tom"e*ter (?), n. [Optic + -meter.] (Physiol.) An instrument for measuring the distance of distinct vision, mainly for the selection of eveglasses.

optometrist.c: Optometrist Op*tom"e*trist (?), n. One who is skilled in or practices optometry, especially one who examines the eyes for defects in vision and prescribes the proper lenses to correct any defects discovered.

optometry.c: Optometry Op*tom"e*try (?), n. 1. (Med.) Measurement of the range of vision, esp. by means of the optometer.

opulence.c: Opulence Op"u*lence (?), n. [L. opulentia: cf. F. opulence. See Opulent.] Wealth; riches; affluence. Swift

opulent.c: Opulent Op"u*lent (?), a. [L. opulens, opulentus, fr. ops, opis, power, wealth, riches, perh. akin to E. apt: cf. F. opulent. Cf. Copious, Couple, Office.] Having a large estate or property; wealthy; rich; affluent; as, an opulent city; an opulent citizen. -- Op"u*lent*ly, adv.

opuntia.c: Opuntia ‖O*pun"ti*a (?), prop. n. [NL.] (Bot.) A genus of cactaceous plants; the prickly pear, or Indian fig.

opus.c: Opus ‖O"pus (?), n.; pl. Opera (#). [L. See Opera.] A work; specif. (Mus.), a musical composition.

opuscule.c: Opuscule Opuscle { O*pus"cle (o*pŭs"'l), O*pus"cule (o*pŭs"kul), } n. [L. opusculum, dim. of opus work: cf. F. opuscule.] A small or petty work.

opusculum.c: Opusculum ‖O*pus"cu*lum (o*pŭs"ku*lŭm), n.; pl. Opuscula (#). [L.] An opuscule. Smart.

oquassa.c: Oquassa O*quas"sa (?), n. (Zool.) A small, handsome trout (Salvelinus oquassa), found in some of the lakes in Maine; -- called also blueback trout.

or.c: -or -or suff. [L. -or: cf. OF. -or, -ur, -our, F. -eur.] 1. A noun suffix denoting an act; a state or quality; as in error, fervor, pallor, candor, etc.

Or Or (ôr), conj. [OE. or, outher, other, auther, either, or, AS. āwðer, contr. from āhwaeðer; ā aye + hwaeðer whether. See Aye, and Whether, and cf. Either.] A particle that marks an alternative; as, you may read or may write, -- that is, you may do one of the things at your pleasure, but not both. It corresponds to either. You may ride either to London or to Windsor. It often connects a series of words or propositions, presenting a choice of either; as, he may study law, or medicine, or divinity, or he may enter into trade.
Or Or, prep. & adv. [AS.?r ere, before. √204. See Ere, prep. & adv.] Ere; before; sooner than. [Obs.]
Or Or, n. [F., fr. L. aurum gold. Cf. Aureate.] (Her.) Yellow or gold color, -- represented in drawing or engraving by small dots.

ora.c: Ora O"ra (?), n. [AS. See 2d Ore.] A money of account among the Anglo-Saxons, valued, in the Domesday Book, at twenty pence sterling.

orabassu.c: Orabassu ‖O`ra*bas"su (?), n. (Zool.) A South American monkey of the genus Callithrix, esp. Callithrix Moloch.

orache.c: Orache Orach { Or"ach, Or"ache} (?), n. [F. arroche, corrupted fr. L. atriplex, Gr.?. Cf. Arrach.] (Bot.) A genus (Atriplex) of herbs or low shrubs of the Goosefoot family, most of them with a mealy surface.

oracle.c: Oracle Or"a*cle (?), n. [F., fr. L. oraculum, fr. orare to speak, utter, pray, fr. os, oris, mouth. See Oral.]
Oracle Or"a*cle, v. i. [imp. & p. p. Oracled (?); p. pr. & vb. n. Oracling (?).] To utter oracles. [Obs.]

oracular.c: Oracular O*rac"u*lar (?), a. [L. oracularius. See Oracle.] 1. Of or pertaining to an oracle; uttering oracles; forecasting the future; as, an oracular tongue.

oraculous.c: Oraculous O*rac"u*lous (?), a. Oracular; of the nature of an oracle. [R.] “Equivocations, or oraculous speeches.” Bacon. “The oraculous seer.” Pope. -- O*rac"u*lous*ly, adv. -- O*rac"u*lous*ness, n.

oral.c: Oral O"ral (?), a. [L. os, oris, the mouth, akin to Skr. ās. Cf. Adore, Orison, Usher.] 1. Uttered by the mouth, or in words; spoken, not written; verbal; as, oral traditions; oral testimony; oral law.

orally.c: Orally O"ral*ly, adv. 1. In an oral manner. Tillotson.

orange.c: Orange Or"ange (ŏr"ĕnj), n. [F.; cf. It. arancia, arancio, LL. arangia, Sp. naranjia, Pg. laranja; all fr. Ar. nāranj, Per. nāranj, nārang; cf. Skr. nāranga orange tree. The o- in F. orange is due to confusion with or gold, L. aurum, because the orange resembles gold in color.]
orange or"ange, a. Of or pertaining to an orange; of the color of an orange; reddish yellow; as, an orange ribbon.

orangeade.c: Orangeade Or`ange*ade" (?), n. [F., fr. orange.] A drink made of orange juice and water, corresponding to lemonade; orange sherbet.

orangeat.c: Orangeat Or`an*geat" (?), n. [F., fr. orange.] Candied orange peel; also, orangeade.

orangeism.c: Orangeism Or"ange*ism (?), n. Attachment to the principles of the society of Orangemen; the tenets or practices of the Orangemen.

orangeman.c: Orangeman Or"ange*man (?), n.; pl. -men (?). One of a secret society, organized in the north of Ireland in 1795, the professed objects of which are the defense of the reigning sovereign of Great Britain, the support of the Protestant religion, the maintenance of the laws of the kingdom, etc.; -- so called in honor of William, Prince of Orange, who became William III. of England.

orangeroot.c: Orangeroot Or"ange*root` (?), n. (Bot.) An American ranunculaceous plant (Hidrastis Canadensis), having a yellow tuberous root; -- also called yellowroot, golden seal, etc.

orangery.c: Orangery Or"an*ger*y (?), n. [F. orangerie, fr. orange. See Orange.] A place for raising oranges; a plantation of orange trees.

orangetawny.c: Orangetawny Or"ange*taw`ny (?), a. & n. Deep orange-yellow; dark yellow. Shak.

orangite.c: Orangite Or"an*gite (?), (Min.) An orange-yellow variety of the mineral thorite, found in Norway.

orangutan.c: Orang-utan Orang-outang O*rang"-ou*tang`, O*rang"-u*tan` (?), n. [Malayan ōrang ūtan, i. e., man of the woods; ōrang man + ūtan a forest, wood, wild, savage.] (Zool.) An arboreal anthropoid ape (Pongo pygmaeus, formerly Simia satyrus), which inhabits Borneo and Sumatra. Often called simply orang. It is now an endangered species. [Written also orangutan, orangutang, orang-utan, ourang-utang, and oran-utan.]

orarian.c: Orarian O*ra"ri*an (?), a. [L. orarius, fr. ora coast.] Of or pertaining to a coast.

oration.c: Oration O*ra"tion (?), n.[L. oratio, fr. orare to speak, utter, pray. See Oral, Orison.] An elaborate discourse, delivered in public, treating an important subject in a formal and dignified manner; especially, a discourse having reference to some special occasion, as a funeral, an anniversary, a celebration, or the like; -- distinguished from an argument in court, a popular harangue, a sermon, a lecture, etc.; as, Webster's oration at Bunker Hill.
Oration O*ra"tion, v. i. To deliver an oration. Donne.

orator.c: Orator Or"a*tor (?), n. [L., fr. orare to speak, utter. See Oration.] 1. A public speaker; one who delivers an oration; especially, one distinguished for his skill and power as a public speaker; one who is eloquent.

oratorian.c: Oratorian Or`a*to"ri*an, n. [Cf. F. oratorien.] (R. C. Ch.) See Fathers of the Oratory, under Oratory.

oratorical.c: Oratorical Or`a*tor"ic*al (?), a. Of or pertaining to an orator or to oratory; characterized by oratory; rhetorical; becoming to an orator; as, an oratorical triumph; an oratorical essay. -- Or`a*tor"ic*al*ly, adv.

oratorio.c: Oratorio Or`a*to"ri*o (?), n. [It., fr. L. oratorius belonging to praying. See Orator, and cf. Oratory.]

oratorious.c: Oratorious Or`a*to"ri*ous (?), a. [LL. oratorius.] Oratorical. [Obs.] Jer. Taylor. -- Or`a*to"ri*ous*ly, adv. [Obs.]

oratorize.c: Oratorize Or"a*tor*ize (?), v. i. To play the orator. [Jocose or derisive] Dickens.

oratory.c: Oratory Or"a*to*ry (?), n.; pl. Oratories (#). [OE. oratorie, fr. L. oratorium, fr. oratorius of praying, of an orator: cf. F. oratoire. See Orator, Oral, and cf. Oratorio.] A place of orisons, or prayer; especially, a chapel or small room set apart for private devotions.

Oratory Or"a*to*ry, n. [L. oratoria (sc. ars) the oratorical art.] The art of an orator; the art of public speaking in an eloquent or effective manner; the exercise of rhetorical skill in oral discourse; eloquence. “The oratory of Greece and Rome.” Milton.

oratress.c: Oratress Or"a*tress (?), n. A woman who makes public addresses. Warner.

oratrix.c: Oratrix Or"a*trix (?), n. [L.] A woman plaintiff, or complainant, in equity pleading. Burrill.

orb.c: Orb Orb (ôrb), n. [OF. orb blind, fr. L. orbus destitute.] (Arch.) A blank window or panel. [Obs.] Oxf. Gloss.
Orb Orb, n. [F. orbe, fr. L. orbis circle, orb. Cf. Orbit.]
Orb Orb (ôrb), v. t. [imp. & p. p. Orbed (ôrbd); p. pr. & vb. n. Orbing.] 1. To form into an orb or circle. [Poetic] Milton. Lowell.
Orb Orb, v. i. To become round like an orb. [Poetic]

orbate.c: Orbate Or"bate (?), a. [L. orbatus, p. p. of orbare to bereave, fr. orbus bereaved of parents or children. See Orphan.] Bereaved; fatherless; childless. [Obs.]

orbation.c: Orbation Or*ba"tion (?), n. [L. orbatio.] The state of being orbate, or deprived of parents or children; privation, in general; bereavement. [Obs.] Bp. Hall.

orbed.c: Orbed Orbed (?), a. Having the form of an orb; round.

orbical.c: Orbical Orbic { Or"bic (?), Or"bic*al (?), } a. [L. orbicus, or orbitus, fr. orbis orb.] Spherical; orbicular; orblike; circular. [R.] Bacon.

orbicle.c: Orbicle Or"bi*cle (?), n. [L. orbiculus, dim. of orbis orb.] A small orb, or sphere. [Obs.] G. Fletcher.

orbicula.c: Orbicula ‖Or*bic"u*la (?), n. [NL. See Orbicle.] (Zool.) Same as Discina.

orbicular.c: Orbicular Or*bic"u*lar (?), a. [L. orbicularis, fr. orbiculus, dim. of orbis orb: cf. F. orbiculaire.] Resembling or having the form of an orb; spherical; circular; orbiculate. -- Or*bic"u*lar*ly, adv. -- Or*bic"u*lar*ness, n.

orbiculate.c: Orbiculate Or*bic"u*late (?), n. That which is orbiculate; especially, a solid the vertical section of which is oval, and the horizontal section circular.

orbiculated.c: Orbiculated Orbiculate { Or*bic"u*late (?), Or*bic"u*la`ted (?), } a. [L. orbiculatus. See Orbicular.] Made, or being, in the form of an orb; having a circular, or nearly circular, or a spheroidal, outline.

orbiculation.c: Orbiculation Or*bic`u*la"tion (?), n. The state or quality of being orbiculate; orbicularness. Dr. H. More.

orbit.c: Orbit Or"bit (?), n. [L. orbita a track or rut made by a wheel, course, circuit, fr. orbis a circle: cf. F. orbite. See 2d Orb.] 1. (Astron.) The path described by a heavenly body in its periodical revolution around another body; as, the orbit of Jupiter, of the earth, of the moon.

orbital.c: Orbital Or"bit*al (?), a. Of or pertaining to an orbit. “Orbital revolution.” J. D. Forbes.

orbitar.c: Orbitar Or"bit*ar (?), a. [Cf. F. orbitaire.] Orbital. [R.] Dunglison.

orbitary.c: Orbitary Or"bit*a*ry (?), a. Situated around the orbit; as, the orbitary feathers of a bird.

orbitelae.c: Orbitelae ‖Or`bi*te"lae (?), n. pl. [NL., fr. L. orbis an orb + tela a web.] (Zool.) A division of spiders, including those that make geometrical webs, as the garden spider, or Epeira.

orbitolites.c: Orbitolites Or`bi*to*li"tes (?), prop. n. [NL. See Orbit, and -lite.] (Zool.) A genus of living Foraminifera, forming broad, thin, circular disks, containing numerous small chambers.

orbitonasal.c: Orbitonasal Or`bi*to*na"sal (?), a. [Orbit + nasal.] (Anat.) Of or pertaining to the orbit and the nose; as, the orbitonasal, or ophthalmic, nerve.

orbitosphenoid.c: Orbitosphenoid Or`bi*to*sphe"noid (?), a. [Orbit + sphenoid.] (Anat.) Of or pertaining to the sphenoid bone and the orbit, or to the orbitosphenoid bone. -- n. The orbitosphenoid bone, which is situated in the orbit on either side of the presphenoid. It generally forms a part of the sphenoid in the adult.

orbitosphenoidal.c: Orbitosphenoidal Or`bi*to*sphe*noid"al (?), a. (Anat.) Of or pertaining to the orbitosphenoid bone; orbitosphenoid.

orbity.c: Orbity Orbitude { Or"bi*tude (?), Or"bi*ty (?), } n. [L. orbitudo, orbitas, fr. orbus: cf. F. orbité. See Orbate.] Orbation. [Obs.] Bp. Hall.

orbulina.c: Orbulina ‖Or`bu*li"na (?), prop. n. [NL., dim. of L. orbis orb.] (Zool.) A genus of minute living Foraminifera having a globular shell.

orby.c: Orby Orb"y (?), a. [From 2d Orb.] Orblike; having the course of an orb; revolving. [Obs.] “Orby hours.” Chapman.

orc.c: orc orc (ôrk), n. [L. orca, a kind of whale: cf. F. orque.] 1. (Zool.) Any of several cetaceans, especialy the grampus (Grampus griseus) of the dolphin family. [Written also ork and orch.] Milton.

orcadian.c: Orcadian Or*ca"di*an (?), a. [L. Orcades the Orkney Islands.] Of or pertaining to the Orkney Islands.

orcein.c: Orcein Or"ce*in (?), n. (Chem.) A reddish brown amorphous dyestuff, C7H7NO3, obtained from orcin, and forming the essential coloring matter of cudbear and archil. It is closely related to litmus.

orchanet.c: Orchanet Or"cha*net (?), n. [F. orcanète.] (Bot.) Same as Alkanet, 2. Ainsworth.

orchard.c: Orchard Or"chard (?), n. [AS. ortgeard, wyrtgeard, lit., wortyard, i. e., a yard for herbs; wyrt herb + geard yard. See Wort, Yard inclosure.] 1. A garden. [Obs.]

orcharding.c: Orcharding Or"chard*ing (?), n. 1. The cultivation of orchards.

orchardist.c: Orchardist Or"chard*ist, n. One who cultivates an orchard.

orchesography.c: Orchesography Or`che*sog"ra*phy (?), n. [Gr.? dance + -graphy.] A treatise upon dancing. [R.]

orchestian.c: Orchestian Or*ches"tian (?), n. [From Gr.? a dancer. See Orchestra.] (Zool.) Any species of amphipod crustacean of the genus Orchestia, or family Orchestidae. See Beach flea, under Beach.

orchestra.c: Orchestra Or"ches*tra (?), n. [L. orchestra, Gr.?, orig., the place for the chorus of dancers, from? to dance: cf. F. orchestre.] 1. The space in a theater between the stage and the audience; -- originally appropriated by the Greeks to the chorus and its evolutions, afterward by the Romans to persons of distinction, and by the moderns to a band of instrumental musicians. Now commonly called orchestra pit, to distinguish it from the section of the main floor occupied by spectators.

orchestral.c: Orchestral Or"ches*tral (?), a. Of or pertaining to an orchestra; suitable for, or performed in or by, an orchestra.

orchestration.c: Orchestration Or`ches*tra"tion (?), n. (Mus.) The arrangement of music for an orchestra; orchestral treatment of a composition; -- called also instrumentation.

orchestrion.c: Orchestrion Or*ches"tri*on (?), n. A large music box imitating a variety of orchestral instruments.

orchid.c: Orchid Or"chid (?), n. [See Orchis.] (Bot.) Any plant of the order Orchidaceae. See Orchidaceous.

orchidaceous.c: Orchidaceous Or`chi*da"ceous (?), a. (Bot.) Pertaining to, or resembling, a natural order (Orchidaceae) of endogenous plants of which the genus Orchis is the type. They are mostly perennial herbs having the stamens and pistils united in a single column, and normally three petals and three sepals, all adherent to the ovary. The flowers are curiously shaped, often resembling insects, the odd or lower petal (called the lip) being unlike the others, and sometimes of a strange and unexpected appearance. About one hundred species occur in the United States, but several thousand in the tropics.

orchidologist.c: Orchidologist Or`chid*ol"o*gist (?), n. One versed in orchidology.

orchidology.c: Orchidology Or`chid*ol"o*gy (?), n. [Gr.? the orchis + -logy.] The branch of botany which treats of orchids.

orchilla.c: Orchilla weed Or*chil"la weed` (?). (Bot.) The lichen from which archil is obtained. See Archil.

orchis.c: Orchis Or"chis (?), prop. n.; pl. Orchises (#). [L., fr. Gr.? a testicle, the orchis; -- so called from its tubers.]

orchitis.c: Orchitis ‖Or*chi"tis (?), n. [NL., fr. Gr.? a testicle + -itis.] (Med.) Inflammation of the testicles.

orchotomy.c: Orchotomy Or*chot"o*my (?), n. [Gr.? a testicle + te`mnein to cut.] (Surg.) The operation of cutting out or removing a testicle by the knife; castration.

orcin.c: Orcin Or"cin (?), n. [Etymology uncertain: cf. F. orcine.] (Chem.) A colorless crystalline substance, C6H3.CH3.(OH)2, which is obtained from certain lichens (Roccella, Lecanora, etc.), also from extract of aloes, and artificially from certain derivatives of toluene. It changes readily into orcein.

ord.c: Ord Ord (ôrd), n. [AS. ord point.] An edge or point; also, a beginning. [ Obs. or Prov. Eng.] Chaucer.

ordain.c: Ordain Or*dain" (?), v. t. [imp. & p. p. Ordained (?); p. pr. & vb. n. Ordaining.] [OE. ordeinen, OF. ordener, F. ordonner, fr. L. ordinare, from ordo, ordinis, order. See Order, and cf. Ordinance.] 1. To set in order; to arrange according to rule; to regulate; to set; to establish. “Battle well ordained.” Spenser.

ordainable.c: Ordainable Or*dain"a*ble (?), a. Capable of being ordained; worthy to be ordained or appointed. Bp. Hall.

ordalian.c: Ordalian Or*da"li*an (?), a. [LL. ordalium.] Of or pertaining to trial by ordeal. [Obs.] Bp. Hall.

ordeal.c: Ordeal Or"de*al (ôr"de*ail), n. [AS. ordāl, ordǣl, a judgment; akin to D. oordeel, G. urteil, urtheil; orig., what is dealt out, the prefix or- being akin to ā- compounded with verbs, G. er-, ur-, Goth. us-, orig. meaning, out. See Deal, v. & n., and cf. Arise, Ort.] 1. An ancient form of test to determine guilt or innocence, by appealing to a supernatural decision, -- once common in Europe, and still practiced in the East and by savage tribes.
Ordeal Or"de*al, a. Of or pertaining to trial by ordeal.

order.c: Order Or"der (?), n. [OE. ordre, F. ordre, fr. L. ordo, ordinis. Cf. Ordain, Ordinal.]

Order Or"der (?), v. t. [imp. & p. p. Ordered (?); p. pr. & vb. n. Ordering.] [From Order, n.] 1. To put in order; to reduce to a methodical arrangement; to arrange in a series, or with reference to an end. Hence, to regulate; to dispose; to direct; to rule.
Order Or"der, v. i. To give orders; to issue commands.

orderable.c: Orderable Or"der*a*ble (?), a. Capable of being ordered; tractable. [R.]

orderer.c: Orderer Or"der*er (?), n. 1. One who puts in order, arranges, methodizes, or regulates.

ordering.c: Ordering Or"der*ing, n. Disposition; distribution; management. South.

orderless.c: Orderless Or"der*less, a. Being without order or regularity; disorderly; out of rule.

orderliness.c: Orderliness Or"der*li*ness (?), n. The state or quality of being orderly.

orderly.c: Orderly Or"der*ly, a. 1. Conformed to order; in order; regular; as, an orderly course or plan. Milton.
Orderly Or"der*ly (?), adv. According to due order; regularly; methodically; duly.
Orderly Or"der*ly, n.; pl. Orderlies (?). 1. (Mil.) A noncommissioned officer or soldier who attends a superior officer to carry his orders, or to render other service.

ordinability.c: Ordinability Or`di*na*bil"i*ty (?), n. Capability of being ordained or appointed. [Obs.] Bp. Bull.

ordinable.c: Ordinable Or"di*na*ble (?), a. [See Ordinate, Ordain.] Capable of being ordained or appointed. [Obs.]

ordinal.c: Ordinal Or"di*nal (?), a. [L. ordinalis, fr. ordo, ordinis, order. See Order.] 1. Indicating order or succession; as, the ordinal numbers, first, second, third, etc. Contrasted to cardinal.
Ordinal Or"di*nal, n. 1. A word or number denoting order or succession.

ordinalism.c: Ordinalism Or"di*nal*ism (?), n. The state or quality of being ordinal. [R.] Latham.

ordinance.c: Ordinance Or"di*nance (?), n. [OE. ordenance, OF. ordenance, F. ordonnance. See Ordain, and cf. Ordnance, Ordonnance.]

ordinand.c: Ordinand Or"di*nand` (?), n. [L. ordinandus, gerundive of ordinare. See Ordain.] One about to be ordained.

ordinant.c: Ordinant Or"di*nant (?), a. [L. ordinans, p. pr. of ordinare. See Ordain.] Ordaining; decreeing. [Obs.] Shak.
Ordinant Or"di*nant, n. One who ordains. F. G. Lee.

ordinarily.c: Ordinarily Or"di*na*ri*ly (?), adv. According to established rules or settled method; as a rule; commonly; usually; in most cases; as, a winter more than ordinarily severe.

ordinary.c: Ordinary Or"di*na*ry (?), a. [L. ordinarius, fr. ordo, ordinis, order: cf. F. ordinaire. See Order.] 1. According to established order; methodical; settled; regular. “The ordinary forms of law.” Addison.

Ordinary Or"di*na*ry, n.; pl. Ordinaries (-rĭz). 1. (Law) (a) (Roman Law) An officer who has original jurisdiction in his own right, and not by deputation. (b) (Eng. Law) One who has immediate jurisdiction in matters ecclesiastical; an ecclesiastical judge; also, a deputy of the bishop, or a clergyman appointed to perform divine service for condemned criminals and assist in preparing them for death. (c) (Am. Law) A judicial officer, having generally the powers of a judge of probate or a surrogate.

ordinaryship.c: Ordinaryship Or"di*na*ry*ship (?), n. The state of being an ordinary. [R.] Fuller.

ordinate.c: Ordinate Or"di*nate (?), a. [L. ordinatus, p. p. of ordinare. See Ordain.] Well-ordered; orderly; regular; methodical. “A life blissful and ordinate.” Chaucer.

Ordinate Or"di*nate, n. (Geom.) The distance of any point in a curve or a straight line, measured on a line called the axis of ordinates or on a line parallel to it, from another line called the axis of abscissas, on which the corresponding abscissa of the point is measured.
Ordinate Or"di*nate (?), v. t. To appoint, to regulate; to harmonize. Bp. Hall.

ordinately.c: Ordinately Or"di*nate*ly (?), adv. In an ordinate manner; orderly. Chaucer. Skelton.

ordination.c: Ordination Or`di*na"tion (?), n. [L. ordinatio: cf. F. ordination.] 1. The act of ordaining, appointing, or setting apart; the state of being ordained, appointed, etc.

ordinative.c: Ordinative Or"di*na*tive (?), a. [L. ordinativus.] Tending to ordain; directing; giving order. [R.] Gauden.

ordinator.c: Ordinator Or"di*na`tor (?), n. [L.] One who ordains or establishes; a director. [R.] T. Adams.

ordnance.c: Ordnance Ord"nance (?), n. [From OE. ordenance, referring orig. to the bore or size of the cannon. See Ordinance.] Heavy weapons of warfare; cannon, or great guns, mortars, and howitzers; artillery; sometimes, a general term for all weapons, ammunitiion, and appliances used in war.

ordonnance.c: Ordonnance Or"don*nance (?), n. [F. See Ordinance.] (Fine Arts) The disposition of the parts of any composition with regard to one another and the whole.

ordonnant.c: Ordonnant Or"don*nant (?), a. [F., p. pr. of ordonner. See Ordinant.] Of or pertaining to ordonnance. Dryden.

ordovician.c: Ordovician Or`do*vi"cian (?), a. [From L. Ordovices, a Celtic people in Wales.] (Geol.) Of or pertaining to a division of the Silurian formation, corresponding in general to the Lower Silurian of most authors, exclusive of the Cambrian. -- n. The Ordovician formation.

ordure.c: Ordure Or"dure (?), n. [F. ordure, OF. ord filthy, foul, fr. L. horridus horrid. See Horrid.]

ordurous.c: Ordurous Or"dur*ous (?), a. Of or pertaining to ordure; filthy. Drayton.

ore.c: Ore Ore (ōr), n. [AS. ār.] Honor; grace; favor; mercy; clemency; happy augury. [Obs.] Chaucer.
Ore Ore, n. [AS. ōra; cf. ār brass, bronze, akin to OHG. ēr, G. ehern brazen, Icel. eir brass, Goth. ais, L. aes, Skr. ayas iron. √210. Cf. Ora, Era.]

oread.c: Oread O"re*ad (?), n. [L. Oreas, -adis, Gr. 'Oreia`s, -a`dos, fr. 'o`ros mountain: cf. F. oréade.] (Class. Myth.) One of the nymphs of mountains and grottoes.

oreades.c: Oreades ‖O*re"a*des (?), n. pl. [NL.] (Zool.) A group of butterflies which includes the satyrs. See Satyr, 2.

orectic.c: Orectic O*rec"tic (?), a. [Gr. 'orektiko`s, fr. 'o`rexis, yearning after, from 'ore`gein to reach after.] (Philos.) Of or pertaining to the desires; hence, impelling to gratification; appetitive.

oregon.c: Oregon grape Or"e*gon grape` (ŏr"e*gŏn grāp`). (Bot.) An evergreen species of barberry (Berberis Aquifolium), of Oregon and California; also, its roundish, blue-black berries.

oreodon.c: Oreodon O"re*o*don (?), prop. n. [Gr. 'o`ros, -eos, mountain + 'odoy`s, 'odo`ntos, tooth.] (Paleon.) A genus of extinct herbivorous mammals, abundant in the Tertiary formation of the Rocky Mountains. It is more or less related to the camel, hog, and deer.

oreodont.c: Oreodont O"re*o*dont (?), a. (Paleon.) Resembling, or allied to, the genus Oreodon.

oreographic.c: Oreographic O`re*o*graph"ic (?), a. Of or pertaining to oreography.

oreography.c: Oreography O`re*og"ra*phy (?), n. [Gr. 'o`ros, -eos, mountain + -graphy.] The science of mountains; orography.

oreoselin.c: Oreoselin O`re*os"e*lin (?), n. (Chem.) A white crystalline substance which is obtained indirectly from the root of an umbelliferous plant (Imperatoria Oreoselinum), and yields resorcin on decomposition.

oreosoma.c: Oreosoma ‖O`re*o*so"ma (?), n. pl. [NL., from Gr. 'o`ros, -eos, mountain + sw^ma body.] (Zool.) A genus of small oceanic fishes, remarkable for the large conical tubercles which cover the under surface.

orfe.c: Orfe Orf { Orf (?), Or"fe (?), } n. (Zool.) A bright-colored domesticated variety of the id. See Id.

orfgild.c: Orfgild Orf"gild` (?), n. [AS. orf, yrfe, cattle, property + gild, gield, money, fine.] (O. Eng. Law) Restitution for cattle; a penalty for taking away cattle. Cowell.

orfray.c: Orfray Or"fray (?), n. [F. orfraie. Cf. Osprey, Ossifrage.] (Zool.) The osprey. [Obs.] Holland.

orfrays.c: Orfrays Or"frays (?), n. [OF. orfrais, F. orfroi; F. or gold + fraise, frise, fringe, ruff. See Fraise, and cf. Auriphrygiate.] See Orphrey. [Obs.] Rom. of R.

organ.c: Organ Or"gan (ôr"gain), n. [L. organum, Gr. 'o`rganon; akin to 'e`rgon work, and E. work: cf. F. organe. See Work, and cf. Orgue, Orgy.] 1. An instrument or medium by which some important action is performed, or an important end accomplished; as, legislatures, courts, armies, taxgatherers, etc., are organs of government.
Organ Or"gan, v. t. To supply with an organ or organs; to fit with organs; to organize. [Obs.]

organdy.c: Organdy Organdie { Or"gan*die, Or"gan*dy } (?), n. [F. organdi.] A kind of transparent light but stiff muslin.

organic.c: Organic Or*gan"ic (ôr*găn"ĭk), a. [L. organicus, Gr. 'organiko`s: cf. F. organique.] 1. (Biol.) Of or pertaining to an organ or its functions, or to objects composed of organs; consisting of organs, or containing them; as, the organic structure of animals and plants; exhibiting characters peculiar to living organisms; as, organic bodies, organic life, organic remains. Cf. Inorganic.

organically.c: Organically Or*gan"ic*al*ly, adv. In an organic manner; by means of organs or with reference to organic functions; hence, fundamentally. Gladstone.

organicalness.c: Organicalness Or*gan"ic*al*ness, n. The quality or state of being organic.

organicism.c: Organicism Or*gan"i*cism (?), n. (Med.) The doctrine of the localization of disease, or which refers it always to a material lesion of an organ. Dunglison.

organific.c: Organific Or`gan*if"ic (?), a. [Organ + L. -ficare (in comp.) to make. See fy.] Making an organic or organized structure; producing an organism; acting through, or resulting from, organs. Prof. Park.

organism.c: Organism Or"gan*ism (?), n. [Cf. F. organisme.] 1. Organic structure; organization. “The advantageous organism of the eye.” Grew.

organist.c: Organist Or"gan*ist, n. [Cf. F. organiste.] 1. (Mus.) One who plays on the organ.

organista.c: Organista ‖Or`ga*nis"ta (?), n. [Sp., an organis.] (Zool.) Any one of several South American wrens, noted for the sweetness of their song.

organizability.c: Organizability Or`gan*i`za*bil"i*ty (ôr`gain*ī`zȧ*bĭl"ĭ*ty̆), n. Quality of being organizable; capability of being organized.

organizable.c: Organizable Or"gan*i`za*ble (ôr"gain*ī`zȧ*b'l), a. Capable of being organized; esp. (Biol.), capable of being formed into living tissue; as, organizable matter.

organize.c: Organize Or"gan*ize (ôr"gain*īz), v. t. [imp. & p. p. Organized (ôr"gain*īzd); p. pr. & vb. n. Organizing (ôr"gain*ī*zĭng).] [Cf. F. organiser, Gr. 'organi`zein. See Organ.] 1. (Biol.) To furnish with organs; to give an organic structure to; to endow with capacity for the functions of life; as, an organized being; organized matter; -- in this sense used chiefly in the past participle.

organling.c: Organling Or"gan*ling (?), n. (Zool.) A large kind of sea fish; the orgeis.

organo.c: Organo- Or"ga*no- (?). [See Organ.] A combining form denoting relation to, or connection with, an organ or organs.

organogen.c: Organogen Or*gan"o*gen (?), n. [Organo- + -gen.] (Chem.) A name given to any one of the four elements, carbon, hydrogen, oxygen, and nitrogen, which are especially characteristic ingredients of organic compounds; also, by extension, to other elements sometimes found in the same connection; as sulphur, phosphorus, etc.

organogenesis.c: Organogenesis Or`ga*no*gen"e*sis (?), n. [Organo- + genesis.] 1. (Biol.) The origin and development of organs in animals and plants.

organogenic.c: Organogenic Or`ga*no*gen"ic (?), a. (Biol.) Of or pertaining to organogenesis.

organographical.c: Organographical Organographic { Or`ga*no*graph"ic (?), Or`ga*no*graph"ic*al (?), } a. [Cf. F. organographique.] Of or pertaining to organography.

organographist.c: Organographist Or`ga*nog"ra*phist (?), n. One versed in organography.

organography.c: Organography Or`ga*nog"ra*phy (?), n. [Organo- + -graphy: cf. F. organographie.] A description of the organs of animals or plants.

organoleptic.c: Organoleptic Or`ga*no*lep"tic (?), a. [F. organoleptique, fr. Gr.? an organ +? to lay hold of.] (Physiol.) Making an impression upon an organ; plastic; -- said of the effect or impression produced by any substance on the organs of touch, taste, or smell, and also on the organism as a whole.

organological.c: Organological Or`ga*no*log"ic*al (?), a. Of or relating to organology.

organology.c: Organology Or`ga*nol"o*gy (?), n. [Organ + -logy: cf. F. organologie.] 1. The science of organs or of anything considered as an organic structure.

organometallic.c: organometallic or`ga*no*me*tal"lic (?), a. (Chem.) Pertaining to, or denoting, any one of a series of compounds of certain metallic elements bound to organic radicals; such as, methylmercury, zinc methyl, sodium ethyl, etc.; formerly refered to as metalorganic.

organum.c: Organum Organon { ‖Or"ga*non (?), ‖Or"ga*num (?), } n. [NL. organon, L. organum. See Organ.] An organ or instrument; hence, a method by which philosophical or scientific investigation may be conducted; -- a term adopted from the Aristotelian writers by Lord Bacon, as the title (“Novum Organon”) of part of his treatise on philosophical method. Sir. W. Hamilton.

organonymy.c: Organonymy Or`ga*non"y*my (?), n. [Organo- + Gr.?, for?, a name.] (Biol.) The designation or nomenclature of organs. B. G. Wilder.

organophyly.c: Organophyly Or`ga*noph"y*ly (?), n. [Organo- + Gr.? clan.] (Biol.) The tribal history of organs, -- a branch of morphophyly. Haeckel.

organoplastic.c: Organoplastic Or`ga*no*plas"tic (?), a. [Organo- + -plastic.] (Biol.) Having the property of producing the tissues or organs of animals and plants; as, the organoplastic cells.

organotrophic.c: Organotrophic Or`ga*no*troph"ic (?), a. [Organo- + Gr.? to nourish.] (Biol.) Relating to the creation, organization, and nutrition of living organs or parts.

organule.c: Organule Or"gan*ule (?), n. [Dim. of organ.] (Anat.) One of the essential cells or elements of an organ. See Sense organule, under Sense. Huxley.

organy.c: Organy Or"ga*ny (?), n. [AS. Organe, from the Latin. See Origan.] (Bot.) See Origan.

organzine.c: organzine or"gan*zine (ôr"gain*zĭn), n. [F. organsin; cf. Sp. organsino, It. organzino.] A kind of double thrown silk of very fine texture, that is, silk twisted like a rope with different strands, so as to increase its strength.

orgasm.c: orgasm or"gasm (ôr"găz'm), n. [F. orgasme; cf. Gr. 'orgasmo`s a kneading, softening, prob. confused with 'orga^n to swell, especially with lust; to feel an ardent desire.] (Physiol.) Eager or immoderate excitement or action; the state of turgescence of any organ; erethism.

orgeat.c: Orgeat Or"geat (?), n. [F., fr. orge barley, L. hordeum.] A sirup in which, formerly, a decoction of barley entered, but which is now prepared with an emulsion of almonds, -- used to flavor beverages or edibles.

orgiastic.c: Orgiastic Or`gi*as"tic (?), a. [Gr.?. See Orgy.] Pertaining to, or of the nature of, orgies. Elton.

orgy.c: Orgy Or"gy (?), n.; sing. Orgies (?). [F. orgie, orgies, L. orgia, pl., Gr.?; akin to? work. See Organ, and Work.]
Orgy Or"gy (?), n.; pl. Orgies (?). A frantic revel; drunken revelry. See Orgies

orgillous.c: Orgillous Or"gil*lous (?), a. [OF. orguillous, F. orgueilleux, fr. OF. orgoil pride, F. orgueil.] Proud; haughty. [Obs.] Shak.

orgue.c: Orgue Orgue (?), n. [F., fr. L. organum organ, Gr.?. See Organ.] (Mil.) (a) Any one of a number of long, thick pieces of timber, pointed and shod with iron, and suspended, each by a separate rope, over a gateway, to be let down in case of attack. (b) A piece of ordnance, consisting of a number of musket barrels arranged so that a match or train may connect with all their touchholes, and a discharge be secured almost or quite simultaneously.

orgyia.c: Orgyia ‖Or*gy"i*a (?), prop. n. [NL., fr. Gr.? the length of the outstretched arms. So named because, when at rest, it stretches forward its fore legs like arms.] (Zool.). A genus of bombycid moths whose caterpillars (esp. those of Orgyia leucostigma) are often very injurious to fruit trees and shade trees. The female is wingless. Called also vaporer moth.

orichalceous.c: Orichalceous Or`i*chal"ce*ous (?), a. Pertaining to, or resembling, orichalch; having a color or luster like that of brass. Maunder.

orichalch.c: Orichalch Or"i*chalch (?), n. [L. orichalcum, Gr.?; 'o`ros, mountain + chalko`s brass: cf. F. orichalque.] A metallic substance, resembling gold in color, but inferior in value; a mixed metal of the ancients, resembling brass; -- called also aurichalcum, orichalcum, etc.

oriel.c: Oriel O"ri*el (?), n. [OF. oriol gallery, corridor, LL. oriolum portico, hall, prob. fr. L. aureolus gilded, applied to an apartment decorated with gilding. See Oriole.] [Formerly written also oriol, oryal, oryall.]

oriency.c: Oriency O"ri*en*cy (?), n. [See Orient.] Brightness or strength of color. [R.] E. Waterhouse.

orient.c: Orient O"ri*ent (ō"rĭ*eint), a. [F., fr. L. oriens, -entis, p. pr. of oriri to rise. See Origin.] 1. Rising, as the sun.
Orient O"ri*ent, n. 1. The part of the horizon where the sun first appears in the morning; the east.
Orient O"ri*ent (ō"rĭ*ĕnt), v. t. [F. orienter. Cf. Orientate.] 1. To define the position of, in relation to the orient or east; hence, to ascertain the bearings of.

oriental.c: Oriental O`ri*en"tal (ō`rĭ*ĕn"tail), a. [L. orientalis: cf. F. oriental.] Of or pertaining to the orient or east; eastern; concerned with the East or Orientalism; -- opposed to occidental; as, Oriental countries.
Oriental O`ri*en"tal, n. 1. A native or inhabitant of the Orient or some Eastern part of the world; an Asiatic.

orientality.c: Orientality O`ri*en*tal"i*ty (?), n. The quality or state of being oriental or eastern. Sir T. Browne.

orientalize.c: Orientalize O`ri*en"tal*ize (?), v. t. [imp. & p. p. Orientalized (?); p. pr. & vb. n. Orientalizing (?).] to render Oriental; to cause to conform to Oriental manners or conditions.

orientate.c: Orientate O"ri*en*tate (?), v. t. [imp. & p. p. Orientated (?); p. pr. & vb. n. Orientating.] [From Orient.]
Orientate O"ri*en*tate, v. i. To move or turn toward the east; to veer from the north or south toward the east.

orientness.c: Orientness O"ri*ent*ness (?), n. The quality or state of being orient or bright; splendor. [Obs.] Fuller.

orifice.c: Orifice Or"i*fice (?), n. [F., from L. orificium; os, oris, a mouth + facere to make. See Oral, and Fact.] A mouth or aperture, as of a tube, pipe, etc.; an opening; as, the orifice of an artery or vein; the orifice of a wound. Shak.

oriflamme.c: Oriflamme Oriflamb { Or"i*flamb, Or"i*flamme } (?), n. [F. oriflamme, OF. oriflambe, LL. auriflamma; L. aurum gold + flamma flame; cf. L. flammula a little banner. So called because it was a flag of red silk, split into many points, and borne on a gilded lance.] 1. The ancient royal standard of France.

origanum.c: Origanum Origan { Or"i*gan (?), ‖O*rig"a*num (?), } prop. n. [L. origanum, Gr.?,?, prob. fr. 'o`ros, mountain +? brightness, beauty. Cf. Organy.] (Bot.) A genus of aromatic labiate plants, including the sweet marjoram (Origanum Marjorana) and the wild marjoram (Origanum vulgare). Spenser.

origenism.c: Origenism Or"i*gen*ism (?), n. (Eccl. Hist.) The opinions of Origen of Alexandria, who lived in the 3d century, one of the most learned of the Greek Fathers. Prominent in his teaching was the doctrine that all created beings, including Satan, will ultimately be saved.

origenist.c: Origenist Or"i*gen*ist, n. A follower of Origen of Alexandria.

origin.c: Origin Or"i*gin (?), n. [F. origine, L. origo, -iginis, fr. oriri to rise, become visible; akin to Gr. 'orny`nai to stir up, rouse, Skr. ṛ, and perh. to E. run.]

originable.c: Originable O*rig"i*na*ble (?), a. Capable of being originated.

originalist.c: Originalist O*rig"i*nal*ist, n. One who is original. [R.]

originality.c: Originality O*rig`i*nal"i*ty (?), n. [Cf. F. originalité.] 1. The quality or state of being original. Macaulay.

originally.c: Originally O*rig"i*nal*ly (?), adv. 1. In the original time, or in an original manner; primarily; from the beginning or origin; not by derivation, or imitation.

originalness.c: Originalness O*rig"i*nal*ness (?), n. The quality of being original; originality. [R.] Johnson.

originary.c: Originary O*rig"i*na*ry (?), a. [L. originarius: cf. F. originaire.] 1. Causing existence; productive. [R.]

originate.c: Originate O*rig"i*nate (?), v. t. [imp. & p. p. Originated (?); p. pr. & vb. n. Originating.] [From Origin.] To give an origin or beginning to; to cause to be; to bring into existence; to produce as new.
Originate O*rig"i*nate, v. i. To take first existence; to have origin or beginning; to begin to exist or act; as, the scheme originated with the governor and council.

originative.c: Originative O*rig"i*na*tive (?), a. Having power, or tending, to originate, or bring into existence; originating. H. Bushnell. -- O*rig"i*na*tive*ly, adv.

orillon.c: Orillon O*ril"lon (?), n. [F., lit., a little ear, from oreille an ear, fr. L. oricula, auricula, dim. of auris an ear. See Ear.] (Fort.) A semicircular projection made at the shoulder of a bastion for the purpose of covering the retired flank, -- found in old fortresses.
