oriole.c: Oriole O"ri*ole (?), n. [OF. oriol, oriouz, orieus, F. loriot (for l'oriol), fr. L. aureolus golden, dim. of aureus golden, fr. aurum gold. Cf. Aureole, Oriel, Loriot.] (Zool.) (a) Any one of various species of Old World singing birds of the family Oriolidae. They are usually conspicuously colored with yellow and black. The European or golden oriole (Oriolus galbula, or Oriolus oriolus) has a very musical flutelike note. (b) In America, any one of several species of the genus Icterus, belonging to the family Icteridae. See Baltimore oriole, and Orchard oriole, under Orchard.

orion.c: Orion O*ri"on (o*rī"ŏn), n. [L., fr. Gr. 'Wri`wn, orig., a celebrated hunter in the oldest Greek mythology, after whom this constellation was named.] (Astron.) A large and bright constellation on the equator, between the stars Aldebaran and Sirius. It contains a remarkable nebula visible to the naked eye.

oriskany.c: Oriskany O*ris"ka*ny (?), a. [From Oriskany, in New York.] (Geol.) Designating, or pertaining to, certain beds, chiefly limestone, characteristic of the latest period of the Silurian age.

orismological.c: Orismological O*ris`mo*log"ic*al (o*rĭs`mŏ*loj"ĭ*kail), a. (Nat. Hist.) Of or pertaining to orismology.

orismology.c: Orismology O`ris*mol"o*gy (ō`rĭs*mŏl"o*jy̆), n. [Gr. "orismo`s a marking out by boundaries, the definition of a word + -logy. See Horizon.] That department of natural history which treats of technical terms; the science of defining technical terms.

orison.c: Orison Or"i*son (?), n. [OF. orison, oreson, oreison, F. oraison, fr. L. oratio speech, prayer. See Oration.] A prayer; a supplication. [Poetic] Chaucer. Shak.

orkneyan.c: Orkneyan Ork"ney*an (?), prop. a. Of or pertaining to the Orkney islands. “Orkneyan skerries.” Longfellow.

orle.c: Orle Orle (?), n. [F. orle an orle, a fillet, fr. LL. orla border, dim. of L. ora border, margin.]

orleans.c: Orleans Or"le*ans (?), n. [So called from the city of Orléans, in France.] 1. A cloth made of worsted and cotton, -- used for wearing apparel.

orlo.c: Orlo ‖Or"lo (?), n. [Sp.] (Mus.) A wind instrument of music in use among the Spaniards.

orlop.c: Orlop Or"lop (?), n. [D. overloop the upper deck, lit., a running over or overflowing, fr. overloopen to run over. See Over, and Leap, and cf. Overloop.] (Naut.) The lowest deck of a vessel, esp. of a ship of war, consisting of a platform laid over the beams in the hold, on which the cables are coiled.

ormolu.c: ormolu or`mo*lu" (ôr`mo*lü"), n. [F. or moulu; or gold (L. aurum) + moulu, p. p. of moudre to grind, to mill, L. molere. See Aureate, and Mill.] A variety of brass made to resemble gold by the use of less zinc and more copper in its composition than ordinary brass contains. Its golden color is often heightened by means of lacquer of some sort, or by use of acids. Called also mosaic gold.

ormuzd.c: Ormuzd ‖Or"muzd (ôr"mŭzd), prop. n. [Zend Ahuramazda.] The good principle, or being, of the ancient Persian religion; same as Ormazd. See also Ahriman.

orn.c: orn orn (ôrn), v. t. To ornament; to adorn. [Obs.] Joye.

ornament.c: ornament or"na*ment (?), n. [OE. ornement, F. ornement, fr. L. ornamentum, fr. ornare to adorn.] That which embellishes or adorns; that which adds grace or beauty; embellishment; decoration; adornment.
ornament or"na*ment (?), v. t. [imp. & p. p. Ornamented; p. pr. & vb. n. Ornamenting.] To adorn; to deck; to embellish; to beautify; as, to ornament a room, or a city.

ornamental.c: ornamental or`na*men"tal (?), a. [Cf. F. ornemental.] Serving to ornament; characterized by ornament; beautifying; embellishing.

ornamentally.c: ornamentally or`na*men"tal*ly, adv. By way of ornament.

ornamentation.c: Ornamentation Or`na*men*ta"tion (?), n. 1. The act or art of ornamenting, or the state of being ornamented.

ornamenter.c: Ornamenter Or"na*ment*er (?), n. One who ornaments; a decorator.

ornate.c: Ornate Or*nate" (?), a. [L. ornatus, p. p. of ornare to adorn.] 1. Elaborately adorned or decorated; beautifully sumptuous. “So bedecked, ornate, and gay.” Milton.
Ornate Or*nate", v. t. To adorn; to honor. [R.]

ornately.c: Ornately Or*nate"ly, adv. In an ornate manner. Sir T. More.

ornateness.c: Ornateness Or*nate"ness, n. The quality of being ornate.

ornature.c: Ornature Or"na*ture (?), n. [L. ornatura.] Decoration; ornamentation. [R.] Holinshed.

ornithic.c: Ornithic Or*nith"ic (?), a. [Gr. 'o`rnis, 'o`rniqos, a bird.] Of or pertaining to birds; as, ornithic fossils. Owen.

ornithichnite.c: Ornithichnite Or`nith*ich"nite (?), n. [Ornitho- + Gr. 'i`chnos track.] (Paleon.) The footmark of a bird occurring in strata of stone. Hitchcock.

ornithichnology.c: Ornithichnology Or`nith*ich*nol"o*gy (?), n. [Ornitho- + ichnology.] (Paleon.) The branch of science which treats of ornithichnites. Hitchcock.

ornitho.c: Ornitho- Ornitho-. [Cf. Ern.] A combining form fr. Gr. 'o`rnis, 'o`rniqos, a bird.

ornithodelphia.c: Ornithodelphia ‖Or*ni`tho*del"phi*a (?), n. pl. [NL., fr. Gr. 'o`rnis + delfy`s the womb.] Same as Monotremata. -- Or`ni*tho*del"phid (#), a.

ornithoidichnite.c: Ornithoidichnite Or`ni*thoid*ich"nite (?), n. [Ornitho- + -oid + Gr. 'i`chnos footstep, track.] (Paleon.) A fossil track resembling that of a bird. Hitchcock.

ornitholite.c: Ornitholite Or*nith"o*lite (?), n. [Ornitho- + -lite.] (Paleon.) (a) The fossil remains of a bird. (b) A stone of various colors bearing the figures of birds.

ornithological.c: Ornithological Ornithologic { Or`ni*tho*log"ic (?), Or`ni*tho*log"ic*al (?), } a. [Cf. F. ornithologique.] Of or pertaining to ornithology; as, her ornithological interests.

ornithologist.c: Ornithologist Or`ni*thol"o*gist (?), n. [Cf. F. ornithologiste.] One skilled in ornithology; a student of ornithology; one who describes birds.

ornithology.c: Ornithology Or`ni*thol"o*gy (?), n. [Ornitho- + -logy: cf. F. ornithologie.] 1. That branch of Zoology which treats of the natural history of birds and their classification.

ornithomancy.c: Ornithomancy Or*nith"o*man`cy (?), n. [Gr.?; 'o`rnis, 'o`rniqos, a bird +? divination: cf. F. ornithomancie.] Divination by means of birds, their flight, etc.

ornithon.c: Ornithon ‖Or*ni"thon (?), n. [L., fr. Gr.?, fr. 'o`rnis, 'o`rniqos, a bird.] An aviary; a poultry house. Weale.

ornithopappi.c: Ornithopappi ‖Or*ni`tho*pap"pi (?), prop. n. pl. [NL., from Gr. 'o`rnis a bird +? an ancestor.] (Zool.) An extinct order of birds. It includes only the Archaeopteryx.

ornithopoda.c: Ornithopoda ‖Or`ni*thop"o*da (?), prop. n. pl. [NL. See Ornitho-, and -poda.] (Paleon.) An order of herbivorous dinosaurs with birdlike characteristics in the skeleton, esp. in the pelvis and hind legs, which in some genera had only three functional toes, and supported the body in walking as in Iguanodon. See Illust. in Appendix.

ornithorhynchus.c: Ornithorhynchus Or`ni*tho*rhyn"chus (?), prop. n. [NL., fr. Gr. 'o`rnis, 'o`rniqos, a bird +? snout, beak.] (Zool.) A genus of monotremes including the platypus (Ornithorhyncus anatinus). See Duck mole, under Duck.

ornithosauria.c: Ornithosauria ‖Or*ni`tho*sau"ri*a (?), prop. n. pl. [NL. See Ornitho-, and Sauria.] (Paleon.) An order of extinct flying reptiles; -- called also Pterosauria.

ornithoscelida.c: Ornithoscelida ‖Or*ni`tho*scel"i*da (?), n. pl. [NL., fr. Gr. 'o`rnis, 'o`rniqos, a bird +? a leg.] (Zool.) A group of extinct Reptilia, intermediate in structure (especially with regard to the pelvis) between reptiles and birds. -- Or`ni*tho*scel"i*dan (#), a.

ornithoscopy.c: Ornithoscopy Or`ni*thos"co*py (?), n. [Ornitho- + -scopy: cf. Gr.? divination from birds.] Observation of birds and their habits. [R.] De Quincey.

ornithotomical.c: Ornithotomical Or`ni*tho*tom"ic*al (?), a. Of or pertaining to ornithotomy.

ornithotomist.c: Ornithotomist Or`ni*thot"o*mist (?), n. One who is skilled in ornithotomy.

ornithotomy.c: Ornithotomy Or`ni*thot"o*my (?), n. [Gr. 'o`rnis, 'o`rniqos, a bird + te`mnein to cut.] The anatomy or dissection of birds.

orograph.c: Orograph Or"o*graph (?), n. [Gr. 'o`ros mountain + -graph.] (Surveying) A machine for use in making topographical maps. It is operated by being pushed across country, and not only records distances, like the perambulator, but also elevations.

orographical.c: Orographical Orographic { Or`o*graph"ic (?), Or`o*graph"ic*al (?), } a. Of or pertaining to orography.

orography.c: Orography O*rog"ra*phy (?), n. [Gr. 'o`ros, a mountain + -graphy.] That branch of science which treats of mountains and mountain systems; orology; as, the orography of Western Europe.

oroheliograph.c: Oroheliograph Or`o*he"li*o*graph (?), n. [Gr. 'o`ros mountain + helio- + -graph.] (Photog.) A camera for obtaining a circular panoramic view of the horizon. The photographic plate is placed horizontally with a vertical lens above. A mirror of peculiar shape reflects light from the entire horizon to the lens, by means of which it is focused upon the plate.

orohippus.c: Orohippus ‖Or`o*hip"pus (?), n. [NL., fr. Gr. 'o`ros, mountain (referring to the Rocky Mountain region) + "i`ppos horse.] (Paleon.) A genus of American Eocene mammals allied to the horse, but having four toes in front and three behind.

oroide.c: Oroide O"roide (?), n. [F. or gold (L. aurum) + Gr. e'i^dos form.] An alloy, chiefly of copper and zinc or tin, resembling gold in color and brilliancy. [Written also oreide.]

orological.c: Orological Or`o*log"ic*al (?), a. [Cf. F. orologique.] Of or pertaining to orology.

orologist.c: Orologist O*rol"o*gist (?), n. One versed in orology.

orology.c: Orology O*rol"o*gy (?), n. [Gr. 'o`ros mountain + -logy: cf. F. orologie.] The science or description of mountains.

orometer.c: Orometer O*rom"e*ter (?), n. [Gr. 'o`ros mountain + -meter.] (Meteor.) An aneroid barometer having a second scale that gives the approximate elevation above sea level of the place where the observation is made.

orotund.c: Orotund O"ro*tund` (?), a. [L. os, oris, the mouth + rotundus round, smooth.] Characterized by fullness, clearness, strength, and smoothness; ringing and musical; -- said of the voice or manner of utterance. -- n. The orotund voice or utterance Rush.

orotundity.c: Orotundity O`ro*tun"di*ty (?), n. The orotund mode of intonation.

orphan.c: Orphan Or"phan (?), n. [L. orphanus, Gr.?, akin to L. orbus. Cf. Orb a blank window.] A child bereaved of both father and mother; sometimes, also, a child who has but one parent living.
Orphan Or"phan, a. Bereaved of parents, or (sometimes) of one parent.
Orphan Or"phan, v. t. [imp. & p. p. Orphaned (?); p. pr. & vb. n. Orphaning.] To cause to become an orphan; to deprive of parents. Young.

orphanage.c: Orphanage Or"phan*age (?), n. 1. The state of being an orphan; orphanhood; orphans, collectively.

orphancy.c: Orphancy Or"phan*cy (?), n. Orphanhood. Sir P. Sidney.

orphanet.c: Orphanet Or"phan*et (?), n. A little orphan. Drayton.

orphanhood.c: Orphanhood Or"phan*hood (?), n. The state or condition of being an orphan; orphanage.

orphanotrophism.c: Orphanotrophism Or`phan*ot"ro*phism (?), n. The care and support of orphans. [R.] Cotton Mather (1711).

orphanotrophy.c: Orphanotrophy Or`phan*ot"ro*phy (?), n. [L. orphanotrophium, Gr.?;? an orphan +? to feed, bring up.]

orpharion.c: Orpharion Or*pha"ri*on (?), n. (Mus.) An old instrument of the lute or cittern kind. [Spelt also orpheoreon.]

orphean.c: Orphean Or*phe"an (?), a. [L. Orphēus, Gr.?.] Of or pertaining to Orpheus, the mythic poet and musician; as, Orphean strains. Cowper.

orpheline.c: Orpheline Or"phe*line (?), n. [F. orphelin. See Orphan.] An orphan. [Obs.] Udcll.

orpheus.c: Orpheus Or"phe*us (?), prop. n. [L. Orpheus, Gr.?.] (Gr. Myth.) The famous mythic Thracian poet, son of the Muse Calliope, and husband of Eurydice. He is reputed to have had power to entrance beasts and inanimate objects by the music of his lyre.

orphic.c: Orphic Or"phic (?), prop. a. [L. Orphicus, Gr.?.] Pertaining to Orpheus; Orphean; as, Orphic hymns.

orphrey.c: Orphrey Or"phrey (?), n. [See Orfrays.] A band of rich embroidery, wholly or in part of gold, affixed to vestments, especially those of ecclesiastics. Pugin.

orpiment.c: Orpiment Or"pi*ment (?), n. [F., fr. L. auripigmentum; aurum gold + pigmentum pigment. Cf. Aureate, Pigment, Orpin, Orpine.] (Chem.) Arsenic sesquisulphide, produced artificially as an amorphous lemon-yellow powder, and occurring naturally as a yellow crystalline mineral; -- formerly called auripigment. It is used in king's yellow, in white Indian fire, and in certain technical processes, as indigo printing.

orpin.c: Orpin Or"pin, n. [F., orpiment, also, the plant orpine. See Orpiment.] 1. A yellow pigment of various degrees of intensity, approaching also to red.

orpine.c: orpine or"pine (?), n. [F. orpin the genus of plants which includes orpine; -- so called from the yellow blossoms of a common species (Sedum acre). See Orpiment.] (Bot.) A low plant with fleshy leaves (Sedum telephium), having clusters of purple flowers. It is found on dry, sandy places, and on old walls, in England, and has become naturalized in America. Called also stonecrop, and live-forever. [Written also orpin.]

orrery.c: Orrery Or"re*ry (?), n.; pl. Orreries (#). [So named in honor of the Earl of Orrery.] An apparatus which illustrates, by the revolution of balls moved by wheelwork, the relative size, periodic motions, positions, orbits, etc., of bodies in the solar system.

orris.c: Orris Or"ris (?), n. [Prob. corrupted from It. ireos iris. See Iris.] (Bot.) A plant of the genus Iris (Iris Florentina); a kind of flower-de-luce. Its rootstock has an odor resembling that of violets.
Orris Or"ris (?), n. 1. [Contr. from orfrays, or from arras.] A sort of gold or silver lace. Johnson.

orsedue.c: Orsedue Orsedew { Orse"dew (?), Or"se*due (?), } n. Leaf metal of bronze; Dutch metal. See under Dutch.

orsellic.c: Orsellic Or*sel"lic (?), a. [From F. orseille archil. See Archil.] (Chem.) Pertaining to, or designating, an acid found in certain lichens, and called also lecanoric acid. [Formerly written also orseillic.]

orsellinic.c: Orsellinic Or`sel*lin"ic (?), a. (Chem.) Pertaining to, or designating, an organic acid obtained by a partial decomposition of orsellic acid as a white crystalline substance, and related to protocatechuic acid.

ort.c: Ort Ort (ôrt), n.; pl. Orts (ôrts). [Akin to LG. ort, ortels, remnants of food, refuse, OFries. ort, OD. oorete, ooraete; prob. from the same prefix as in E. ordeal + a word akin to eat.] A morsel left at a meal; a fragment; refuse; -- commonly used in the plural. Milton.

ortalidian.c: Ortalidian Or`ta*lid"i*an (?), n. (Zool.) Any one of numerous small two-winged flies of the family Ortalidae. The larvae of many of these flies live in fruit; those of others produce galls on various plants.

orthid.c: Orthid Or"thid (?), n. (Zool.) A brachiopod shell of the genus Orthis, and allied genera, of the family Orthidae.

orthis.c: Orthis ‖Or"this (ôr"thĭs), prop. n. [NL., fr. Gr. 'orqo`s straight.] (Zool.) An extinct genus of Brachiopoda, abundant in the Paleozoic rocks.

orthite.c: Orthite Or"thite (?), n. [Gr. 'orqo`s straight.] (Min.) A variety of allanite occurring in slender prismatic crystals.

ortho.c: Ortho- Or"tho- (ôr"tho-) pref. [Gr. 'orqo`s straight; akin to Skr. ūrdhva upright, vṛdh to grow, to cause to grow.]

orthocarbonic.c: Orthocarbonic Or`tho*car*bon"ic (?), a. [Ortho- + carbonic.] (Chem.) Designating a complex ether, C.(OC2H5)4, which is obtained as a liquid of a pleasant ethereal odor by means of chlorpicrin, and is believed to be a derivative of the hypothetical normal carbonic acid, C.(OH)4.

orthocenter.c: Orthocenter Or`tho*cen"ter (?), n. [Ortho- + center.] (Geom.) That point in which the three perpendiculars let fall from the angles of a triangle upon the opposite sides, or the sides produced, mutually intersect.

orthoceras.c: Orthoceras ‖Or*thoc"e*ras (?), n. [NL., fr. Gr. 'orqo`s straight + ke`ras a horn.] (Paleon.) An extinct genus of Paleozoic Cephalopoda, having a long, straight, conical shell. The interior is divided into numerous chambers by transverse septa.

orthoceratite.c: Orthoceratite Or`tho*cer"a*tite (?), n. [Ortho- + Gr.?,?, a horn.] (Zool.) An orthoceras; also, any fossil shell allied to Orthoceras.

orthoclase.c: Orthoclase Or"tho*clase (?), n. [Ortho- + Gr.? to break.] (Min.) Common or potash feldspar crystallizing in the monoclinic system and having two cleavages at right angles to each other. See Feldspar.

orthoclastic.c: Orthoclastic Or`tho*clas"tic (?), a. (Crystallog.) Breaking in directions at right angles to each other; -- said of the monoclinic feldspars.

orthodiagonal.c: Orthodiagonal Or`tho*di*ag"o*nal (?), n. [Ortho- + diagonal.] (Crystallog.) The diagonal or lateral axis in a monoclinic crystal which is at right angles with the vertical axis.

orthodome.c: Orthodome Or"tho*dome (?), n. [Ortho- + dome.] (Crystallog.) See the Note under Dome, 4.

orthodox.c: Orthodox Or"tho*dox (?), a. [L. orthodoxus, Gr. 'orqo`doxos; 'orqo`s right, true + do`xa opinion, dokei^n to think, seem; cf. F. orthodoxe. See Ortho-, Dogma.] 1. Sound in opinion or doctrine, especially in religious doctrine; hence, holding the Christian faith; believing the doctrines taught in the Scriptures; -- opposed to heretical and heterodox; as, an orthodox Christian.

orthodoxal.c: Orthodoxal Or"tho*dox`al (ôr"tho*dŏks`ail), a. Pertaining to, or evincing, orthodoxy; orthodox. [R.] Milton.

orthodoxical.c: Orthodoxical Or`tho*dox"ic*al (?), a. Pertaining to, or evincing, orthodoxy; orthodox.

orthodoxly.c: Orthodoxly Or"tho*dox`ly (?), adv. In an orthodox manner; with soundness of faith. Sir W. Hamilton.

orthodoxness.c: Orthodoxness Or"tho*dox`ness, n. The quality or state of being orthodox; orthodoxy. Waterland.

orthodoxy.c: Orthodoxy Or"tho*dox`y (?), n. [Gr.?: cf. F. orthodoxie. See Orthodox.] 1. Soundness of faith; a belief in the doctrines taught in the Scriptures, or in some established standard of faith; -- opposed to heterodoxy or to heresy.

orthodromic.c: Orthodromic Or`tho*drom"ic (?), a. [Ortho- + Gr.? to run.] Of or pertaining to orthodromy.

orthodromics.c: Orthodromics Or`tho*drom"ics (?), n. The art of sailing in a direct course, or on the arc of a great circle, which is the shortest distance between any two points on the surface of the globe; great-circle sailing; orthodromy.

orthodromy.c: Orthodromy Or"tho*drom`y (ôr"tho*drŏm`y̆; 277), n. [Cf. F. orthodromie.] The act or art of sailing on a great circle.

orthoepical.c: Orthoepical Orthoepic { Or`tho*ep"ic (?), Or`tho*ep"ic*al (?), } a. Of or pertaining to orthoepy, or correct pronunciation. -- Or`tho*ep"ic*al*ly, adv.

orthoepist.c: orthoepist or"tho*e*pist (ôr"tho*e*pĭst), n. One who is skilled in orthoepy.

orthoepy.c: orthoepy or"tho*e*py (ôr"tho*e*py̆; 277), n. [Gr. 'orqoe`peia; 'orqo`s right + 'e`pos a word: cf. F. orthoépie. See Ortho-, and Epic.] The art of uttering words correctly; a correct pronunciation of words; also, mode of pronunciation.

orthogamy.c: orthogamy or*thog"a*my (?), n. [Ortho- + Gr.? marriage.] (Bot.) Direct fertilization in plants, as when the pollen fertilizing the ovules comes from the stamens of the same blossom; -- opposed to heterogamy.

orthognathism.c: Orthognathism Or*thog"na*thism (?), n. (Anat.) The quality or state of being orthognathous. Huxley.

orthognathous.c: Orthognathous Or*thog"na*thous (?), a. [Ortho- + Gr. gna`qos the jaw.] (Anat.) Having the front of the head, or the skull, nearly perpendicular, not retreating backwards above the jaws; -- opposed to prognathous. See Gnathic index, under Gnathic.

orthogon.c: Orthogon Or"tho*gon (?), n. [Ortho- + Gr. gwni`a angle: cf. F. orthogone, a.] (Geom.) A rectangular figure.

orthogonal.c: Orthogonal Or*thog"o*nal (?), a. [Cf. F. orthogonal.] Right-angled; rectangular; as, an orthogonal intersection of one curve with another.

orthogonally.c: Orthogonally Or*thog"o*nal*ly, adv. Perpendicularly; at right angles; as, a curve cuts a set of curves orthogonally.

orthograph.c: Orthograph Or"tho*graph (?), n. [Ortho- + -graph.] (Arch.) An orthographic projection, sometimes partly in section, esp. of a building.

orthographer.c: Orthographer Or*thog"ra*pher (?), n. One versed in orthography; one who spells words correctly.

orthographical.c: Orthographical Orthographic { Or`tho*graph"ic (?), Or`tho*graph"ic*al (?), } a. [Cf. F. orthographique, L. orthographus, Gr.?.] 1. Of or pertaining to orthography, or right spelling; also, correct in spelling; as, orthographical rules; the letter was orthographic.

orthographically.c: Orthographically Or`tho*graph"ic*al*ly, adv. In an orthographical manner: (a) according to the rules of proper spelling; (b) according to orthographic projection.

orthographist.c: Orthographist Or*thog"ra*phist (?), n. One who spells words correctly; an orthographer.

orthographize.c: Orthographize Or*thog"ra*phize (?), v. t. To spell correctly or according to usage; to correct in regard to spelling.

orthography.c: Orthography Or*thog"ra*phy (?), n. [OE. ortographie, OF. orthographie, L. orthographia, Gr.?, fr.? writing correctly; 'orqo`s right + gra`fein to write. See Ortho-, and Graphic.]

orthology.c: Orthology Or*thol"o*gy (?), n. [Gr.?; 'orqo`s right + lo`gos speech, description: cf. F. orthologie.] The right description of things. [R.] Fotherby.

orthometric.c: Orthometric Or`tho*met"ric (?), a. [See Orthometry.] (Crystallog.) Having the axes at right angles to one another; -- said of crystals or crystalline forms.

orthometry.c: Orthometry Or*thom"e*try (?), n. [Ortho- + -metry.] The art or practice of constructing verses correctly; the laws of correct versification.

orthomorphic.c: Orthomorphic Or`tho*mor"phic (?), a. [Ortho- + morphic.] (Geom.) Having the right form.

orthopedical.c: Orthopedical Orthopedic { Or`tho*ped"ic (?), Or`tho*ped"ic*al (?), } a. (Med.) Of, pertaining to, or employed in, orthopedics; relating to the prevention or cure of deformities of children, or, in general, of the human body at any age; as, orthopedic surgery; an orthopedic hospital.

orthopedist.c: Orthopedist Or*thop"e*dist (?), n. (Med.) One who prevents, cures, or remedies deformities, esp. in children.

orthopedy.c: Orthopedy Or*thop"e*dy (?), n. [Ortho- + Gr.?,?, a child.] (Med.) Same as orthopedics.

orthophony.c: Orthophony Or*thoph"o*ny (?), n. [Ortho- + Gr. fwnh` voice.] The art of correct articulation; voice training.

orthopinacoid.c: Orthopinacoid Or`tho*pin"a*coid (?), n. [Ortho- + pinacoid.] (Crystallog.) A name given to the two planes in the monoclinic system which are parallel to the vertical and orthodiagonal axes.

orthopny.c: Orthopny Orthopnoea { ‖Or`thop*nœ"a (?), Or*thop"ny (?), } n. [L. orthopnoea, Gr.?; 'orqo`sstraight, right + pnei^n to breathe: cf. F. orthopnée.] (Med.) Specifically, a morbid condition in which respiration can be performed only in an erect posture; by extension, any difficulty of breathing.

orthopoda.c: Orthopoda ‖Or*thop"o*da (?), prop. n. pl. [NL. See Ortho-, and -poda.] (Zool.) An extinct order of reptiles which stood erect on the hind legs, and resembled birds in the structure of the feet, pelvis, and other parts.

orthopraxy.c: Orthopraxy Or"tho*prax`y (?), n. [Gr. 'orqo`s straight +? a doing.] (Med.) The treatment of deformities in the human body by mechanical appliances.

orthoptera.c: Orthoptera ‖Or*thop"te*ra (?), prop. n. pl. [NL., fr. Gr. 'orqo`s straight +? feather, wing.] (Zool.) An order of mandibulate insects including grasshoppers, locusts, cockroaches, mantids, crickets, katydids, etc. See Illust. under Insect.

orthopteran.c: Orthopteran Or*thop"ter*an (?), n. (Zool.) One of the Orthoptera.

orthopterous.c: Orthopterous Or*thop"ter*ous (?), a. (Zool.) Of or pertaining to the Orthoptera.

orthorhombic.c: Orthorhombic Or`tho*rhom"bic (?), a. [Ortho- + rhombic.] (Crystallog.) Noting the system of crystallization which has three unequal axes at right angles to each other; trimetric. See Crystallization.

orthoscope.c: Orthoscope Or"tho*scope (?), n. [Ortho- + -scope.] (Physiol.) An instrument designed to show the condition of the superficial portions of the eye.

orthoscopic.c: Orthoscopic Or`tho*scop"ic (?), a. (Opt.) Giving an image in correct or normal proportions; giving a flat field of view; as, an orthoscopic eyepiece.

orthosilicic.c: Orthosilicic Or`tho*si*lic"ic (?), a. [Ortho- + silicic.] (Chem.) Designating the form of silicic acid having the normal or highest number of hydroxyl groups.

orthospermous.c: Orthospermous Or`tho*sper"mous (?), a. [Ortho- + Gr.? seed.] (Bot.) Having the seeds straight, as in the fruits of some umbelliferous plants; -- opposed to coelospermous. Darwin.

orthostade.c: Orthostade Or"tho*stade (?), n. [Gr.?; 'orqo`s straight +? to place.] (Anc. Costume) A chiton, or loose, ungirded tunic, falling in straight folds.

orthostichy.c: Orthostichy Or*thos"ti*chy (?), n.; pl. Orthostichies (#). [Ortho- + Gr. sti`chos row.] (Bot.) A longitudinal rank, or row, of leaves along a stem.

orthotomic.c: Orthotomic Or`tho*tom"ic (?), a. [Ortho- + Gr.? to cleave.] (Geom.) Cutting at right angles.

orthotomous.c: Orthotomous Or*thot"o*mous (?), a. (Crystallog.) Having two cleavages at right angles with one another.

orthotomy.c: Orthotomy Or*thot"o*my (?), n. (Geom.) The property of cutting at right angles.

orthotone.c: Orthotone Or"tho*tone (?), a. [Ortho- + Gr.? tone, accent.] (Gr. Gram.) Retaining the accent; not enclitic; -- said of certain indefinite pronouns and adverbs when used interrogatively, which, when not so used, are ordinarilly enclitic.

orthotropous.c: Orthotropous Orthotropal { Or*thot"ro*pal (?), Or*thot"ro*pous (?), } a. [Ortho- + Gr.? to turn: cf. F. orthotrope.] (Bot.) Having the axis of an ovule or seed straight from the hilum and chalaza to the orifice or the micropyle; atropous.

orthotropic.c: Orthotropic Or`tho*trop"ic (?), a. [See Orthotropal.] (Bot.) Having the longer axis vertical; -- said of erect stems. Encyc. Brit.

orthoxylene.c: Orthoxylene Or`tho*xy"lene (?), n. [Ortho- + xylene.] (Chem.) That variety of xylene (C6H4(CH3)2) in which the two methyl groups are in the ortho position; a colorless, liquid, combustible hydrocarbon resembling benzene.

ortive.c: Ortive Or"tive (?), a. [L. ortivus, fr. oriri, ortus, to rise: cf. F. ortive.] Of or relating to the time or act of rising; eastern; as, the ortive amplitude of a planet.

ortolan.c: Ortolan Or"to*lan (?), n. [F., fr. It. ortolano ortolan, gardener, fr. L. hortulanus gardener, fr. hortulus, dim. of hortus garden. So called because it frequents the hedges of gardens. See Yard an inclosure, and cf. Hortulan.] (Zool.) (a) A European singing bird (Emberiza hortulana), about the size of the lark, with black wings. It is esteemed delicious food when fattened. Called also bunting. (b) In England, the wheatear (Saxicola oenanthe). (c) In America, the sora, or Carolina rail (Porzana Carolina). See Sora.

ortygan.c: Ortygan Or"ty*gan (?), n. [Gr.?,?, a quail.] (Zool.) One of several species of East Indian birds of the genera Ortygis and Hemipodius. They resemble quails, but lack the hind toe. See Turnix.

orval.c: Orval Or"val (?), n. [F. orvale.] (Bot.) A kind of sage (Salvia Horminum).

orvietan.c: Orvietan Or`vi*e"tan (?), n. [F. orviétan: cf. It. orvietano. So called because invented at Orvieto, in Italy.] A kind of antidote for poisons; a counter poison formerly in vogue. [Obs.]

ory.c: -ory -o*ry (?) suff. [L. -orius: cf. F. -oire.] 1. An adjective suffix meaning of or pertaining to, serving for; as in auditory, pertaining to or serving for hearing; prohibitory, amendatory, etc.

oryall.c: Oryall Oryal { O"ry*al (?), O"ry*all (?) }, n. See Oriel.

oryctere.c: Oryctere Or"yc*tere (?), n. [Gr. 'orykth`r digger: cf. F. oryctère.] (Zool.) The aard-vark (Orycteropus afer).

orycterope.c: Orycterope O*ryc"ter*ope (?), n. [Gr. 'orykth`r digger + poy`s foot.] (Zool.) Same as Oryctere (the aardvark, Orycteropus afer).

oryctognosy.c: Oryctognosy Or`yc*tog"no*sy (?), n. [Gr. 'orykto`s dug (? to dig) + gnw^sis knowledge.] Mineralogy. [Obs.] -- Or`yc*tog*nos"tic (#), a. -- Or`yc*tog*nos"tic*al (#), a. [Obs.] -- Or`yc*tog*nos"tic*al*ly (#), adv. [Obs.]

oryctography.c: Oryctography Or`yc*tog"ra*phy (?), n. [Gr. 'orykto`s dug + -graphy.] Description of fossils. [Obs.]

oryctological.c: Oryctological Or`yc*to*log"ic*al (?), a. [Cf. F. oryctologique.] Of or pertaining to oryctology. [Obs.]

oryctologist.c: Oryctologist Or`yc*tol"o*gist (?), n. One versed in oryctology. [Obs.]

oryctology.c: Oryctology Or`yc*tol"o*gy (?), n. [Gr. 'orykto`s dug + -logy: cf. F. oryctologie.] 1. An old name for paleontology.

oryx.c: Oryx O"ryx (ō"rĭks), prop. n. [NL., from Gr. 'o`ryx a kind of gazelle or antelope.] (Zool.) A genus of African antelopes which includes the gemsbok, the leucoryx, the bisa antelope (Oryx beisa), and the beatrix antelope (Oryx beatrix) of Arabia.

oryza.c: Oryza ‖O*ry"za (?), prop. n. [L., rice, Gr.? See Rice.] (Bot.) A genus of grasses including the rice plant; rice.

os.c: Os ‖Os, n.; pl. Ora (#). [L.] A mouth; an opening; an entrance.

Os Os (?), n.; pl. Osar (#). [Sw. ås ridge, chain of hills, pl. åsar.] (Geol.) One of the ridges of sand or gravel found in Sweden, etc., supposed by some to be of marine origin, but probably formed by subglacial waters. The osar are similar to the kames of Scotland and the eschars of Ireland. See Eschar.

osage.c: Osage orange O"sage or"ange (?). (Bot.) An ornamental tree of the genus Maclura (Maclura aurantiaca), closely allied to the mulberry (Morus); also, its fruit. The tree was first found in the country of the Osage Indians, and bears a hard and inedible fruit of an orangelike appearance. See Bois d'arc.

osages.c: Osages O*sa"ges (?), n. pl.; sing. Osage (?). (Ethnol.) A tribe of southern Sioux Indians, now living in the Indian Territory.

oscan.c: Oscan Os"can (?), a. Of or pertaining to the Osci, a primitive people of Campania, a province of ancient Italy. -- n. The language of the Osci.

oscillancy.c: Oscillancy Os"cil*lan*cy (?), n. The state of oscillating; a seesaw kind of motion. [R.]

oscillaria.c: Oscillaria ‖Os`cil*la"ri*a (?), prop. n. [NL., fr. L. oscillare to swing.] (Bot.) A genus of dark green, or purplish black, filamentous, fresh-water algae, the threads of which have an automatic swaying or crawling motion. Called also Oscillatoria.

oscillate.c: Oscillate Os"cil*late (ŏs"sĭl*lāt), v. i. [imp. & p. p. Oscillated (ŏs"sĭl*lā`tĕd); p. pr. & vb. n. Oscillating (ŏs"sĭl*lā`tĭng).] [L. oscillare to swing, fr. oscillum a swing, a little mask or puppet made to be hung from trees and swing in the wind, prob. orig., a little mouth, a dim. from os mouth. See Oral, and cf. Osculate.]

oscillating.c: Oscillating Os"cil*la`ting (ŏs"sĭl*lā`tĭng), a. That oscillates; vibrating; swinging.
Oscillating current Os"cil*lat`ing current. (Elec.) A current alternating in direction.

oscillative.c: Oscillative Os"cil*la*tive (?), a. Tending to oscillate; vibratory. [R.] I. Taylor.

oscillator.c: oscillator os"cil*la`tor (ŏs"sĭl*lā`tẽr), n. 1. One that oscillates; specif.: (Electronics) Any device or circuit for producing electric oscillations, whether of current or voltage; esp., an apparatus for generating electric waves in a system of wireless telegraphy.

oscillatoria.c: Oscillatoria ‖Os`cil*la*to"ri*a (?), n. pl. [NL. See Oscillatory.] (Bot.) Same as Oscillaria.

oscillatory.c: Oscillatory Os"cil*la*to*ry (?), a. [Cf. F. oscillatoire. See Oscillate.] Moving, or characterized by motion, backward and forward like a pendulum; swinging; oscillating; vibratory; as, oscillatory motion.

oscillogram.c: Oscillogram Os"cil*lo*gram (?), n. [L. oscillare + -gram.] (Elec.) An autographic record made by an oscillograph.

oscillograph.c: Oscillograph Os"cil*lo*graph (?), n. [L. oscillare to swing + -graph.] (Elec.) An apparatus for recording or indicating alternating-current wave forms or other electrical oscillations, especially of voltages or currents; it usually consists of a galvanometer with strong field, in which the mass of the moving part is very small and frequency of vibration very high. -- Os`cil*lo*graph"ic (#), a.

oscillometer.c: Oscillometer Os`cil*lom"e*ter (?), n. [L. oscillare to swing + -meter.] An instrument for measuring the angle through which a ship rolls or pitches at sea.

oscine.c: Oscine Os"cine (?), a. (Zool.) Relating to the Oscines.

oscines.c: Oscines ‖Os"ci*nes (?), n. pl. [L. oscen, -inis.] (Zool.) Singing birds; a group of the Passeres, having numerous syringeal muscles, conferring musical ability.

oscinian.c: Oscinian Os*cin"i*an (?), n. (Zool.) One of the Oscines, or singing birds.
Oscinian Os*cin"i*an, n. (Zool.) Any one of numerous species of dipterous flies of the family Oscinidae.

oscinine.c: Oscinine Os"ci*nine (?), a. (Zool.) Of or pertaining to the Oscines.

oscitant.c: Oscitant Os"ci*tant (?), a. [L. oscitans, -antis, p. pr. of oscitare: cf. F. oscitant.] 1. Yawning; gaping.

oscitantly.c: Oscitantly Os"ci*tant*ly, adv. In an oscitant manner.

oscitate.c: Oscitate Os"ci*tate (?), v. i. [L. oscitare; os the mouth + citare, v. intens. fr. ciere to move.] To gape; to yawn.

oscitation.c: Oscitation Os`ci*ta"tion (?), n. [L. oscitatio: cf. F. oscitation.] The act of yawning or gaping. Addison.

osculant.c: Osculant Os"cu*lant (?), a. [L. osculans, -antis, p. pr. of osculari to kiss. See Osculate.]

osculate.c: Osculate Os"cu*late (?), v. t. [imp. & p. p. Osculated (?); p. pr. & vb. n. Osculating.] [L. osculatus, p. p. of osculari to kiss, fr. osculum a little mouth, a kiss, dim. of os mouth. See Oral, and cf. Oscillate.]
Osculate Os"cu*late, v. i. 1. To kiss one another; to kiss.

osculation.c: Osculation Os`cu*la"tion (?), n. [L. osculatio a kissing: cf. F. osculation.] 1. The act of kissing; a kiss.

osculatory.c: Osculatory Os"cu*la*to*ry (?), a. 1. Of or pertaining to kissing; kissing. “The osculatory ceremony.” Thackeray.
Osculatory Os"cu*la*to*ry, n. [LL. osculatorium. See Osculate.] (R. C. Ch.) Same as Pax, 2.

osculatrix.c: Osculatrix Os`cu*la"trix (?), n.; pl. Osculatrixes (#). [NL.] (Geom.) A curve whose contact with a given curve, at a given point, is of a higher order (or involves the equality of a greater number of successive differential coefficients of the ordinates of the curves taken at that point) than that of any other curve of the same kind.

oscule.c: Oscule Os"cule (?), n. [Cf. F. oscule. See Osculum.] (Zool.) One of the excurrent apertures of sponges.

osculum.c: Osculum ‖Os"cu*lum (?), n.; pl. Oscula (#). [L., a little mouth.] (Zool.) Same as Oscule.

osier.c: Osier O"sier (?), n. [F. osier: cf. Prov. F. oisis, Armor. ozil, aozil, Gr.?,?,?, L. vitex, and E. withy.] (Bot.) (a) A kind of willow (Salix viminalis) growing in wet places in Europe and Asia, and introduced into North America. It is considered the best of the willows for basket work. The name is sometimes given to any kind of willow. (b) One of the long, pliable twigs of this plant, or of other similar plants.
Osier O"sier, a. Made of osiers; composed of, or containing, osiers. “This osier cage of ours.” Shak.

osiered.c: Osiered O"siered (?), a. Covered or adorned with osiers; as, osiered banks. [Poetic] Collins.

osiris.c: Osiris O*si"ris (?), prop. n. [L., fr. Gr.?; of Egyptian origin.] (Myth.) One of the principal divinities of Egypt, the brother and husband of Isis. He was figured as a mummy wearing the royal cap of Upper Egypt, and was symbolized by the sacred bull, called Apis. Cf. Serapis. -- O*sir"i*an (#), a.

osmanli.c: Osmanli Os"man*li (?), n.; pl. Osmanlis (#). [So called from Osman. See Ottoman.] A Turkish official; one of the dominant tribe of Turks; loosely, any Turk.

osmate.c: Osmate Os"mate (?), n. (Chem.) A salt of osmic acid. [Formerly written also osmiate.]

osmaterium.c: Osmaterium ‖Os`ma*te"ri*um (?), n.; pl. Osmateria (#). [NL., fr. Gr.? smell.] (Zool.) One of a pair of scent organs which the larvae of certain butterflies emit from the first body segment, either above or below.

osmazome.c: Osmazome Os"ma*zome (?), n. [Gr.? smell, odor +? broth: cf. F. osmazôme.] (Old Chem.) A substance formerly supposed to give to soup and broth their characteristic odor, and probably consisting of one or several of the class of nitrogenous substances which are called extractives.

osmiamate.c: Osmiamate Os`mi*am"ate (?), n. (Chem.) A salt of osmiamic acid.

osmiamic.c: Osmiamic Os`mi*am"ic (?), a. [Osmium + amido.] (Chem.) Of, pertaining to, or designating, a nitrogenous acid of osmium, H2N2Os2O5, forming a well-known series of yellow salts.

osmic.c: Osmic Os"mic (?), a. (Chem.) Pertaining to, derived from, or containing, osmium; specifically, designating those compounds in which it has a valence higher than in other lower compounds; as, osmic oxide.

osmidrosis.c: Osmidrosis ‖Os`mi*dro"sis (?), n. [NL., from Gr. 'osmh` smell +? to sweat.] (Med.) The secretion of fetid sweat.

osmious.c: Osmious Os"mi*ous (?), a. (Chem.) Denoting those compounds of osmium in which the element has a valence relatively lower than in the osmic compounds; as, osmious chloride. [Written also osmous.]

osmite.c: osmite os"mite (?), n. (Chem.) A salt of osmious acid.

osmium.c: osmium os"mi*um (ŏz"mĭ*ŭm), n. [Gr. 'osmh` a smell, odor, akin to 'o`zein to smell. So named in allusion to the strong chlorinelike odor of osmic tetroxide. See Odor.] (Chem.) A rare metallic element of the platinum group with atomic number 76. It is found native as an alloy in platinum ore, and in iridosmine. It is a hard, infusible, bluish or grayish white metal, and the heaviest substance known. Its tetroxide is used in histological experiments to stain tissues. Symbol Os. Atomic weight 190.2. Specific gravity 22.477.

osmogene.c: osmogene os"mo*gene (ŏs"mo*jēn or ŏz"mo*jēn), n. [Osmose + root of Gr. ge`nos race.] An apparatus, consisting of a number of cells whose sides are of parchment paper, for conducting the process of osmosis. It is used especially in sugar refining to remove potassium salts from the molasses.

osmograph.c: osmograph os"mo*graph (ŏz"mo*grȧf), n. [Osmose + -graph.] (Physics) An instrument for recording the height of the liquid in an endosmometer or for registering osmotic pressures.

osmometer.c: osmometer os*mom"e*ter (ŏz"mŏm"e*tẽr or ŏs"mŏm"e*tẽr), n. [Gr. 'wsmo`s impulse + -meter.] (Physics) An instrument for measuring the amount of osmotic action in different liquids.

osmometry.c: Osmometry Os*mom"e*try (ŏz"mŏm"e*try̆ or ŏs"mŏm"e*try̆), n. (Physics) The study of osmosis by means of the osmometer.

osmose.c: Osmose Os"mose (ŏz"mōs), n. [Gr.?, equiv. to? impulse, fr.? to push.] (Chemical Physics) (a) The tendency in fluids to mix, or become equably diffused, when in contact. Same as osmosis, which see.

osmosis.c: osmosis os*mo"sis (ŏz*mō"sĭs), n. [NL., fr. Gr. 'wsmo`s, equiv. to 'w^sis impulse, fr. 'wqei^n to push.] (Chemical Physics) (a) The tendency in fluids to mix, or become equably diffused, when in contact. It was first observed between fluids of differing densities, and as taking place through a membrane or an intervening porous structure. An older term for the phenomenon was Osmose. (b) The action produced by this tendency.

osmotic.c: osmotic os*mot"ic (?), a. Pertaining to, or having the property of, osmosis; as, osmotic force.

osmund.c: Osmund Os"mund (?), n. (Bot.) A fern of the genus Osmunda, or flowering fern. The most remarkable species is the osmund royal, or royal fern (Osmunda regalis), which grows in wet or boggy places, and has large bipinnate fronds, often with a panicle of capsules at the top. The rootstock contains much starch, and has been used in stiffening linen.

osnaburg.c: Osnaburg Os"na*burg (?), n. A species of coarse linen, originally made in Osnaburg, Germany.

osoberry.c: Oso-berry O"so-ber`ry (?), n. (Bot.) The small, blueblack, drupelike fruit of the Nuttallia cerasiformis, a shrub of Oregon and California, belonging to the Cherry tribe of Rosaceae.

osphradium.c: Osphradium ‖Os*phra"di*um (?), n.; pl. Osphradia (#). [NL., fr. Gr.? strong scent, fr.? to smell.] (Zool.) The olfactory organ of some Mollusca. It is connected with the organ of respiration.

ospray.c: Ospray Osprey { Os"prey, Os"pray } (?), n. [Through OF. fr. L. ossifraga (orig., the bone breaker); prob. influenced by oripelargus (mountain stork, a kind of eagle, Gr.?); cf. OF. orpres, and F. orfraie. See Ossifrage.] (Zool.) The fishhawk (Pandion haliaetus).

oss.c: Oss Oss (?), v. i. [See Osse, n.] To prophesy; to presage. [R. & Obs.] R. Edgeworth.

osse.c: Osse Osse (?), n. [Gr.?.] A prophetic or ominous utterance. [R. & Obs.] Holland.

ossean.c: Ossean Os"se*an (?), n. (Zool.) A fish having a bony skeleton; a teleost.

ossein.c: Ossein Os"se*in (?), n. [L. os bone.] (Physiol. Chem.) The organic basis of bone tissue; the residue after removal of the mineral matters from bone by dilute acid; in embryonic tissue, the substance in which the mineral salts are deposited to form bone; bone collagen; -- called also ostein. Chemically it is the same as collagen.

osseous.c: Osseous Os"se*ous (?), a. [L. osseus, from os, ossis bone; akin to Gr. 'oste`on, Skr. asthi. Cf. Oyster.] Composed of bone; resembling bone; capable of forming bone; bony; ossific.

osseter.c: Osseter Os"se*ter (?), n. [Russ, osetr' sturgeon.] (Zool.) A species of sturgeon.

ossianic.c: Ossianic Os`si*an"ic (?), prop. a. Of or pertaining to, or characteristic of, Ossian, a legendary Erse or Celtic bard.

ossicle.c: Ossicle Os"si*cle (?), n. [L. ossiculum, dim. of os, ossis, a bone.] 1. A little bone; as, the auditory ossicles in the tympanum of the ear.

ossiculum.c: Ossiculum ‖Os*sic"u*lum (?), n.; pl. Ossicula (#). [L., a little bone.] (Zool.) Same as Ossicle.

ossiferous.c: Ossiferous Os*sif"er*ous (?), a. [L. os, ossis, a bone + -ferous: cf. F. ossifère.] Containing or yielding bone.

ossific.c: Ossific Os*sif"ic (?), a. [L. os, ossis, bone + facere to make: cf. F. ossifique. See Fact.] Capable of producing bone; having the power to change cartilage or other tissue into bone.

ossification.c: Ossification Os`si*fi*ca"tion (?), n. [Cf. F. ossification. See Ossify.] 1. (Physiol.) The formation of bone; the process, in the growth of an animal, by which inorganic material (mainly lime salts) is deposited in cartilage or membrane, forming bony tissue; ostosis.

ossified.c: Ossified Os"si*fied (?), a. Changed to bone or something resembling bone; hardened by deposits of mineral matter of any kind; -- said of tissues.

ossifrage.c: Ossifrage Os"si*frage (?), n. [L. ossifraga, ossifragus, osprey, fr. ossifragus bone breaking; os, ossis, a bone + frangere, fractum, to break. See Osseous, Break, and cf. Osprey, Ossifragous.] (Zool.) (a) The lammergeir. (b) The young of the sea eagle or bald eagle. [Obs.]

ossifragous.c: Ossifragous Os*sif"ra*gous (?), a. [L. ossifragus. See Ossifrage.] Serving to break bones; bone-breaking.

ossify.c: Ossify Os"si*fy (?), v. t. [imp. & p. p. Ossified (?); p. pr. & vb. n. Ossifying (?).] [L. os, ossis, bone + -fy: cf. F. ossifier. See Osseous.] 1. (Physiol.) To form into bone; to change from a soft animal substance into bone, as by the deposition of lime salts.
Ossify Os"si*fy, v. i. (Physiol.) To become bone; to change from a soft tissue to a hard bony tissue.

ossifying.c: Ossifying Os"si*fy`ing (?), a. (Physiol.) Changing into bone; becoming bone; as, the ossifying process.

ossivorous.c: Ossivorous Os*siv"o*rous (?), a. [L. os, ossis, bone + vorare to devour: cf. F. ossivore.] Feeding on bones; eating bones; as, ossivorous quadrupeds. Derham.

ossuarium.c: Ossuarium ‖Os`su*a"ri*um (?), n. [L.] A charnel house; an ossuary. Walpole.

ossuary.c: Ossuary Os"su*a*ry (?), n.; pl. -ries (#). [L. ossuarium, fr. ossuarius of or bones, fr. os, ossis, bone: cf. F. ossuaire.] A place where the bones of the dead are deposited; a charnel house. [Obs.] Sir T. Browne.

osteitis.c: Osteitis ‖Os`te*i"tis (?), n. [NL. See Osteo-, and -itis.] (Med.) Inflammation of bone.

osteler.c: Osteler Os"tel*er (?), n. Same as Hosteler. Wyclif.

ostend.c: Ostend Os*tend" (?), v. t. [L. ostendere to show.] To exhibit; to manifest. [Obs.]

ostensibility.c: Ostensibility Os*ten`si*bil"i*ty (?), n. The quality or state of being ostensible.

ostensible.c: Ostensible Os*ten"si*ble (ŏs*tĕn"sĭ*b'l), a. [From L. ostensus, p. p. of ostendere to show, prop., to stretch out before; fr. prefix obs- (old form of ob-) + tendere to stretch. See Tend.]

ostensibly.c: Ostensibly Os*ten"si*bly (ŏs*tĕn"sĭ*bly̆), adv. In an ostensible manner; avowedly; professedly; apparently. Walsh.

ostension.c: Ostension Os*ten"sion (?), n. [L. ostensio a showing: cf. F. ostension. See Ostend.] (Eccl.) The showing of the sacrament on the altar in order that it may receive the adoration of the communicants.

ostensively.c: Ostensively Os*ten"sive*ly, adv. In an ostensive manner.

ostensory.c: Ostensory Ostensorium { ‖Os`ten*so"ri*um (?), Os*ten"so*ry (?), } n.; pl. L. -soria (#), E. -sories (#). [NL. ostensorium: cf. F. ostensoir. See Ostensible.] (R. C. Ch.) Same as Monstrance.

ostent.c: Ostent Os"tent (?), n. [L. ostentus, ostentum, fr. ostendere (p. p. ostensus and ostentus) to show. See Ostensible.]

ostentate.c: Ostentate Os"ten*tate (?), v. t. [L. ostentatus, p. p. of ostentare, v. intens. fr. ostendere. See Ostent.] To make an ambitious display of; to show or exhibit boastingly. [R.] Jer. Taylor.

ostentation.c: Ostentation Os`ten*ta"tion (?), n. [L. ostentatio: cf. F. ostentation.] 1. The act of ostentating or of making an ambitious display; unnecessary show; pretentious parade; -- usually in a detractive sense. “Much ostentation vain of fleshly arm.” Milton.

ostentatious.c: Ostentatious Os`ten*ta"tious (?), a. Fond of, or evincing, ostentation; unduly conspicuous; pretentious; boastful.

ostentator.c: Ostentator Os"ten*ta`tor (?), n. [L.] One fond of display; a boaster. Sherwood.

osteo.c: osteo- os"te*o- pref. A combining form of Gr. 'oste`on a bone.

osteoblast.c: Osteoblast Os"te*o*blast (?), n. [Osteo- + -blast.] (Anat.) One of the protoplasmic cells which occur in the osteogenetic layer of the periosteum, and from or around which the matrix of the bone is developed; an osteoplast.

osteoclasis.c: osteoclasis ‖os`te*o*cla"sis (?), n. [NL. See Osteoclast.] (Surg.) The operation of breaking a bone in order to correct deformity.

osteoclast.c: osteoclast os"te*o*clast (?), n. [Osteo- + Gr. kla^n to break.] 1. (Physiol.) Same as myeloplax, a large multinucleate cell within the bone, which functions in the absroption and removal of bone tissue.

osteocomma.c: Osteocomma ‖Os`te*o*com"ma (?), n.; pl. L. Osteocommata (#), E. Osteocommas (#). [NL. See Osteo-, and Comma.] (Anat.) A metamere of the vertebrate skeleton; an osteomere; a vertebra. Owen.

osteocope.c: Osteocope Os"te*o*cope (?), n. [Gr.?; 'oste`on a bone +? a striking, pain: cf. F. ostéocope.] (Med.) Pain in the bones; a violent fixed pain in any part of a bone. -- Os`te*o*cop"ic (#), a.

osteocranium.c: Osteocranium Os`te*o*cra"ni*um (?), n. [Osteo- + cranium.] (Anat.) The bony cranium, as distinguished from the cartilaginous cranium.

osteodentine.c: Osteodentine Os`te*o*den"tine (?), n. [Osteo- + dentine.] (Anat.) A hard substance, somewhat like bone, which is sometimes deposited within the pulp cavity of teeth.

osteogen.c: Osteogen Os"te*o*gen (?), n. [Osteo- + -gen.] (Physiol.) The soft tissue, or substance, which, in developing bone, ultimately undergoes ossification.

osteogeny.c: Osteogeny Osteogenesis { Os`te*o*gen"e*sis (?), Os`te*og"e*ny (?), } n. [Osteo- + genesis, or the root of Gr. gi`gnesqai to be born: cf. F. ostéogénie.] (Physiol.) The formation or growth of bone.

osteogenetic.c: Osteogenetic Os`te*o*ge*net"ic (?), a. (Physiol.) Connected with osteogenesis, or the formation of bone; producing bone; as, osteogenetic tissue; the osteogenetic layer of the periosteum.

osteography.c: Osteography Os`te*og"ra*phy (?), n. [Osteo- + -graphy.] The description of bones; osteology.

osteoid.c: Osteoid Os"te*oid (?), a. [Osteo- + -oid: cf. Gr.?.] (Anat.) Resembling bone; bonelike.

osteolite.c: Osteolite Os"te*o*lite (?), n. [Osteo- + -lite.] (Min.) A massive impure apatite, or calcium phosphate.

osteologer.c: Osteologer Os`te*ol"o*ger (?), n. One versed in osteology; an osteologist.

osteological.c: Osteological Osteologic { Os`te*o*log"ic (?), Os`te*o*log"ic*al (?), } a. [Cf. F. ostéologique.] Of or pertaining to osteology. -- Os`te*o*log"ic*al*ly, adv.

osteologist.c: Osteologist Os`te*ol"o*gist (?), n. One who is skilled in osteology; an osteologer.

osteology.c: Osteology Os`te*ol"o*gy (?), n. [Osteo- + -logy: cf. F. ostéologie.] The science which treats of the bones of the vertebrate skeleton.

osteolysis.c: Osteolysis ‖Os`te*ol"y*sis (?), n. [NL. osteo- + Gr. ly`sis a loosing.] Softening and absorption of bone. -- Os`te*o*lyt"ic (#), a.

osteoma.c: Osteoma ‖Os`te*o"ma (?), n.; pl. Osteomata (#). [NL. See Osteo-, and -oma.] (Med.) A tumor composed mainly of bone; a tumor of a bone.

osteomalacia.c: Osteomalacia ‖Os`te*o*ma*la"ci*a (?), n. [NL., fr. Gr. 'oste`on bone +? softness.] (Med.) A disease of the bones, in which they lose their earthy material, and become soft, flexible, and distorted. Also called malacia.

osteomanty.c: Osteomanty Os"te*o*man`ty (?), n. [Osteo- Gr. mantei`a divination.] Divination by means of bones. [R.]

osteopath.c: Osteopath Os"te*o*path (?), n. A practitioner of osteopathy.

osteopathic.c: Osteopathic Os`te*o*path"ic (?), a. (Med.) Of or pertaining to osteopathy. -- Os`te*o*path"ic*al*ly (#), adv.

osteopathist.c: Osteopathist Os`te*op"a*thist (?), n. One who practices osteopathy; an osteopath.

osteopathy.c: osteopathy os`te*op"a*thy (?), n. [Osteo- + Gr. pa`qos suffering.] (Med.) (a) Any disease of the bones. [R.] (b) A system of treatment based on the theory that diseases are chiefly due to deranged mechanism of the bones, nerves, blood vessels, and other tissues, and can be remedied by manipulations of these parts. Modern practitioners use the therapeutic and diagnostic techniques of modern medicine as well as manipulative procedures.

osteoperiostitis.c: Osteoperiostitis ‖Os`te*o*per`i*os*ti"tis (?), n. [NL.; osteo- + periosteum + -itis.] (Med.) Inflammation of a bone and its periosteum.

osteophone.c: Osteophone Os"te*o*phone (?), n. [Gr. 'oste`on bone + fwnh` voice.] An instrument for transmission of auditory vibrations through the bones of the head, so as to be appreciated as sounds by persons deaf from causes other than those affecting the nervous apparatus of hearing.

osteoplast.c: Osteoplast Os"te*o*plast (?), n. [Osteo- + Gr. pla`ssein to form.] (Anat.) An osteoblast.

osteoplasty.c: Osteoplasty Os"te*o*plas`ty (?), n. [Osteo- + -plasty.] (Med.) An operation or process by which the total or partial loss of a bone is remedied. Dunglison.

osteoporosis.c: Osteoporosis ‖Os`te*o*po*ro"sis (?), n. [NL.; osteo- + Gr. po`ros pore.] (Med. & Physiol.) An absorption of bone so that the bone tissue becomes unusually porous. It occurs especially in elderly men and postmenopausal women, and predisposes the elderly to fractures of the bones.

osteopterygious.c: Osteopterygious Os`te*op`ter*yg"i*ous (?), a. [Osteo- Gr.? a fin.] (Zool.) Having bones in the fins, as certain fishes.

osteosarcoma.c: Osteosarcoma ‖Os`te*o*sar*co"ma (?), n.; pl. Osteosarcomata (#). [NL. See Osteo-, and sarcoma.] (Med.) A tumor having the structure of a sarcoma in which there is a deposit of bone; sarcoma connected with bone.

osteosclerosis.c: Osteosclerosis ‖Os`te*o*scle*ro"sis (?), n. [NL.; osteo- + sclerosis.] Abnormal hardness and density of bone.

osteotome.c: Osteotome Os"te*o*tome (?), n. [Osteo- + Gr. te`mnein.] (Surg.) Strong nippers or a chisel for dividing bone.

osteotomist.c: Osteotomist Os`te*ot"o*mist (?), n. One skilled in osteotomy.

osteotomy.c: Osteotomy Os`te*ot"o*my (?), n. 1. The dissection or anatomy of bones; osteology.

osteozoa.c: Osteozoa ‖Os`te*o*zo"a (?), n. pl. [NL., fr. Gr. 'oste`on a bone + zw^,on an animal.] (Zool.) Same as Vertebrata.

ostiary.c: Ostiary Os"ti*a*ry (?), n.; pl. -ries (#). [L. ostium door, entrance. See Usher.] 1. The mouth of a river; an estuary. [R.] Sir T. Browne.

ostic.c: Ostic Os"tic (?), a. [From North American Indian oshtegwon a head.] Pertaining to, or applied to, the language of the Tuscaroras, Iroquois, Wyandots, Winnebagoes, and a part of the Sioux Indians. Schoolcraft.

ostiole.c: Ostiole Os"ti*ole (?), n. [L. ostiolum a little door, dim. of ostium a door: cf. F. ostiole.] (Bot.) (a) The exterior opening of a stomate. See Stomate. (b) Any small orifice.

ostium.c: Ostium ‖Os"ti*um (?), n.; pl. Ostia (#). [L.] (Anat.) An opening; a passage.

ostleress.c: Ostleress Ost"ler*ess, n. A female ostler. [R.] Tennyson.

ostmen.c: Ostmen Ost"men (?), n. pl.; sing. Ostman. [See East, and Man.] East men; Danish settlers in Ireland, formerly so called. Lyttelton.

ostosis.c: Ostosis ‖Os*to"sis (?), n. [NL., from Gr. 'oste`on a bone.] (Physiol.) Bone formation; ossification. See Ectostosis, and Endostosis.

ostracea.c: Ostracea ‖Os*tra"ce*a (?), n. pl. [NL., fr. Gr. 'o`strakon shell of a testacean.] (Zool.) A division of bivalve mollusks including the oysters and allied shells.

ostracean.c: Ostracean Os*tra"cean (?), n. [L. ostrea an oyster. See Oyster.] (Zool.) Any one of a family of bivalves, of which the oyster is the type.

ostracion.c: Ostracion ‖Os*tra"ci*on (?), prop. n. [NL., fr. Gr. 'ostra`kion small shell.] (Zool.) A genus of plectognath fishes of the family Ostraciontidae having the body covered with solid, immovable, bony plates. It includes the trunkfishes (also called boxfish).

ostraciont.c: Ostraciont Os*tra"ci*ont (?), n. (Zool.) A fish of the genus Ostracion and allied genera.

ostracism.c: ostracism os"tra*cism (?), n. [Gr. 'ostrakismo`s, fr. 'ostraki`zein to ostracize. See Ostracize.] 1. (Gr. Antiq.) Banishment by popular vote, -- a means adopted at Athens to rid the city of a person whose talent and influence gave umbrage.

ostracize.c: Ostracize Os"tra*cize (?), v. t. [imp. & p. p. Ostracized (?); p. pr. & vb. n. Ostracizing (?).] [Gr. 'ostraki`zein, fr. 'o`strakon a tile, a tablet used in voting, a shell; cf. 'o`streon oyster, 'oste`on bone. Cf. Osseous, Oyster.] 1. (Gr. Antiq.) To exile by ostracism; to banish by a popular vote, as at Athens. Grote.

ostracoda.c: Ostracoda ‖Os*trac"o*da (?), prop. n. pl. (Zool.) An order of Entomostraca possessing shrimplike bodies enclosed in hard bivalve shells; called also seed shrimp and mussel shrimp. They were formerly referred to as Ostracoidea. They are of small size, and swim freely about; many are less than 1 mm in length. Microfossils of certain extinct orders have been found extending back to the Cambrian age.

ostracodermi.c: Ostracodermi ‖Os`tra*coder"mi (?), prop. n. pl. [NL., fr. Gr. 'o`strakon shell of a testacean +? skin.] (Zool.) A suborder of fishes of which Ostracion is the type.

ostracoid.c: ostracoid os"tra*coid (?), a. (Zool.) Of or pertaining to the Ostracoidea (now Ostracoda). -- n. One of the Ostracoidea (now Ostracoda).

ostracoidea.c: Ostracoidea ‖Os`tra*coi"de*a (?), n. pl. [NL., fr. Gr. 'o`strakon shell of a testacean + -oid.] (Zool.) An order of Entomostraca possessing hard bivalve shells. They are of small size, and swim freely about. Now usually written Ostracoda. [archaic]

ostrea.c: Ostrea ‖Os"tre*a (?), n. [L., an oyster.] (Zool.) A genus of bivalve Mollusca which includes the true oysters.

ostreaceous.c: Ostreaceous Os`tre*a"ceous (?), a. [L. ostrea an oyster. See Oyster.] (Zool.) Of or pertaining to an oyster, or to a shell; shelly.

ostreaculture.c: Ostreaculture Os"tre*a*cul`ture (?), n. The artificial cultivation of oysters.

ostreophagist.c: Ostreophagist Os`tre*oph"a*gist (?), n. [Gr. 'o`streon an oyster + fagei^n to eat.] One who feeds on oysters.

ostrich.c: ostrich os"trich (ŏs"trich), n. [OE. ostriche, ostrice, OF. ostruche, ostruce, F. autruche, L. avis struthio; avis bird + struthio ostrich, fr. Gr.?, fr.? bird, sparrow. Cf. Aviary, Struthious.] [Formerly written also estrich.] (Zool.) A large bird of the genus Struthio, of which Struthio camelus of Africa is the best known species. It has long and very strong legs, adapted for rapid running; only two toes; a long neck, nearly bare of feathers; and short wings incapable of flight. The adult male is about eight feet high.

ostriferous.c: Ostriferous Os*trif"er*ous (?), a. [L. ostrifer; ostrea oyster + ferre.] Producing oysters; containing oysters.

ostrogoth.c: Ostrogoth Os"tro*goth (?), prop. n. [L. Ostrogothi, pl. See East, and Goth.] One of the Eastern Goths. See Goth.

ostrogothic.c: Ostrogothic Os`tro*goth"ic (?), prop. a. Of or pertaining to the Ostrogoths.

oswego.c: Oswego tea Os*we"go tea" (?). (Bot.) An American aromatic herb (Monarda didyma), with showy, bright red, labiate flowers.

otacoustic.c: otacoustic ot`a*cous"tic (?), a. [Oto- + acoustic: cf. F. otacoustique.] Assisting the sense of hearing; as, an otacoustic instrument.

otacousticon.c: otacousticon otacoustic { ot`a*cous"tic (?), ot`a*cous"ti*con (?), } n. An instrument to facilitate hearing, as an ear trumpet.

otaheite.c: Otaheite apple O`ta*hei"te ap"ple (?). [So named from Otaheite, or Tahiti, one of the Society Islands.] (Bot.) (a) The fruit of a Polynesian anacardiaceous tree (Spondias dulcis), also called vi-apple. It is rather larger than an apple, and the rind has a flavor of turpentine, but the flesh is said to taste like pineapples. (b) A West Indian name for a myrtaceous tree (Jambosa Malaccensis) which bears crimson berries.

otalgia.c: Otalgia ‖O*tal"gi*a (?), n. [NL., fr. Gr. 'wtalgi`a; o'y^s, 'wto`s, the ear + 'a`lgos pain: cf. F. otalgie.] (Med.) Pain in the ear; earache.

otalgic.c: Otalgic O*tal"gic (?), a. (Med.) Of or pertaining to otalgia. -- n. A remedy for otalgia.

otalgy.c: Otalgy O*tal"gy (?), n. Pain in the ear; otalgia.

otary.c: Otary O"ta*ry (?), n.; pl. Otaries (#). [Gr. 'wtaro`s large-eared, fr. o'y^s, 'wto`s, ear: cf. F. otarie.] (Zool.) Any eared seal.

otheoscope.c: Otheoscope O"the*o*scope (?), n. [Gr. 'wqei^n to push + -scope.] (Physics) An instrument for exhibiting the repulsive action produced by light or heat in an exhausted vessel; a modification of the radiometer. W. Crookes.

other.c: Other Oth"er (ŭth"ẽr), conj. [See Or.] Either; -- used with other or or for its correlative (as either... or are now used). [Obs.]

Other Oth"er, pron. & a. [AS. ōðer; akin to OS. āðar, ōðar, D. & G. ander, OHG. andar, Icel. annarr, Sw. annan, Dan. anden, Goth. anþar, Skr. antara: cf. L. alter; all orig. comparatives: cf. Skr. anya other. √180. Cf. Alter.] [Formerly other was used both as singular and plural.]
Other Oth"er (ŭth"ẽr), adv. Otherwise. “It shall none other be.” Chaucer. “If you think other.” Shak.

othergates.c: Othergates Oth"er*gates` (ŭth"ẽr*gāts`), adv. [Other + gate way. See wards.] In another manner. [Obs.]

otherguess.c: Otherguess Otherguise { Oth"er*guise` (ŭth"ẽr*gīz`), Oth"er*guess` (?) }, a. & adv. [A corruption of othergates.] Of another kind or sort; in another way. “Otherguess arguments.” Berkeley.

otherness.c: Otherness Oth"er*ness, n. The quality or state of being other or different; alterity; oppositeness.

otherwhere.c: Otherwhere Oth"er*where` (?), adv. In or to some other place, or places; elsewhere. Milton. Tennyson.

otherwhiles.c: Otherwhiles Otherwhile { Oth"er*while` (?), Oth"er*whiles` (?), } adv. At another time, or other times; sometimes; occasionally. [Archaic]

otic.c: Otic O"tic (?), a. [Gr.?, fr. o'y^s, 'wto`s, the ear: cf. F. otique.] Of, pertaining to, or in the region of, the ear; auricular; auditory.

otiose.c: Otiose O"ti*ose` (?), a. [L. otiosus, fr. otium ease.] Being at leisure or ease; unemployed; indolent; idle. “Otiose assent.” Paley.

otiosity.c: Otiosity O`ti*os"ity (?), n. [L. otiositas.] Leisure; indolence; idleness; ease. [R.] Thackeray.

otis.c: Otis ‖O"tis (?), prop. n. [L., a kind of bustard, Gr.?.] (Zool.) A genus of birds including certain of the bustards.

otitis.c: Otitis ‖O*ti"tis (?), n. [NL., fr. Gr. o'y^s, 'wto`s, the ear + -itis.] (Med.) Inflammation of the ear.

oto.c: Oto- O"to- (?). [Gr. o'y^s, 'wto`s, the ear.] A combining form denoting relation to the ear, or situation near the ear or in the ear.

otoba.c: Otoba fat O*to"ba fat` (?). (Chem.) A colorless buttery substance obtained from the fruit of Myristica otoba, a species of nutmeg tree.

otoconite.c: Otoconite O*toc"o*nite (?), n. [Oto- + Gr.? dust.] (Anat.) (a) A mass of otoliths. (b) An otolith.

otocrane.c: Otocrane O"to*crane (?), n. [Oto- + Gr.? skull.] (Anat.) The cavity in the skull in which the parts of the internal ear are lodged.

otocranial.c: Otocranial O`to*cra"ni*al (?), a. (Anat.) Of or pertaining to the otocrane.

otocyst.c: Otocyst O"to*cyst (?), n. [Oto- + cyst.] (Zool. & Anat.) An auditory cyst or vesicle; one of the simple auditory organs of many invertebrates, containing a fluid and otoliths; also, the embryonic vesicle from which the parts of the internal ear of vertebrates are developed.

otography.c: Otography O*tog"ra*phy (?), n. [Oto- + -graphy.] A description of the ear.

otolite.c: Otolite Otolith { O"to*lith (?), O"to*lite (?), } n. [Oto- + -lith, -lite.] (Anat.) One of the small bones or particles of calcareous or other hard substance in the internal ear of vertebrates, and in the auditory organs of many invertebrates; an ear stone. Collectively, the otoliths are called ear sand and otoconite.

otolitic.c: Otolitic Otolithic { O`to*lith"ic (?), O`to*lit"ic (?), } a. (Anat.) Of or pertaining to otoliths.

otological.c: Otological O`to*log"ic*al (?), a. Of or pertaining to otology.

otologist.c: Otologist O*tol"o*gist (?), n. One skilled in otology; an aurist.

otology.c: Otology O*tol"o*gy (?), n. [Oto- + -logy.] The branch of science which treats of the ear and its diseases.

otopathy.c: Otopathy O*top"a*thy (?), n. [Oto- + Gr. paqei^n to suffer.] (Med.) A diseased condition of the ear.

otorrhoea.c: Otorrhoea ‖O`tor*rhœ"a (?), n. [NL., fr. Gr. o'y^s, 'wto`s, the ear +? to flow.] (Med.) A flow or running from the ear, esp. a purulent discharge.

otoscope.c: Otoscope O"to*scope (?), n. [Oto- + -scope.] An instrument for examining the condition of the ear.

otoscopeic.c: Otoscopeic O`to*scope"ic (?), a. Of or pertaining to the otoscope or to otoscopy.

otoscopy.c: Otoscopy O*tos"co*py (?), n. (Med.) The examination of the ear; the art of using the otoscope.

otosteal.c: Otosteal O*tos"te*al (?), n. [Oto- + Gr. 'oste`on a bone.] (Anat.) An auditory ossicle. R. Owen.

otozoum.c: Otozoum ‖O`to*zo"um (?), prop. n. [NL., fr. Gr.?, a fabled giant + zw^,on an animal.] (Paleon.) An extinct genus of huge vertebrates, probably dinosaurs, known only from four-toed tracks in Triassic sandstones.

ottava.c: Ottava rima ‖Ot*ta"va ri"ma (?). [It. See Octave, and Rhyme.] (Pros.) A stanza of eight lines of heroic verse, with three rhymes, the first six lines rhyming alternately and the last two forming a couplet. It was used by Byron in “Don Juan,” by Keats in “Isabella,” by Shelley in “The Witch of Atlas,” etc.

ottawas.c: Ottawas Ot"ta*was (?), n. pl.; sing. Ottawa (?). (Ethnol.) A tribe of Indians who, when first known, lived on the Ottawa River. Most of them subsequently migrated to the southwestern shore of Lake Superior.

otter.c: Otter Ot"ter (ŏt"tẽr), n. [OE. oter, AS. otor; akin to D. & G. otter, Icel. otr, Dan. odder, Sw. utter, Lith. udra, Russ, vuidra, Gr. "y`dra water serpent, hydra, Skr. udra otter, and also to E. water. √137, 215. See Water, and cf. Hydra.]
Otter Ot"ter, n. A corruption of Annotto.

otto.c: Otto cycle Ot"to cy`cle (?). (Thermodynamics) A four-stroke cycle for internal-combustion engines consisting of the following operations: First stroke, suction into cylinder of explosive charge, as of gas and air; second stroke, compression, ignition, and explosion of this charge; third stroke (the working stroke), expansion of the gases; fourth stroke, expulsion of the products of combustion from the cylinder. This is the cycle invented by Beau de Rochas in 1862 and applied by Dr. Otto in 1877 in the Otto-Crossley gas engine, the first commercially successful internal-combustion engine made.
Otto engine Otto engine. An engine using the Otto cycle.

ottoman.c: Ottoman Ot"to*man (?), a. [F. ottoman: cf. It. ottomano, ottomanno; -- from Othoman, Othman, or Osman, the name of a sultan who assumed the government of Turkey about the year 1300. Cf. Osmanli, Ottoman a stuffed seat.] Of or pertaining to the Turks; as, the Ottoman power or empire.
Ottoman Ot"to*man, n.; pl. Ottomans (?). 1. A Turk.

ottrelite.c: Ottrelite Ot"trel*ite (?), n. [From Ottrez, on the borders of Luxembourg.] (Min.) A micaceous mineral occurring in small scales. It is characteristic of certain crystalline schists.

ouakari.c: Ouakari ‖Oua*ka"ri (?), n. [From the native name.] (Zool.) Any South American monkey of the genus Brachyurus, especially Brachyurus ouakari.

ouananiche.c: Ouananiche Oua`na`niche" (?), n. [Canadian F., of Amer. Indian origin.] A small landlocked variety of the Atlantic salmon (Salmo salar ounaniche) of Lake St. John, Canada, and neighboring waters, noted for its vigor and activity, and habit of leaping from the water when hooked.

ouarine.c: Ouarine Oua`rine" (?), n. [F.] (Zool.) A Brazilian monkey of the genus Mycetes.

oubliette.c: Oubliette ‖Ou`bli`ette" (?), n. [F., fr. oublier to forget, fr. (assumed) LL. oblitare, L. oblivisci, p. p. oblitus.] A dungeon with an opening only at the top, found in some old castles and other strongholds, into which persons condemned to perpetual imprisonment, or to perish secretly, were thrust, or lured to fall.

ouch.c: Ouch Ouch (ouch), n. [OE. ouch, nouche (a nouch being taken for an ouch: cf. Adder), fr. OF. nusche, nosche, nousche, buckle, clasp, LL. nusca, fr. OHG. nusca, nuscha.] A socket or bezel holding a precious stone; hence, a jewel or ornament worn on the person.

ought.c: Ought Ought, imp., p. p., or auxiliary. [Orig. the preterit of the verb to owe. OE. oughte, aughte, ahte, AS. āhte. √110. See Owe.] 1. Was or were under obligation to pay; owed. [Obs.]

oughtness.c: Oughtness Ought"ness (?), n. The state of being as a thing ought to be; rightness. [R.] N. W. Taylor.

oughwhere.c: Oughwhere Ough"where` (?), adv. [AS. āhwaer.] Anywhere; somewhere. See Owher. [Obs.]

ounce.c: Ounce Ounce (ouns), n. [F. once, fr. L. uncia a twelfth, the twelfth part of a pound or of a foot: cf. Gr. 'o`gkos bulk, mass, atom. Cf. 2d Inch, Oke.] 1. A unit of mass or weight, the sixteenth part of a pound avoirdupois, and containing 28.35 grams or 437½ grains.

Ounce Ounce, n. [F. once; cf. It. lonza, Sp. onza; prob. for lonce, taken as l'once, fr. L. lynx, Gr.?, or an (assumed) fem. adj. lyncea, from lynx. Cf. Lynx.] (Zool.) A feline quadruped (Felis irbis syn. Felis uncia) resembling the leopard in size, and somewhat in color, but it has longer and thicker fur, which forms a short mane on the back. The ounce is pale yellowish gray, with irregular dark spots on the neck and limbs, and dark rings on the body. It inhabits the lofty mountain ranges of Asia. Called also once.

oundy.c: Oundy Ounded { Ound"ed (?), Oun"dy (?), } a. [F. ondé, -ée, fr. onde, L. unda, a wave.] Wavy; waving; curly. [Obs.] “Owndie hair.” Chaucer.

ouphe.c: Ouphe Ouphe (?), n. [See Auf.] A fairy; a goblin; an elf. [Obs.] “Like urchins, ouphes, and fairies.” Shak.

our.c: Our Our (our), possessive pron. [AS. ūre our, of us; akin to ūs us, to us, and to G. unser our, of us, Goth. unsara. √186. See Us.] Of or pertaining to us; belonging to us; as, our country; our rights; our troops; our endeavors. See I.

ourebi.c: Ourebi ‖Ou"re*bi (?), n. (Zool.) A small, graceful, and swift African antelope, allied to the klipspringer.

ouretic.c: Ouretic Ou*ret"ic (?), a. [Gr.?, from? urine. Cf. Uretic.] (Chem.) Uric.

ours.c: Ours Ours (ourz), possessive pron. See Note under Our.

ourselves.c: Ourselves Our*selves" (?), pron.; sing. Ourself (?). An emphasized form of the pronoun of the first person plural; -- used as a subject, usually with we; also, alone in the predicate, in the nominative or the objective case.

ous.c: -ous -ous (?) suff. [OF. -ous, us, -os, F. -eux, fr. L. -osus, and -us. Cf. -ose.] 1. An adjective suffix meaning full of, abounding in, having, possessing the qualities of, like; as in gracious, abounding in grace; arduous, full of ardor; bulbous, having bulbs, bulblike; riotous, poisonous, piteous, joyous, etc.

ousel.c: Ousel Ou"sel (ŏo"z'l), n. [OE. osel, AS. ōsle; akin to G. amsel, OHG. amsala, and perh. to L. merula blackbird. Cf. Merle, Amsel.] (Zool.) One of several species of European thrushes, especially the blackbird (Merula merula, or Turdus merula), and the mountain or ring ousel (Turdus torquatus). [Written also ouzel.]

oust.c: Oust Oust, v. t. [imp. & p. p. Ousted; p. pr. & vb. n. Ousting.] [OF. oster, F. ôter, prob. fr. L. obstare to oppose, hence, to forbid, take away. See Obstacle, and cf. Ouster.] 1. To take away; to remove.

ouster.c: Ouster Oust"er (?), n. [Prob. fr. the OF. infin. oster, used substantively. See Oust.] A putting out of possession; dispossession; disseizin; -- of a person.

out.c: Out Out (out), adv. [OE. out, ut, oute, ute, AS. ūt, and ūte, ūtan, fr. ūt; akin to D. uit, OS. ūt, G. aus, OHG. ūz, Icel. ūt, Sw. ut, Dan. ud, Goth. ut, Skr. ud. √198. Cf. About, But, prep., Carouse, Utter, a.] In its original and strict sense, out means from the interior of something; beyond the limits or boundary of somethings; in a position or relation which is exterior to something; -- opposed to in or into. The something may be expressed after of, from, etc. (see Out of, below); or, if not expressed, it is implied; as, he is out; or, he is out of the house, office, business, etc.; he came out; or, he came out from the ship, meeting, sect, party, etc. Out is used in a variety of applications, as: --
Out Out (out), n. 1. One who, or that which, is out; especially, one who is out of office; -- generally in the plural.
Out Out, v. t. 1. To cause to be out; to eject; to expel.
Out Out, v. i. To come or go out; to get out or away; to become public. “Truth will out.” Shak.
Out Out, interj. Expressing impatience, anger, a desire to be rid of; -- with the force of command; go out; begone; away; off.
out and out out-and-out out-and-out, out and out adv. Completely; wholly; openly.

outact.c: Outact Out*act" (?), v. t. To do or beyond; to exceed in acting. [R.]

outagamies.c: Outagamies Ou"ta*gam`ies (?), n. pl.; sing. Outagamie (?). (Ethnol.) See 1st Fox, 7.

outargue.c: Outargue Out*ar"gue (?), v. t. To surpass or conquer in argument.

outbabble.c: Outbabble Out*bab"ble (?), v. t. To utter foolishly or excessively; to surpass in babbling. [R.] Milton.

outbalance.c: Outbalance Out*bal"ance (?), v. t. To outweight; to exceed in weight or effect.

outbar.c: Outbar Out*bar" (?), v. t. To bar out. [R.] Spenser.

outbeg.c: Outbeg Out*beg" (?), v. t. To surpass in begging. [R.]

outbid.c: Outbid Out*bid" (?), v. t. [imp. Outbid or Outbade (?); p. p. Outbid or Outbidden (?); p. pr. & vb. n. Outbidding.] To exceed or surpass in bidding; to bid a higher price.

outbidder.c: Outbidder Out*bid"der (?), n. One who outbids. Johnson.

outbleat.c: Outbleat Out*bleat" (?), v. t. To surpass in bleating.

outblown.c: Outblown Out"blown` (?), a. Inflated with wind. Dryden.

outblush.c: Outblush Out*blush" (?), v. t. To exceed in blushing; to surpass in rosy color. T. Shipman.

outboard.c: Outboard Out"board` (?), a. & adv. (Naut.) Beyond or outside of the lines of a vessel's bulwarks or hull; in a direction from the hull or from the keel; -- opposed to inboard; as, outboard rigging; swing the davits outboard.

outbounds.c: Outbounds Out"bounds` (?), n. pl. The farthest or exterior bounds; extreme limits; boundaries. Spenser.

outbow.c: Outbow Out*bow" (?), v. t. To excel in bowing. Young.

outbowed.c: Outbowed Out"bowed` (?), a. Convex; curved outward. “The convex or outbowed side of a vessel.” Bp. Hall.

outbrag.c: Outbrag Out*brag" (?), v. t. To surpass in bragging; hence, to make appear inferior.

outbrave.c: Outbrave Out*brave" (?), v. t. 1. To excel in bravery or in insolence; to defy with superior courage or audacity.

outbray.c: Outbray Out*bray" (?), v. t. 1. To exceed in braying.

outbrazen.c: Outbrazen Out*bra"zen (?), v. t. To bear down with a brazen face; to surpass in impudence. T. Brown.

outbreak.c: outbreak out"break` (?), n. 1. A bursting forth; eruption; insurrection; mutiny; revolt. “Mobs and outbreaks.” J. H. Newman.

outbreaking.c: Outbreaking Out"break`ing, n. 1. The act of breaking out.

outbreast.c: Outbreast Out*breast" (?), v. t. To surpass in singing. See Breast, n., 6. [Obs.]

outbreathe.c: Outbreathe Out*breathe" (?), v. t. 1. To breathe forth. “Outbreathed life.” Spenser.
Outbreathe Out*breathe", v. i. To issue, as breath; to be breathed out; to exhale. Beau. & Fl.

outbribe.c: Outbribe Out*bribe" (?), v. t. To surpass in bribing.

outbring.c: Outbring Out*bring" (?), v. t. To bring or bear out.

outbud.c: Outbud Out*bud" (?), v. i. To sprout. [Poetic] Spenser.

outbuild.c: Outbuild Out*build" (?), v. t. [imp. & p. p. Outbuilt (?) or Outbuilded; p. pr. & vb. n. Outbuilding.] To exceed in building, or in durability of building.

outbuilding.c: Outbuilding Out"build`ing (?), n. A building separate from, and subordinate to, the main house; an outhouse.

outburn.c: Outburn Out*burn", v. t. & i. 1. To exceed in burning.

outburst.c: Outburst Out"burst` (?), n. A bursting forth; as, an outburst of laughter.

outcant.c: Outcant Out*cant" (?), v. t. To surpass in canting. Pope.

outcast.c: Outcast Out"cast` (?), a. [Cf. Sw. utkasta to cast out.] Cast out; degraded. “Outcast, rejected.” Longfellow.
Outcast Out"cast`, n. 1. One who is cast out or expelled; an exile; one driven from home, society, or country; hence, often, a degraded person; a vagabond.

outcasting.c: Outcasting Out"cast`ing, n. That which is cast out. [Obs.]

outcheat.c: Outcheat Out*cheat" (?), v. t. To exceed in cheating.

outclimb.c: Outclimb Out*climb" (?), v. t. To climb beyond; to surpass in climbing. Davenant.

outcome.c: Outcome Out"come (?), n. That which comes out of, or follows from, something else; issue; result; consequence; upshot. “The logical outcome.” H. Spenser.

outcompass.c: Outcompass Out*com"pass (?), v. t. To exceed the compass or limits of. Bacon.

outcourt.c: Outcourt Out"court` (?), n. An outer or exterior court.

outcrafty.c: Outcrafty Out*craft"y (?), v. t. To exceed in cunning. [R.] Shak.

outcrier.c: Outcrier Out"cri`er (?), n. One who cries out or proclaims; a herald or crier.

outcrop.c: Outcrop Out"crop` (?), n. (Geol.) (a) The coming out of a stratum to the surface of the ground. Lyell. (b) That part of inclined strata which appears at the surface; basset.
Outcrop Out*crop" (?), v. i. (Geol.) To come out to the surface of the ground; -- said of strata.

outcry.c: Outcry Out"cry` (?), n. 1. A vehement or loud cry; a cry of distress, alarm, opposition, or detestation; clamor.

outdare.c: Outdare Out*dare" (?), v. t. To surpass in daring; to overcome by courage; to brave. Shak. R. Browning.

outdated.c: Outdated Out*dat"ed (?), a. Being out of date; antiquated; outmoded; unfashionable. [Obs.] Hammond.

outdazzle.c: Outdazzle Out*daz"zle (?), v. t. To surpass in dazzing.

outdo.c: Outdo Out*do" (out*dōo"), v. t. [imp. Outdid (out*dĭd"); p. p. Outdone (out*dŭn"); p. pr. & vb. n. Outdoing.] To go beyond in performance; to excel; to surpass.

outdoor.c: Outdoor Out"door` (?), a. [For out of door.] Being, or done, in the open air; being or done outside of certain buildings, as poorhouses, hospitals, etc.; as, outdoor exercise; outdoor relief; outdoor patients.

outdoors.c: Outdoors Out"doors` (?), adv. Out of the house; out of doors; in the open air; abroad.

outdraw.c: Outdraw Out*draw" (?), v. t. To draw out; to extract. [R.] “He must the teeth outdraw.” Gower.

outdream.c: Outdream Out*dream" (?), v. t. To pass, or escape, while dreaming. “To outdream dangers.” Beau. & Fl.

outdrink.c: Outdrink Out*drink" (?), v. t. To exceed in drinking.

outdwell.c: Outdwell Out*dwell" (?), v. t. To dwell or stay beyond. [Poetic] “He outdwells his hour.” Shak.

outdweller.c: Outdweller Out"dwell`er (?), n. One who holds land in a parish, but lives elsewhere. [Eng.]

outer.c: Outer Out"er (out"ẽr), a. [Compar. of Out.] [AS. ūtor, compar. of ūt, adv., out. See Out, Utter, a.] Being on the outside; external; farthest or farther from the interior, from a given station, or from any space or position regarded as a center or starting place; -- opposed to inner; as, the outer wall; the outer court or gate; the outer stump in cricket; the outer world.
Outer Out"er, n. (a) The part of a target which is beyond the circles surrounding the bull's-eye. (b) A shot which strikes the outer of a target.
Outer Out"er, n. [From Out, v.] One who puts out, ousts, or expels; also, an ouster; dispossession. [R.]

outermost.c: Outermost Out"er*most` (?), a. [See Uttermost, Utmost, and cf. Outmost.] Being on the extreme external part; farthest outward; as, the outermost row. Boyle.

outface.c: Outface Out*face" (out*fās"), v. t. [imp. & p. p. Outfaced (out*fāst"); p. pr. & vb. n. Outfacing (out*fā"sĭng).] To face or look (one) out of countenance; to resist or bear down by bold looks or effrontery; to brave. Shak.

outfall.c: Outfall Out"fall` (out"fäl`), n. 1. The mouth of a river; the lower end of a water course; the open end of a drain, culvert, etc., where the discharge occurs.

outfangthef.c: outfangthef out*fang"thef (out*făng"thĕf), n. [AS. ūt-fangen-þeóf. See Out, Fang, v. t., and Thief.] (Anglo-Saxon & O. Eng. Law) (a) A thief from without or abroad, taken within a lord's fee or liberty. (b) The privilege of trying such a thief. Burrill.

outfawn.c: Outfawn Out*fawn" (out*fän"), v. t. To exceed in fawning.

outfeast.c: Outfeast Out*feast" (out*fēst"), v. t. To exceed in feasting.

outfeat.c: Outfeat Out*feat" (out*fēt"), v. t. To surpass in feats.

outfield.c: Outfield Out"field` (out"fēld`), n. 1. Arable land which has been or is being exhausted. See Infield, 1. [Scot.]

outfit.c: Outfit Out"fit (?), n. 1. A fitting out, or equipment, as of a ship for a voyage, or of a person for an expedition in an unoccupied region or residence in a foreign land; the expense of, or allowance made for, equipment, as by the government of the United States to a diplomatic agent going abroad.

outfitter.c: Outfitter Out"fit`ter (?), n. One who furnishes outfits for a voyage, a journey, or a business.

outflank.c: Outflank Out*flank" (?), v. t. 1. (Mil.) To go beyond, or be superior to, on the flank; to pass around or turn the flank or flanks of.

outflatter.c: Outflatter Out*flat"ter (?), v. t. To exceed in flattering.

outfling.c: Outfling Out"fling`, n. A gibe; a contemptuous remark.

outflow.c: Outflow Out"flow` (?), n. A flowing out; efflux.
Outflow Out*flow" (?), v. i. To flow out. Campbell.

outfly.c: Outfly Out*fly" (?), v. t. [imp. Outflew (?); p. p. Outflown (?); p. pr. & vb. n. Outflying.] To surpass in flying; to fly beyond or faster than. Shak.

outfool.c: Outfool Out*fool", v. t. To exceed in folly. [R.] Young.

outfoot.c: Outfoot Out*foot" (?), v. t. To outrun or outwalk; hence, of a vessel, to outsail. [Colloq.]

outfrown.c: Outfrown Out*frown" (?), v. t. To frown down; to overbear by frowning. Shak.

outgaze.c: Outgaze Out*gaze" (?), v. t. To gaze beyond; to exceed in sharpness or persistence of seeing or of looking; hence, to stare out of countenance.
