outgeneral.c: Outgeneral Out*gen"er*al (?), v. t. [imp. & p. p. Outgeneraled (?) or Outgeneralled; p. pr. & vb. n. Outgeneraling or Outgeneralling.] To exceed in generalship; to gain advantage over by superior military skill or executive ability; to outmaneuver. Chesterfield.

outgive.c: Outgive Out*give" (?), v. t. To surpass in giving. Dryden.

outgo.c: Outgo Out*go" (?), v. t. [imp. Outwent (?); p. p. Outgone (?); p. pr. & vb. n. Outgoing.]

Outgo Out"go` (?), n.; pl. Outgoes (?). That which goes out, or is paid out; outlay; expenditure; -- the opposite of income; as, when one's outgo exceeds one's income, distress follows quickly. Lowell.

outgoer.c: Outgoer Out"go`er (?), n. One who goes out or departs.

outgoing.c: Outgoing Out"go`ing, n. 1. The act or the state of going out.
outgoing out"go`ing, a. 1. Going out; departing; leaving; as, the outgoing administration; an outgoing steamer.

outground.c: Outground Out"ground` (?), n. Ground situated at a distance from the house; outlying land.

outgrow.c: Outgrow Out*grow" (?), v. t. [imp. Outgrew (?); p. p. Outgrown (?); p. pr. & vb. n. Outgrowing.]

outgrowth.c: Outgrowth Out"growth` (?), n. That which grows out of, or proceeds from, anything; an excrescence; an offshoot; hence, a result or consequence.

outguard.c: Outguard Out"guard` (?), n. (Mil.) A guard or small body of troops at a distance from the main body of an army, to watch for the approach of an enemy; hence, anything for defense placed at a distance from the thing to be defended.

outgush.c: Outgush Out"gush` (?), n. A pouring out; an outburst.
Outgush Out*gush" (out*gŭsh"), v. i. To gush out; to flow forth.

outhaul.c: Outhaul Out"haul` (out"häl`), n. (Naut.) A rope used for hauling out a sail upon a spar; -- opposite of inhaul.

outhees.c: Outhees Out*hees" (out*hēs"), n. [Cf. LL. uthesium, hutesium, huesium, OF. hueis, and E. hue, in hue and cry.] Outcry; alarm. [Obs.] Chaucer.

outherod.c: Out-Herod Out-Her"od (?), v. t. To surpass (Herod) in violence or wickedness; to exceed in any vicious or offensive particular. Compare outpope the Pope. “It out-Herods Herod.” Shak.

outhire.c: Outhire Out*hire" (?), v. t. To hire out. [Obs.] Spenser.

outhouse.c: outhouse out"house` (?), n. 1. A small house or building at a little distance from the main house; an outbuilding.

outing.c: Outing Out"ing, n. 1. The act of going out; an airing; an excursion; as, a summer outing.

outjest.c: Outjest Out*jest" (?), v. t. To surpass in jesting; to drive out, or away, by jesting. [R.] Shak.

outjet.c: Outjet Out"jet` (?), n. That which jets out or projects from anything. [R.] H. Miller.

outjuggle.c: Outjuggle Out*jug"gle (?), v. t. To surpass in juggling.

outkeeper.c: Outkeeper Out"keep`er (?), n. (Surv.) An attachment to a surveyor's compass for keeping tally in chaining.

outknave.c: Outknave Out*knave" (?), v. t. To surpass in knavery.

outlabor.c: Outlabor Out*la"bor (?), v. t. To surpass in laboring.

outland.c: Outland Out"land (?), a. [Out + land. See Outlandish.] 1. Foreign; outlandish. [Obs.] Strutt.

outlandish.c: Outlandish Out*land"ish (?), a. [AS. ūtlendisc foreign. See Out, Land, and -ish.] 1. Foreign; not native. [archaic]

outlast.c: Outlast Out*last" (?), v. t. To exceed in duration; to survive; to endure longer than. Milton.

outlaugh.c: Outlaugh Out*laugh" (?), v. t. 1. To surpass or outdo in laughing. Dryden.

outlaw.c: Outlaw Out"law` (out"lä`), n. [AS. ūtlaga, ūtlah. See Out, and Law.] 1. A person excluded from the benefit of the law, or deprived of its protection. Blackstone.
Outlaw Out"law`, v. t. [imp. & p. p. Outlawed (?); p. pr. & vb. n. Outlawing.] [AS.?tlagian.]

outlawry.c: Outlawry Out"law`ry (?), n.; pl. Outlawries (?). 1. The act of outlawing; the putting a man out of the protection of law, or the process by which a man (as an absconding criminal) is deprived of that protection.

outlay.c: Outlay Out*lay" (?), v. t. To lay out; to spread out; to display. [R.] Drayton.
Outlay Out"lay` (?), n. 1. A laying out or expending.

outleap.c: Outleap Out*leap" (?), v. t. To surpass in leaping.

outlearn.c: Outlearn Out*learn" (?), v. t. 1. To excel or surpass in learing.

outlet.c: Outlet Out"let` (?), n. The place or opening by which anything is let out; a passage out; an exit; a vent.
Outlet Out*let" (?), v. t. To let out; to emit. [R.] Daniel.

outlie.c: Outlie Out*lie" (?), v. t. To exceed in lying. Bp. Hall.

outlier.c: Outlier Out"li`er (?), n. 1. One who does not live where his office, or business, or estate, is. Bentley.

outlimb.c: Outlimb Out"limb` (?), n. An extreme member or part of a thing; a limb. [Obs.] Fuller.

outline.c: Outline Out"line` (?), n. 1. (a) The line which marks the outer limits of an object or figure; the exterior line or edge; contour. (b) In art: A line drawn by pencil, pen, graver, or the like, by which the boundary of a figure is indicated. (c) A sketch composed of such lines; the delineation of a figure without shading.
Outline Out"line`, v. t. [imp. & p. p. Outlined (?); p. pr. & vb. n. Outlining.] 1. To draw the outline of.

outlinear.c: Outlinear Out*lin"e*ar (?), a. Of or pertaining to an outline; being in, or forming, an outline. Trench.

outlive.c: Outlive Out*live" (?), v. t. [imp. & p. p. Outlived (?); p. pr. & vb. n. Outliving.] To live beyond, or longer than; to survive.

outlook.c: Outlook Out*look" (?), v. t. 1. To face down; to outstare.
Outlook Out"look`, n. 1. The act of looking out; watch.

outloose.c: Outloose Out"loose` (?), n. A loosing from; an escape; an outlet; an evasion. [Obs.]

outlustre.c: Outlustre Outluster { Out*lus"ter, Out*lus"tre } (?), v. t. To excel in brightness or luster. Shak.

outlying.c: Outlying Out"ly`ing (?), a. Lying or being at a distance from the central part, or the main body; being on, or beyond, the frontier; exterior; remote; detached.

outmanoeuvre.c: Outmanoeuvre Outmaneuver { Out`ma*neu"ver, Out`ma*noeu"vre } (?), v. t. To surpass, or get an advantage of, in maneuvering; to outwit or frustrate by clever stratagems; to outgeneral.

outmantle.c: Outmantle Out*man"tle (?), v. t. To excel in mantling; hence, to excel in splendor, as of dress. [R.]

outmarch.c: Outmarch Out*march" (?), v. t. To surpass in marching; to march faster than, or so as to leave behind.

outmeasure.c: Outmeasure Out*meas"ure (?), v. t. To exceed in measure or extent; to measure more than. Sir T. Browne.

outmost.c: Outmost Out"most` (?), a. [OE. outemest, utmest, AS. ūtemest, a superl. fr. ūte out. See Out, Utmost, and cf. Outermost.] Farthest from the middle or interior; farthest outward; outermost.

outmount.c: Outmount Out*mount" (?), v. t. To mount above. [R.]

outname.c: Outname Out*name" (?), v. t. 1. To exceed in naming or describing. [R.]

outness.c: Outness Out"ness (?), n. 1. The state of being out or beyond; separateness.

outnoise.c: Outnoise Out*noise" (?), v. t. To exceed in noise; to surpass in noisiness. [R.] Fuller.

outnumber.c: Outnumber Out*num"ber (?), v. t. To exceed in number; as, the garrison was badly outnumbered by the attacking forces.

outofdoor.c: Out-of-door Out`-of-door", (?), a. Being out of the house; being, or done, in the open air; suited for the open air; outdoor; as, out-of-door exercise. See Out of door, under Out, adv.

outoftheway.c: Out-of-the-way Out`-of-the-way", a. 1. See under Out, adv.

outpace.c: Outpace Out*pace" (?), v. t. [Cf. Outpass.] 1. To outgo; to move faster than; to leave behind. Lamb.

outparamour.c: Outparamour Out*par"a*mour (?), v. t. To exceed in the number of mistresses. [R.] Shak.

outparish.c: Outparish Out"par`ish (?), n. A parish lying without the walls of, or in a remote part of, a town. Graunt.

outpart.c: Outpart Out"part` (?), n. An outlying part. [R.] Ayliffe.

outpass.c: Outpass Out*pass" (?), v. t. [Cf. Outpace.] To pass beyond; to exceed in progress.

outpassion.c: Outpassion Out*pas"sion (?), v. t. To exceed in passion.

outpatient.c: Out-patient Out"-pa`tient (?), n. 1. A patient who is outside a hospital, but receives medical aid from it.

outpeer.c: Outpeer Out*peer" (?), v. t. To excel. [R.] Shak.

outpension.c: Outpension Out"pen`sion (?), v. t. To grant an outpension to.
Outpension Out"pen`sion, n. A public pension granted to one not required to live in a charitable institution. -- Out"pen`sion*er, n.

outplay.c: Outplay Out*play" (?), v. t. To excel or defeat in a game; to play better than; as, to be outplayed in tennis or ball.

outpoise.c: Outpoise Out*poise" (?), v. t. To outweigh. Howell.

outport.c: Outport Out"port` (?), n. A harbor or port at some distance from the chief town or seat of trade. Macaulay.

outpost.c: Outpost Out"post` (?), n. (Mil.) (a) A post or station without the limits of a camp, or at a distance from the main body of an army, for observation of the enemy. (b) The troops placed at such a station.

outpour.c: Outpour Out*pour" (?), v. t. To pour out. Milton.
outpour out"pour`, n. 1. A flowing out; a free discharge.

outpower.c: outpower out*pow"er (?), v. t. To excel in power; to overpover. [Obs.] Fuller.

outpray.c: Outpray Out*pray" (?), v. t. To exceed or excel in prayer.

outpreach.c: Outpreach Out*preach" (?), v. t. To surpass in preaching.

outprize.c: Outprize Out*prize" (?), v. t. To prize beyong value, or in excess; to exceed in value. [Obs.] Shak.

output.c: Output Out"put` (?), n. 1. The amount or quantity of a material or product that is produced by a mine, factory, or any system for production of commercial goods, such as the amount of coal or ore put out from one or more mines, or the quantity of material produced by, or turned out from, one or more furnaces or mills, in a given time; production.

outquench.c: Outquench Out*quench" (?), v. t. To quench entirely; to extinguish. “The candlelight outquenched.” Spenser.

outrage.c: Outrage Out*rage" (?), v. t. [Out + rage.] To rage in excess of. [R.] Young.

Outrage Out"rage (?), n. [F. outrage; OF. outre, oltre, beyond (F. outre, L. ultra) + -age, as, in courage, voyage. See Ulterior.] 1. Injurious violence or wanton wrong done to persons or things; a gross violation of right or decency; excessive abuse; wanton mischief; gross injury. Chaucer.
Outrage Out"rage (?), v. t. [imp. & p. p. Outragen (?); p. pr. & vb. n. Outraging (?).] [F. outrager. See Outrage, n.]
Outrage Out"rage, v. i. To be guilty of an outrage; to act outrageously.

outrageous.c: Outrageous Out*ra"geous (out*rā"jŭs), a. [OF. outrageus, F. outrageux. See Outrage, n.] Of the nature of an outrage; exceeding the limits of right, reason, or decency; such as to cause outrage; involving or doing an outrage; furious; violent; atrocious. “Outrageous weeping.” Chaucer. “The most outrageous villainies.” Sir P. Sidney. “The vile, outrageous crimes.” Shak. “Outrageous panegyric.” Dryden.

outrance.c: Outrance ‖Ou`trance" (ōo`träNs"), n. [F. See Outré.] The utmost or last extremity.

outrank.c: Outrank Out*rank" (?), v. t. To exceed in rank; hence, to take precedence of.

outray.c: Outray Out*ray" (?), v. t. To outshine. [R.] Skelton.
Outray Out*ray", v. i. To spread out in array. [Obs.]

outraye.c: Outraye Out*raye" (?), v. i. See Outrage, v. i. [Obs.]

outraze.c: Outraze Out*raze" (?), v. t. To obliterate. [Obs.] Sandys.

outre.c: Outre ‖Ou`tré" (?), a. [F., p.p. of outer to exaggerate, fr. L. ultra beyond. See Outrage.] Out of the common course or limits; extravagant{2}; bizarre; outlandish{2}; as, an outré costume.

outreach.c: Outreach Out*reach" (?), v. t. To reach beyond.

outreason.c: Outreason Out*rea"son (?), v. t. To excel or surpass in reasoning; to reason better than. South.

outreckon.c: Outreckon Out*reck"on (?), v. t. To exceed in reckoning or computation. Bp. Pearson.

outrecuidance.c: Outrecuidance ‖Ou`tre*cui`dance" (?), n. [F., fr. outre beyond + cuider to think, L. cogitare.] Excessive presumption. [R.] B. Jonson.

outrede.c: Outrede Out*rede" (?), v. t. To surpass in giving rede, or counsel. [Obs.] See Atrede. Chaucer.

outreign.c: Outreign Out*reign" (?), v. t. To go beyond in reigning; to reign through the whole of, or longer than. [R.] Spenser.

outride.c: Outride Out*ride" (?), v. t. To surpass in speed of riding; to ride beyond or faster than. Shak.
Outride Out"ride`, n. 1. A riding out; an excursion. [R.]

outrider.c: Outrider Out"rid`er (?), n. 1. A summoner whose office is to cite men before the sheriff. [Obs.]

outrigger.c: outrigger out"rig`ger (?), n. 1. Any spar or projecting timber run out for temporary use, as from a ship's mast, to hold a rope or a sail extended, or from a building, to support hoisting teckle.

outright.c: outright out"right` (?), adv. 1. Immediately; without delay; at once; as, he was killed outright.

outring.c: Outring Out*ring" (?), v. t. To excel in volume of ringing sound; to ring louder than.

outrival.c: Outrival Out*ri"val (?), v. t. To surpass in a rivalry.

outrive.c: Outrive Out*rive" (?), v. t. To river; to sever. [Obs.] Fairfax.

outrode.c: Outrode Outroad { Out"road`, Out"rode` } (?), n. An excursion. [Obs.] “Outrodes by the ways of Judea.” Macc. xv. 41 (Geneva Bible).

outroar.c: Outroar Out*roar" (?), v. t. To exceed in roaring.

outromance.c: Outromance Out`ro*mance" (?), v. t. To exceed in romantic character. [R.] Fuller.

outroom.c: Outroom Out"room` (?), n. An outer room. [R.] Fuller.

outroot.c: Outroot Out*root" (?), v. t. 1. To eradicate; to extirpate.

outrun.c: Outrun Out*run" (?), v. t. [imp. Outran (?); p. p. Outrun; p. pr. & vb. n. Outrunning.] To exceed, or leave behind, in running; to run faster than; to outstrip; to go beyond.

outrunner.c: Outrunner Out*run"ner (?), n. An offshoot; a branch. [R.] “Some outrunner of the river.” Lauson.

outrush.c: Outrush Out*rush" (?), v. i. To rush out; to issue, or run out, forcibly. Garth.

outsail.c: Outsail Out*sail" (?), v. t. To excel, or to leave behind, in sailing; to sail faster than. Beau. & Fl.

outscent.c: Outscent Out*scent" (?), v. t. To exceed in odor. Fuller.

outscold.c: Outscold Out*scold" (?), v. t. To exceed in scolding. Shak.

outscorn.c: Outscorn Out*scorn" (?), v. t. To confront, or subdue, with greater scorn. Shak.

outscouring.c: Outscouring Out"scour`ing (?), n. That which is scoured out or washed out. Buckland.

outscout.c: Outscout Out*scout" (?), v. t. To overpower by disdain; to outface. [Obs.] Marston.

outsee.c: Outsee Out*see" (?), v. t. To see beyond; to excel in certainty of seeing; to surpass in foresight.

outsell.c: Outsell Out*sell" (?), v. t. 1. To exceed in amount of sales; to sell more than.

outsentry.c: Outsentry Out"sen`try (?), n. (Mil.) A sentry who guards the entrance or approach to a place; an outguard.

outset.c: Outset Out"set` (?), n. A setting out, starting, or beginning. “The outset of a political journey.” Burke.

outsettler.c: Outsettler Out"set`tler (?), n. One who settles at a distance, or away, from others.

outshine.c: Outshine Out*shine" (?), v. i. To shine forth. “Bright, outshining beams.” Shak.
Outshine Out*shine", v. t. 1. To surpass in splendor, excellence, or achievement.

outshoot.c: Outshoot Out*shoot" (?), v. t. To exceed or excel in shooting; to shoot beyond. Bacon.

outshut.c: Outshut Out*shut" (?), v. t. To shut out. [R.] Donne.

outside.c: Outside Out"side` (?), n. 1. The external part of a thing; the part, end, or side which forms the external surface; that which appears, or is manifest; that which is superficial; the exterior.
Outside Out"side` (?), a. 1. Of or pertaining to the outside; external; exterior; superficial.
Outside Out"side` (?), adv. or prep. On or to the outside (of); without; on the exterior; as, to ride outside the coach; he stayed outside.

outsider.c: Outsider Out`sid"er (?), n. 1. One not belonging to the concern, institution, party, etc., spoken of; one disconnected in interest or feeling. [Recent] A. Trollope.

outsing.c: Outsing Out*sing" (?), v. t. To surpass in singing.

outsit.c: Outsit Out*sit" (?), v. t. To remain sitting, or in session, longer than, or beyond the time of; to outstay.

outskirt.c: Outskirt Out"skirt` (?), n. A part remote from the center, and near the outer edge; border; -- usually in the plural; as, the outskirts of a town. Wordsworth.

outsleep.c: Outsleep Out*sleep" (?), v. t. To exceed in sleeping. Shak.

outslide.c: Outslide Out*slide" (?), v. i. To slide outward, onward, or forward; to advance by sliding. [Poetic]

outsoar.c: Outsoar Out*soar" (?), v. t. To soar beyond or above.

outsole.c: Outsole Out"sole` (?), n. The outside sole of a boot or shoe.

outsound.c: Outsound Out*sound" (?), v. t. To surpass in sounding.

outspan.c: outspan out*span" (?), v. t. & i. [D. uitspannen.] To unyoke or disengage, as oxen from a wagon; to unharness (a horse). [S. Africa]

outsparkle.c: Outsparkle Out*spar"kle (?), v. t. To exceed in sparkling.

outspeak.c: Outspeak Out*speak" (?), v. t. 1. To exceed in speaking.

outspeed.c: Outspeed Out*speed" (?), v. t. To excel in speed.

outspin.c: Outspin Out*spin" (?), v. t. To spin out; to finish.

outspoken.c: Outspoken Out*spo"ken (?), a. Speaking, or spoken, freely, openly, candidly, or boldly; as, an outspoken man; an outspoken rebuke. -- Out*spo"ken*ness, n.

outsport.c: Outsport Out*sport" (?), v. t. To exceed in sporting. [R.] “Not to outsport discretion.” Shak.

outspread.c: Outspread Out*spread" (?), v. t. To spread out; to expand; -- usually as a past part. or adj.

outspring.c: Outspring Out*spring" (?), v. i. To spring out; to issue.

outstand.c: Outstand Out*stand" (?), v. i. To stand out, or project, from a surface or mass; hence, to remain standing out.
Outstand Out*stand", v. t. 1. To resist effectually; to withstand; to sustain without yielding. [R.] Woodward.

outstanding.c: Outstanding Out*stand"ing, a. 1. That stands out; undischarged; uncollected; not paid; as, outstanding obligations.

outstare.c: Outstare Out*stare" (?), v. t. To excel or overcome in staring; to face down.

outstart.c: Outstart Out*start" (?), v. i. To start out or up. Chaucer.

outstay.c: Outstay Out*stay" (?), v. t. To stay beyond or longer than.

outstep.c: Outstep Out*step" (?), v. t. To exceed in stepping.

outstorm.c: Outstorm Out*storm" (?), v. t. To exceed in storming.

outstreet.c: Outstreet Out"street` (?), n. A street remote from the center of a town. Johnson.

outstretch.c: Outstretch Out*stretch" (?), v. t. To stretch out. Milton.

outstride.c: Outstride Out*stride" (?), v. t. To surpass in striding.

outstrike.c: Outstrike Out*strike" (?), v. t. To strike out; to strike faster than. Shak.

outstrip.c: Outstrip Out*strip" (?), v. t. [imp. & p. p. Outstripped (?); p. pr. & vb. n. Outstripping.] 1. To go faster than; to outrun; to advance beyond; to leave behind.

outsuffer.c: Outsuffer Out*suf"fer (?), v. t. To exceed in suffering.

outswear.c: Outswear Out*swear" (?), v. t. To exceed in swearing.

outsweeten.c: Outsweeten Out*sweet"en (?), v. t. To surpass in sweetness. [R.] Shak.

outswell.c: Outswell Out*swell" (?), v. t. 1. To exceed in swelling.

outtake.c: Outtake Out*take" (?), prep. Except. [Obs.] R. of Brunne.

outtaken.c: Outtaken Out*tak"en (?), p. p. or prep. Excepted; save. [Obs.] Wyclif. Chaucer.

outtalk.c: Outtalk Out*talk" (?), v. t. To overpower by talking; to exceed in talking; to talk down. Shak.

outtell.c: Outtell Out*tell" (?), v. t. To surpass in telling, counting, or reckoning. “I have outtold the clock.” Beau. & Fl.

outterm.c: Outterm Out"term` (?), n. An external or superficial thing; outward manner; superficial remark, etc. [Obs.]

outthrow.c: Outthrow Out*throw" (?), v. t. 1. To throw out. Spenser.

outtoil.c: Outtoil Out*toil" (?), v. t. To exceed in toiling.

outtongue.c: Outtongue Out*tongue" (?), v. t. To silence by talk, clamor, or noise. [R.] Shak.

outtravel.c: Outtravel Out*trav"el (?), v. t. To exceed in speed or distance traveled. Mad. D' Arblay.

outvalue.c: Outvalue Out*val"ue (?), v. t. To exceed in value. Boyle.

outvenom.c: Outvenom Out*ven"om (?), v. t. To exceed in venom.

outvie.c: Outvie Out*vie" (?), v. t. To exceed in vying. Dryden.

outvillain.c: Outvillain Out*vil"lain (?), v. t. To exceed in villainy.

outvoice.c: Outvoice Out*voice" (?), v. t. To exceed in noise. Shak.

outvote.c: Outvote Out*vote" (?), v. t. To exceed in the number of votes given; to defeat by votes. South.

outwalk.c: Outwalk Out*walk" (?), v. t. To excel in walking; to leave behind in walking. B. Jonson.

outwall.c: Outwall Out"wall` (?), n. The exterior wall; the outside surface, or appearance. Shak.

outwards.c: Outwards Outward { Out"ward (?), Out"wards (?), } adv. [AS. ūteweard. See Out, and -ward, -wards.] From the interior part; in a direction from the interior toward the exterior; out; to the outside; beyond; off; away; as, a ship bound outward.

outward.c: Outward Out"ward, a. 1. Forming the superficial part; external; exterior; -- opposed to inward; as, an outward garment or layer.

outwatch.c: Outwatch Out*watch" (?), v. t. To exceed in watching.

outway.c: Outway Out"way` (?), n. A way out; exit. [R.]

outwear.c: Outwear Out*wear" (?), v. t. 1. To wear out; to consume or destroy by wearing. Milton.

outweary.c: Outweary Out*wea"ry (?), v. t. To weary out. Cowley.

outweed.c: Outweed Out*weed" (?), v. t. To weed out. [Obs.]

outweep.c: Outweep Out*weep" (?), v. t. To exceed in weeping.

outweigh.c: Outweigh Out*weigh" (?), v. t. To exceed in weight or value.

outwell.c: Outwell Out*well" (?), v. t. To pour out. [Obs.] Spenser.
Outwell Out*well", v. i. To issue forth. Thomson.

outwhore.c: Outwhore Out*whore" (?), v. t. To exceed in lewdness.

outwin.c: Outwin Out*win" (?), v. t. To win a way out of. [Obs.]

outwind.c: Outwind Out*wind" (?), v. t. To extricate by winding; to unloose. [R.] Spenser. Dr. H. More.

outwing.c: Outwing Out*wing" (?), v. t. To surpass, exceed, or outstrip in flying. Garth.

outwit.c: Outwit Out*wit" (?), v. t. 1. To surpass in wisdom, esp. in cunning.
Outwit Out"wit (?), n. The faculty of acquiring wisdom by observation and experience, or the wisdom so acquired; -- opposed to inwit. [Obs.] Piers Plowman.

outwoe.c: Outwoe Out*woe" (?), v. t. To exceed in woe. [Obs.]

outwork.c: Outwork Out*work" (?), v. t. To exceed in working; to work more or faster than.
Outwork Out"work` (?), n. (Fort.) A minor defense constructed beyond the main body of a work, as a ravelin, lunette, hornwork, etc. Wilhelm.

outworth.c: Outworth Out*worth" (?), v. t. To exceed in worth. [R.]

outwrest.c: Outwrest Out*wrest" (?), v. t. To extort; to draw from or forth by violence. [Obs.] Spenser.

outwrite.c: Outwrite Out*write" (?), v. t. To exceed or excel in writing.

outzany.c: Outzany Out*za"ny (?), v. t. To exceed in buffoonery. [Obs.] B. Jonson.

ouvarovite.c: Ouvarovite Ou*va"ro*vite (?), n. [Named from the Russian Count Uvaroff.] (Min.) Chrome garnet.

oval.c: Oval O"val (?), a. [F. ovale, fr. L. ovum egg. Cf. Egg, Ovum.] 1. Of or pertaining to eggs; done in the egg, or inception; as, oval conceptions. [Obs.]
Oval O"val, n. A body or figure in the shape of an egg, or popularly, of an ellipse.

ovalbumen.c: Ovalbumen Ovalbumin { O`val*bu"min (ō`văl*bū"mĭn), O`val*bu"men (ō`văl*bū"mĕn), } n. [Ovum + albumin.] (Physiol. Chem.) The albumin from white of eggs; egg albumin; -- in distinction from serum albumin. See Albumin.

ovaliform.c: Ovaliform O*val"i*form (o`văl"ĭ*fôrm), a. [Oval + -form.] Having the form of an egg; having a figure such that any section in the direction of the shorter diameter will be circular, and any in the direction of the longer diameter will be oval.

ovally.c: Ovally O"val*ly (?), adv. In an oval form.

ovant.c: Ovant O"vant (?), a. [L. ovans triumphant, p. pr. of ovare to exult.] Exultant. [Obs.] Holland.

ovarial.c: Ovarial Ovarian { O*va"ri*an (?), O*va"ri*al (?), } a. Of or pertaining to an ovary.

ovariole.c: Ovariole O*va"ri*ole (?), n. (Zool.) One of the tubes of which the ovaries of most insects are composed.

ovariotomist.c: Ovariotomist O*va`ri*ot"o*mist (?), n. One who performs, or is skilled in, ovariotomy.

ovariotomy.c: Ovariotomy O*va`ri*ot"o*my (?), n. [Ovarium + Gr. te`mnein to cut.] (Surg.) The operation of removing one or both of the ovaries; oophorectomy.

ovarious.c: Ovarious O*va"ri*ous (?), a. Consisting of eggs; as, ovarious food. [R.] Thomson.

ovaritis.c: Ovaritis ‖O`va*ri"tis (?), n. [NL. See Ovarium, and -itis.] (Med.) Inflammation of the ovaries.

ovarium.c: Ovarium ‖O*va"ri*um (?), n.; pl. L. Ovaria (#), E. Ovariums (#). [NL.] An ovary. See Ovary.

ovary.c: Ovary O"va*ry (ō"vȧ*ry̆), n.; pl. Ovaries (ō"vȧ*rĭz). [NL. ovarium, fr. L. ovum egg: cf. F. ovaire. See Oval.] 1. (Bot.) That part of the pistil which contains the seed, and in most flowering plants develops into the fruit. See Illust. of Flower.

ovate.c: Ovate O"vate (?), a. [L. ovatus, from ovum egg. See Oval.]

ovateacuminate.c: Ovate-acuminate O"vate-a*cu"mi*nate (?), a. Having an ovate form, but narrowed at the end into a slender point.

ovatecylindraceous.c: Ovate-cylindraceous O"vate-cyl`in*dra"ceous (?), a. Having a form intermediate between ovate and cylindraceous.

ovatelanceolate.c: Ovate-lanceolate O"vate-lan"ce*o*late (?), a. Having a form intermediate between ovate and lanceolate.

ovateoblong.c: Ovate-oblong O"vate-ob"long (?), a. Oblong, with one end narrower than the other; ovato-oblong.

ovaterotundate.c: Ovate-rotundate O"vate-ro*tund"ate (?), a. Having a form intermediate between that of an egg and a sphere; roundly ovate.

ovatesubulate.c: Ovate-subulate O"vate-su"bu*late (?), a. Having an ovate form, but with a subulate tip or extremity.

ovation.c: Ovation O*va"tion (?), n. [L. ovatio, fr. ovare to exult, rejoice, triumph in an ovation; cf. Gr.? to shout: cf. F. ovation.] 1. (Rom. Antiq.) A lesser kind of triumph allowed to a commander for an easy, bloodless victory, or a victory over slaves.

oven.c: Oven Ov"en (ŭv"'n), n. [AS. ofen; akin to D. oven, OHG. ofan, ovan, G. ofen, Icel. ofn, Dan. ovn, Sw. ugn, Goth. aúhns, Gr. 'ipno`s, Skr. ukhā pot.] A place arched over with brick or stonework, and used for baking, heating, or drying; hence, any structure, whether fixed or portable, which may be heated for baking, drying, etc.; esp., now, a chamber in a stove, used for baking or roasting.

ovenbird.c: Ovenbird Ov"en*bird` (?), n. (Zool.) (a) Any species of the genus Furnarius, allied to the creepers. They inhabit South America and the West Indies, and construct curious oven-shaped nests. (b) In the United States, Seiurus aurocapillus; -- called also golden-crowned thrush. (c) In England, sometimes applied to the willow warbler, and to the long-tailed titmouse.

over.c: Over O"ver (ō"vẽr), prep. [AS. ofer; akin to D. over, G. über, OHG. ubir, ubar, Dan. over, Sw. öfver, Icel. yfir, Goth. ufar, L. super, Gr. "ype`r, Skr. upari. √199. Cf. Above, Eaves, Hyper-, Orlop, Super-, Sovereign, Up.] 1. Above, or higher than, in place or position, with the idea of covering; -- opposed to under; as, clouds are over our heads; the smoke rises over the city.
Over O"ver (?), adv. 1. From one side to another; from side to side; across; crosswise; as, a board, or a tree, a foot over, i. e., a foot in diameter.
Over O"ver, a. 1. Upper; covering; higher; superior; -- chiefly used in composition; as, overshoes, overcoat, over-garment, overlord.

Over O"ver, n. (Cricket) A certain number of balls (usually four) delivered successively from behind one wicket, after which the ball is bowled from behind the other wicket as many times, the fielders changing places.

overabound.c: Overabound O`ver*a*bound" (?), v. i. To be exceedingly plenty or superabundant. Pope.

overact.c: Overact O`ver*act" (?), v. t. 1. To act or perform to excess; to exaggerate in acting; as, he overacted his part.
Overact O`ver*act" (?), v. i. To act more than is necessary; to go to excess in action. B. Jonson.

overaction.c: Overaction O"ver*ac"tion (?), n. Performance to excess; exaggerated or excessive action.

overaffect.c: Overaffect O`ver*af*fect" (?), v. t. To affect or care for unduly. [Obs.] Milton.

overagitate.c: Overagitate O`ver*ag"i*tate (?), v. t. To agitate or discuss beyond what is expedient. Bp. Hall.

overalls.c: Overalls O"ver*alls (?), n. pl. 1. A kind of loose trousers worn over others to protect them from soiling.

overanxiety.c: Overanxiety O"ver*anx*i"e*ty (?), n. The state of being overanxious; excessive anxiety.

overanxious.c: Overanxious O"ver*anx"ious (?), a. Anxious in an excessive or needless degree. -- O"ver*anx"ious*ly, adv.

overarch.c: Overarch O`ver*arch" (?), v. t. & i. To make or place an arch over; to hang over like an arch. “Brown with o'erarching shades.” Pope.

overarm.c: Over-arm O"ver-arm` (?), a. (Cricket, etc.) Done (as bowling or pitching) with the arm raised above the shoulder. See Overhard. “An over-arm with a round-arm bowler.” R. A. Proctor.

overawe.c: Overawe O`ver*awe" (?), v. t. [imp. & p. p. Overawed (?); p. pr. & vb. n. Overawing.] To awe exceedingly; to intimidate or subjugate or restrain by awe or great fear.

overawful.c: Overawful O"ver*aw"ful (?), a. Awful, or reverential, in an excessive degree. [R.] Milton.

overbalance.c: Overbalance O`ver*bal"ance (?), v. t. 1. To exceed equality with; to outweigh. Locke.
Overbalance O"ver*bal`ance (?), n. Excess of weight or value; something more than an equivalent; as, an overbalance of exports. J. Edwards.

overbattle.c: Overbattle O"ver*bat"tle (?), a. [Over + battle, a.] Excessively fertile; bearing rank or noxious growths. [Obs.] “Overbattle grounds.” Hooker.

overbear.c: Overbear O`ver*bear" (?), v. t. 1. To bear down or carry down, as by excess of weight, power, force, etc.; to overcome; to suppress.
Overbear O`ver*bear", v. i. To bear fruit or offspring to excess; to be too prolific.

overbearing.c: Overbearing O`ver*bear"ing, a. 1. Overpowering; subduing; repressing. I. Watts.

overbend.c: Overbend O`ver*bend" (?), v. t. To bend to excess.
Overbend O`ver*bend", v. i. To bend over. [R.]

overbid.c: Overbid O`ver*bid" (?), v. t. To bid or offer beyond, or in excess of. Dryden.

overbide.c: Overbide O`ver*bide" (?), v. t. To outlive. [Obs.] Chaucer.

overblow.c: Overblow O`ver*blow" (?), v. i. 1. To blow over, or be subdued. [R.] Spenser.
Overblow O`ver*blow", v. t. 1. To blow away; to dissipate by wind, or as by wind.

overboard.c: Overboard O"ver*board` (?), adv. Over the side of a ship; hence, from on board of a ship, into the water; as, to fall overboard.

overboil.c: Overboil O`ver*boil" (?), v. i. To boil over or unduly.

overbold.c: Overbold O`ver*bold" (?), a. Excessively or presumptuously bold; impudent. Shak. -- O"ver*bold"ly, adv.

overbow.c: Overbow O`ver*bow" (?), v. t. To bend or bow over; to bend in a contrary direction. [Obs.] Fuller.

overbreed.c: Overbreed O`ver*breed" (?), v. t. To breed to excess; as, the bulls were so huge and overbred no matador wanted to fight them.

overbrim.c: Overbrim O`ver*brim" (?), v. i. To flow over the brim; to be so full as to overflow. [R.]

overbrow.c: Overbrow O`ver*brow" (?), v. t. To hang over like a brow; to impend over. [Poetic] Longfellow.

overbuild.c: Overbuild O`ver*build" (?), v. t. 1. To build over. Milton.

overbuilt.c: Overbuilt O`ver*built" (?), a. Having too many buildings; as, an overbuilt part of a town.

overbulk.c: Overbulk O`ver*bulk" (?), v. t. To oppress by bulk; to overtower. [Obs. & R.] Shak.

overburden.c: Overburden O`ver*bur"den (?), v. t. To load with too great weight or too much care, etc. Sir P. Sidney.
Overburden O"ver*bur`den, n. The waste which overlies good stone in a quarry. Raymond.

overburn.c: Overburn O`ver*burn" (?), v. t. & i. To burn too much; to be overzealous.

overbuy.c: Overbuy O`ver*buy" (?), v. t. 1. To buy too much.

overcanopy.c: Overcanopy O`ver*can"o*py (?), v. t. To cover as with a canopy. Shak.

overcarking.c: Overcarking O"ver*cark"ing (ō"vẽr*kärk"ĭng), a. Too anxious; too full of care. [Archaic] Fuller.

overcarry.c: Overcarry O`ver*car"ry (ō"vẽr*kăr"ry̆), v. t. & i. To carry too far; to carry beyond the proper point. Hayward.

overcast.c: Overcast O`ver*cast" (ō`vẽr*kȧst"), v. t. 1. To cast or cover over; hence, to cloud; to darken.

overcautious.c: Overcautious O"ver*cau"tious (?), a. Too cautious; cautious or prudent to excess. -- O"ver*cau"tious*ly, adv. -- O"ver*cau"tious*ness, n.

overchange.c: Overchange O"ver*change` (?), n. Too much or too frequent change; fickleness. [R.] Beau. & Fl.

overcharge.c: Overcharge O`ver*charge", v. i. To make excessive charges.

overclimb.c: Overclimb O`ver*climb" (?), v. t. To climb over. Surrey.

overcloud.c: Overcloud O`ver*cloud" (?), v. t. To cover or overspread with clouds; to becloud; to overcast.

overcloy.c: Overcloy O`ver*cloy" (?), v. t. To fill beyond satiety. Shak.

overcoat.c: overcoat o"ver*coat` (?), n. [Cf. Surcoat.] A coat worn over the other clothing; a greatcoat; a topcoat.

overcold.c: Overcold O"ver*cold" (?), a. Cold to excess. Wiseman.

overcolor.c: Overcolor O`ver*col"or (?), v. t. To color too highly.

overcome.c: Overcome O`ver*come" (?), v. t. [imp. Overcame (?); p. p. Overcome; p. pr & vb. n. Overcoming.] [AS. ofercuman. See Over, Come, and cf. Supervene.]
Overcome O`ver*come", v. i. To gain the superiority; to be victorious. Rev. iii. 21.

overcoming.c: Overcoming O`ver*com"ing (?), a. Conquering; subduing. -- O`ver*com"ing*ly, adv.

overconfidence.c: Overconfidence O"ver*con"fi*dence (?), n. Excessive confidence; too great reliance or trust.

overconfident.c: Overconfident O"ver*con"fi*dent (?), a. Confident to excess. -- O"ver*con"fi*dent*ly, adv.

overcount.c: overcount o`ver*count" (?), v. t. 1. To rate too high. Shak.

overcover.c: Overcover O`ver*cov"er (?), v. t. To cover up. Shak.

overcrow.c: overcrow o`ver*crow" (?), v. t. To crow, exult, or boast, over; to overpower. Spenser. Shak.

overcrowd.c: Overcrowd O`ver*crowd" (?), v. t. To crowd too much.

overcunning.c: Overcunning O"ver*cun"ning (?), a. Exceedingly or excessively cunning.

overdare.c: Overdare O`ver*dare" (?), v. t. & i. To dare too much or rashly; to be too daring.

overdate.c: Overdate O`ver*date" (?), v. t. To date later than the true or proper period; to postdate. Milton.

overdevelop.c: Overdevelop O`ver*de*vel"op (?), v. t. To develop excessively; specif. (Photog.), to subject (a plate or film) too long to the developing process.

overdo.c: Overdo O`ver*do" (?), v. t. [imp. Overdid (?); p. p. Overdone (?); p. pr. & vb. n. Overdoing.] 1. To do too much; to exceed what is proper or true in doing; to exaggerate; to carry too far.
Overdo O`ver*do", v. i. To labor too hard; to do too much.

overdose.c: Overdose O`ver*dose" (?), v. t. To dose to excess; to give an overdose, or too many doses, to.
Overdose O"ver*dose`, n. Too great a dose; an excessive dose.

overdraft.c: Overdraft O"ver*draft` (?), n. (Banking) The act of overdrawing; a draft in excess of the credit balance; also, the amount or sum overdrawn.

overdraw.c: Overdraw O`ver*draw" (?), v. t. [imp. Overdrew (?); p. p. Overdrawn (?); p. pr. & vb. n. Overdrawing.] 1. To exaggerate; to overdo.

overdress.c: overdress o`ver*dress" (?), v. t. To dress or adorn to excess; to dress too much; to dress too formally for an informal occasion. Pope.

overdrink.c: Overdrink O`ver*drink" (?), v. t. & i. To drink to excess.

overdrive.c: Overdrive O`ver*drive" (?), v. t. & i. To drive too hard, or far, or beyond strength.

overdrown.c: Overdrown O`ver*drown" (?), v. t. To wet or drench to excess. [Obs.] W. Browne.

overdry.c: Overdry O`ver*dry" (?), v. t. To dry too much. Burton.

overdue.c: overdue o"ver*due" (?), a. Due and more than due; delayed beyond the proper time of arrival, payment, return, etc.; as, an overdue vessel; an overdue note; a book overdue at the library; an overdue payment.

overdye.c: Overdye O`ver*dye" (?), v. t. To dye with excess of color; to put one color over (another). Shak.

overeager.c: Overeager O`ver*ea"ger (?), a. Too eager; too impatient. -- O`ver*ea"ger*ly, adv. -- O"ver*ea"ger*ness, n.

overearnest.c: Overearnest O`ver*ear"nest (?), a. Too earnest. -- O"ver*ear"nest*ly, adv. -- O"ver*ear"nest*ness, n.

overeat.c: Overeat O`ver*eat" (?), v. t. & i. 1. To gnaw all over, or on all sides. [Obs.] Shak.

overempty.c: Overempty O`ver*emp"ty (?), v. t. To make too empty; to exhaust. [R.] Carew.

overest.c: Overest O"ver*est (?), a. [Superl. of Over.] Uppermost; outermost.

overestimate.c: Overestimate O`ver*es"ti*mate (?), v. t. 1. To estimate too highly.
Overestimate O`ver*es"ti*mate (?), n. An estimate that is too high; as, an overestimate of the vote.

overexcite.c: Overexcite O`ver*ex*cite" (?), v. t. To excite too much.

overexcitement.c: Overexcitement O"ver*ex*cite"ment (?), n. Excess of excitement; the state of being overexcited.

overexert.c: Overexert O`ver*ex*ert" (?), v. t. To exert too much.

overexertion.c: Overexertion O"ver*ex*er"tion (?), n. Excessive exertion; as, he strained his back from overexertion.

overexpose.c: Overexpose O`ver*ex*pose" (?), v. t. To expose excessively; specif. (Photog.), to subject (a plate or film) too long to the light used in producing a picture. -- O`ver*ex*po"sure (#), n.

overexquisite.c: Overexquisite O"ver*ex"qui*site (?), a. Too exquisite; too exact or nice; too careful.

overeye.c: Overeye O`ver*eye" (?), v. t. 1. To superintend; to oversee; to inspect. [Obs.]

overfall.c: Overfall O"ver*fall` (?), n. 1. A cataract; a waterfall. [Obs.]

overfatigue.c: Overfatigue O`ver*fa*tigue", v. t. To fatigue to excess; to tire out.

overfeed.c: Overfeed O`ver*feed" (?), v. t. & i. [imp. & p. p. Overfed (?); p. pr. & vb. n. Overfeeding.] To feed to excess; to surfeit.

overfill.c: overfill o`ver*fill" (?), v. t. To fill to excess; to surcharge.

overfish.c: Overfish O`ver*fish" (?), v. t. 1. To fish to excess.

overfloat.c: Overfloat O`ver*float" (?), v. t. To overflow. [R.] Dryden.

overflourish.c: Overflourish O`ver*flour"ish (?), v. t. 1. To make excessive display or flourish of. Collier.

overflow.c: Overflow O`ver*flow" (?), v. t. [imp. & p. p. Overflowed (?); p. pr. & vb. n. Overflowing.] [AS. oferfl?wan. See Over, and Flow.] 1. To flow over; to cover woth, or as with, water or other fluid; to spread over; to inundate; to overwhelm.
Overflow O`ver*flow", v. i. 1. To run over the bounds.
Overflow O"ver*flow` (?), n. 1. A flowing over, as of water or other fluid; an inundation. Bacon.

overflowing.c: Overflowing O`ver*flow"ing (?), n. An overflow; that which overflows; exuberance; copiousness.

overflowingly.c: Overflowingly O`ver*flow"ing*ly, adv. In great abundance; exuberantly. Boyle.

overflush.c: Overflush O`ver*flush" (?), v. t. To flush to excess. [R.]

overflutter.c: Overflutter O`ver*flut"ter (?), v. t. To flutter over.

overfly.c: Overfly O`ver*fly" (?), v. t. [imp. Overflew (?); p. p. Overflown (?); p. pr. & vb. n. Overflying.] To cross or pass over by flight. Byron.

overfond.c: Overfond O"ver*fond" (?), a. Fond to excess. Milton.

overforward.c: Overforward O"ver*for"ward (?), a. Forward to excess; too forward. -- O"ver*for"ward*ness, n.

overfree.c: Overfree O"ver*free" (?), a. Free to excess; too liberal; too familiar. -- O"ver*free"ly, adv.

overfreight.c: Overfreight O`ver*freight" (?), v. t. [imp. & p. p. Overfreighted (Overfraught (?), obs.); p. pr. & vb. n. Overfreighting.] To put too much freight in or upon; to load too full, or too heavily; to overload.

overfrieze.c: Overfrieze O`ver*frieze" (?), v. t. To cover with a frieze, or as with a frieze. E. Hall.

overfront.c: Overfront O`ver*front" (?), v. t. To confront; to oppose; to withstand. [Obs.] Milton.

overfull.c: Overfull O"ver*full" (?), a. [AS. oferfull.] Too full; filled to overflowing; excessively full; surfeited. Shak.

overfullness.c: Overfullness O"ver*full"ness, n. The state of being excessively or abnormally full, so as to cause overflow, distention, or congestion; excess of fullness; surfeit.

overgarrison.c: Overgarrison O`ver*gar"ri*son (?), v. t. To garrison to excess.

overgaze.c: Overgaze O`ver*gaze" (?), v. t. To gaze; to overlook. [Poetic] “Earth's o'ergazing mountains.” Byron.

overget.c: Overget O`ver*get" (?), v. t. 1. To reach; to overtake; to pass. [Obs.]

overgild.c: Overgild O`ver*gild" (?), v. t. [AS. ofergyldan.] To gild over; to varnish.

overgird.c: Overgird O`ver*gird" (?), v. t. To gird too closely. [R.]

overgive.c: Overgive O`ver*give" (?), v. t. To give over; to surrender; to yield. [Obs.] Spenser.

overglad.c: Overglad O"ver*glad" (?), a. Excessively or unduly glad.

overglance.c: Overglance O`ver*glance" (?), v. t. To glance over.

overglaze.c: Overglaze O"ver*glaze` (?), a. (Ceramics) (a) Applied over the glaze; -- said of enamel paintings, which sometimes are seen to project from the surface of the ware. (b) Suitable for applying upon the glaze; -- said of vitrifiable colors used in ceramic decoration.

overglide.c: Overglide O`ver*glide" (?), v. t. To glide over. Wyatt.

overgloom.c: Overgloom O`ver*gloom" (?), v. t. To spread gloom over; to make gloomy; to overshadow. [R.]

overgo.c: Overgo O`ver*go" (?), v. t. [imp. Overwent (?); p. p. Overgone (?); p. pr. & vb. n. Overgoing.] [AS. ofergān.]

overgorge.c: Overgorge O`ver*gorge" (?), v. t. To gorge to excess.

overgrace.c: Overgrace O`ver*grace" (?), v. t. To grace or honor exceedingly or beyond desert. [R.] Beau. & Fl.

overgrassed.c: Overgrassed O"ver*grassed" (?), a. Overstocked, or overgrown, or covered, with grass. [Obs.] Spenser.

overground.c: Overground O"ver*ground" (?), a. Situated over or above ground; as, the overground portion of a plant.

overgrow.c: Overgrow O`ver*grow" (?), v. t. [imp. Overgrew (?); p. p. Overgrown (?); p. pr. & vb. n. Overgrowing.]
Overgrow O`ver*grow", v. i. To grow beyond the fit or natural size; to grow too large; as, a huge, overgrown ox. L'Estrange.

overhand.c: Overhand O"ver*hand` (?), n. 1. The upper hand; advantage; superiority; mastery.
Overhand O"ver*hand`, a. 1. (Sewing) Over and over; -- applied to a style of sewing, or to a seam, in which two edges, usually selvedges, are sewed together by passing each stitch over both.
Overhand O"ver*hand`, adv. In an overhand manner or style.

overhandle.c: Overhandle O`ver*han"dle (?), v. t. To handle, or use, too much; to mention too often. Shak.

overhang.c: Overhang O`ver*hang" (?), v. t. [imp. & p. p. Overhung (?); p. pr. & vb. n. Overhanging.] 1. To impend or hang over. [R.] Beau. & Fl.
Overhang O`ver*hang", v. i. To jut over. Milton.
Overhang O`ver*hang`, n. (Arch.) 1. In a general sense, that which just out or projects; a projection; also, the measure of the projection; as, the overhang is five feet.

overharden.c: Overharden O`ver*hard"en (?), v. t. To harden too much; to make too hard. Boyle.

overhasty.c: Overhasty O"ver*has"ty (?), a. Too hasty; precipitate; rash. -- O"ver*has"ti*ly (#), adv. -- O`ver*has"ti*ness, n.

overhaul.c: Overhaul O`ver*haul" (?), v. t. [imp. & p. p. Overhauled (?); p. pr. & vb. n. Overhauling.] 1. To haul or drag over; hence, to turn over for examination; to inspect; to examine thoroughly with a view to corrections or repairs.

overhauling.c: Overhauling Overhaul { O"ver*haul` (?), O`ver*haul"ing, } n. 1. A strict examination with a view to correction or repairs.

overhead.c: Overhead O`ver*head" (?), adv. Aloft; above; in or attached to the ceiling or roof; in the story or upon the floor above; in the zenith.

Overhead expenses Overhead charges { O`ver*head" char"ges, O`ver*head" expenses, etc. } (Accounting) Those general charges or expenses in any business which cannot be charged up as belonging exclusively to any particular part of the work or product, as where different kinds of goods are made, or where there are different departments in a business; -- called also fixed charges, establishment charges, or (in a manufacturing business) administration charges, selling charges, and distribution charges, etc.

overhear.c: Overhear O`ver*hear" (?), v. t. [imp. & p. p. Overheard (?); p. pr. & vb. n. Overhearing.] [AS. oferhiéran.]

overheat.c: Overheat O`ver*heat" (?), v. t. [Cf. Superheat.] To heat to excess; to superheat. Cowper.

overhele.c: Overhele O`ver*hele" (?), v. t. [AS. oferhelian.] To hele or cover over. [Obs.] B. Jonson.

overhent.c: Overhent O`ver*hent", v. t. [See Hent.] To overtake. [Obs.]

overhighly.c: Overhighly O"ver*high"ly, adv. Too highly; too greatly.

overhip.c: Overhip O`ver*hip" (?), v. t. [imp. & p. p. Overhipped (?); p. pr. & vb. n. Overhipping.] [Over + a word akin to E. hop to skip.] To pass over by, or as by a hop; to skip over; hence, to overpass. [Obs.] “When the time is overhipt.” Holland.

overhold.c: Overhold O`ver*hold" (ō"vẽr*hōld`), v. t. To hold or value too highly; to estimate at too dear a rate. [Obs.] Shak.

overhung.c: Overhung O"ver*hung" (?), a. 1. Covered over; ornamented with hangings. Carlyle.

overinfluence.c: Overinfluence O`ver*in"flu*ence (?), v. t. To influence in an excessive degree; to have undue influence over.

overinform.c: Overinform O`ver*in*form" (?), v. t. To inform, fill, or animate, excessively. [R.] Johnson.

overissue.c: Overissue O"ver*is"sue (?), n. An excessive issue; an issue, as of notes or bonds, exceeding the limit of capital, credit, or authority.
Overissue O`ver*is"sue, v. t. To issue in excess.

overjealous.c: Overjealous O`ver*jeal"ous (?), a. [Over + jealous. Cf. Overzealous.] Excessively jealous; too jealous.

overjoy.c: Overjoy O`ver*joy" (?), v. t. To make excessively joyful; to gratify extremely.

overjump.c: Overjump O`ver*jump" (?), v. t. To jump over; hence, to omit; to ignore. Marston.

overking.c: Overking O"ver*king` (?), n. A king who has sovereignty over inferior kings or ruling princes. J. R. Green.

overknowing.c: Overknowing O"ver*know"ing (?), a. Too knowing or too cunning.

overlabor.c: Overlabor O`ver*la"bor (?), v. t. [imp. & p. p. Overlabored (?); p. pr. & vb. n. Overlaboring.]

overlade.c: Overlade O`ver*lade" (?), v. t. [imp. Overladed; p. p. Overladen (?); p. pr. & vb. n. Overlading.] [Cf. Overload.] To load with too great a cargo; to overburden; to overload. Spenser.

overland.c: Overland O"ver*land` (?), a. Being, or accomplished, over the land, instead of by sea; as, an overland journey.
Overland O"ver*land`, adv. By, upon, or across, land.

overlander.c: Overlander O"ver*land`er (?), n. One who travels over lands or countries; one who travels overland.

overlanguaged.c: Overlanguaged O"ver*lan"guaged (?), a. Employing too many words; diffuse. Lowell.

overlap.c: Overlap O`ver*lap" (?), v. t. 1. To lay (one thing) over another; to lap.
Overlap O"ver*lap` (?), n. 1. The lapping of one thing over another; as, an overlap of six inches; an overlap of a slate on a roof.

overlarge.c: Overlarge O"ver*large" (?), a. Too large; too great.

overlargeness.c: Overlargeness O"ver*large"ness, n. Excess of size or bulk.

overlash.c: Overlash O`ver*lash" (?), v. i. [Cf. Prov. E. lash extravagant, lashing lavish.] To drive on rashly; to go to excess; hence, to exaggerate; to boast. [Obs.] Barrow.

overlate.c: Overlate O"ver*late" (?), a. Too late; exceedingly late.

overlave.c: Overlave O`ver*lave" (?), v. t. To lave or bathe over.

overlay.c: Overlay O`ver*lay" (?), v. t. [imp. & p. p. Overlaid (?); p. pr. & vb. n. Overlaying.] 1. To lay, or spread, something over or across; hence, to cover; to overwhelm; to press excessively upon.
Overlay O"ver*lay` (?), n. 1. A covering. Sir W. Scott.

overlayer.c: Overlayer O"ver*lay"er (?), n. One who overlays; that with which anything is overlaid.

overlaying.c: Overlaying O"ver*lay"ing, n. A superficial covering; a coating.

overlead.c: Overlead O`ver*lead" (?), v. t. To domineer over; to affront; to treat with indignity. [Obs.] Chaucer.

overleap.c: Overleap O`ver*leap" (?), v. t. [AS. oferhleápan. See Over, and Leap.] To leap over or across; hence, to omit; to ignore. “Let me o'erleap that custom.” Shak.

overlearned.c: Overlearned O"ver*learn"ed (?), a. Too learned. -- O"ver*learn"ed, adv. -- O"ver*learn"ed*ness, n.

overleaven.c: Overleaven O`ver*leav"en (?), v. t. To leaven too much; hence, to change excessively; to spoil. [Obs.]

overliberally.c: Overliberally O"ver*lib"er*al*ly, adv. In an overliberal manner.

overlick.c: Overlick O`ver*lick" (?), v. t. To lick over.

overlie.c: Overlie O`ver*lie" (?), v. t. [imp. Overlay (?); p. p. Overlain (?); p. pr. & vb. n. Overlying.] To lie over or upon; specifically, to suffocate by lying upon; as, to overlie an infant. Quain.

overlight.c: Overlight O"ver*light` (?), n. Too strong a light. Bacon.
Overlight O"ver*light", a. Too light or frivolous; giddy.

overliness.c: Overliness O"ver*li*ness (?), n. The quality or state of being overly; carelessness. [Obs.] Bp. Hall.

overlinger.c: Overlinger O"ver*lin"ger (?), v. t. To cause to linger; to detain too long. [Obs.] Fuller.

overlip.c: Overlip O"ver*lip` (?), n. [AS. oferlibban.] The upper lip. [Obs.] Chaucer.

overlive.c: Overlive O`ver*live" (?), v. t. To outlive. Sir P. Sidney.
Overlive O`ver*live" (?), v. i. To live too long, too luxuriously, or too actively. Milton. “Overlived in this close London life.” Mrs. Browning.

overload.c: Overload O`ver*load" (?), v. t. [imp. & p. p. Overloaded; p. pr. & vb. n. Overloading.] [Cf. Overlade.] To load or fill to excess; to load too heavily.
Overload O"ver*load` (?), n. An excessive load; the excess beyond a proper load.

overlogical.c: Overlogical O"ver*log"ic*al (?), a. Excessively logical; adhering too closely to the forms or rules of logic.

overlong.c: Overlong O"ver*long" (?), a. & adv. Too long. Shak.

overlook.c: Overlook O`ver*look" (?), v. t. [imp. & p. p. Overlooked (?); p. pr. & vb. n. Overlooking.] 1. To look down upon from a place that is over or above; to look over or view from a higher position; to be situated above, so as to command a view of; as, to overlook a valley from a hill; a hotel room that overlooks the marketplace. “The pile o'erlooked the town.” Dryden.

overlord.c: Overlord O"ver*lord` (?), n. One who is lord over another or others; a superior lord; a master. Freeman.

overlordship.c: Overlordship O"ver*lord"ship (?), n. Lordship or supremacy of a person or a people over others. J. R. Green.

overlove.c: Overlove O`ver*love" (?), v. t. To love to excess.

overlusty.c: Overlusty O"ver*lust"y (?), a. Too lusty, or lively. Shak.

overly.c: Overly O"ver*ly, a. 1. Careless; negligent; inattentive; superfical; not thorough. [Archaic] Bp. Hall.
overly o"ver*ly, adv. 1. In an overly manner. [Archaic]

overlying.c: Overlying O`ver*ly"ing (?), a. Lying over or upon something; as, overlying rocks.

overmagnify.c: Overmagnify O`ver*mag"ni*fy (?), v. t. To magnify too much. Bp. Hall.

overmalapert.c: Overmalapert O"ver*mal"a*pert (?), a. Excessively malapert or impudent. [Obs.] Prynne.

overman.c: Overman O"ver*man (?), n.; pl. -men (?). 1. One in authority over others; a chief; usually, an overseer or boss.

overmanner.c: Overmanner O"ver*man`ner (?), adv. In an excessive manner; excessively. [Obs.] Wiclif.

overmarch.c: Overmarch O`ver*march" (?), v. t. & i. To march too far, or too much; to exhaust by marching. Baker.

overmast.c: Overmast O`ver*mast" (?), v. t. (Naut.) To furnish (a vessel) with too long or too heavy a mast or masts.

overmaster.c: Overmaster O`ver*mas"ter (?), v. t. To overpower; to subdue; to vanquish; to govern.

overmatch.c: Overmatch O`ver*match" (?), v. t. 1. To be more than equal to or a match for; hence, to vanquish. Drayton.
Overmatch O"ver*match` (?), n. One superior in power; also, an unequal match; a contest in which one of the opponents is overmatched. Milton. D. Webster.

overmeasure.c: Overmeasure O`ver*meas"ure (?), v. t. To measure or estimate too largely.
Overmeasure O"ver*meas`ure (?), n. Excessive measure; the excess beyond true or proper measure; surplus.

overmeddle.c: Overmeddle O`ver*med"dle (?), v. t. To meddle unduly.

overmeddling.c: Overmeddling O`ver*med"dling (?), n. Excessive interference. “Justly shent for their overmeddling.” Fuller.

overmickle.c: Overmickle O"ver*mic"kle (?), a. & adv. Overmuch. [Obs. or Prov. Eng. & Scot.]

overmix.c: Overmix O`ver*mix" (?), v. t. To mix with too much.

overmodest.c: Overmodest O"ver*mod"est (?), a. Modest to excess; bashful. -- O"ver*mod"est*ly, adv.

overmorrow.c: Overmorrow O"ver*mor"row (?), n. The day after or following to-morrow. [Obs.] Bible (1551).

overmost.c: Overmost O"ver*most` (?), a. Over the rest in authority; above all others; highest. [Obs.] Fabyan.

overmount.c: Overmount O`ver*mount" (?), v. t. [Cf. Surmount.] To mount over; to go higher than; to rise above.

overmuch.c: Overmuch O"ver*much" (?), a. Too much. -- adv. In too great a degree; too much. -- n. An excess; a surplus.

overmuchness.c: Overmuchness O`ver*much"ness (?), n. The quality or state of being in excess; superabundance. [R.] B. Jonson.

overmultiply.c: Overmultiply O`ver*mul"ti*ply (?), v. t. & i. To multiply or increase too much; to repeat too often.

overname.c: Overname O`ver*name" (?), v. t. To name over or in a series; to recount. [Obs.] Shak.

overnice.c: Overnice O"ver*nice" (?), a. Excessively nice; fastidious. Bp. Hall. -- O"ver*nice"ly, adv. -- O"ver*nice"ness, n.

overnight.c: Overnight O"ver*night` (?), n. The fore part of the night last past; the previous evening. [R.] Shak.
overnight o"ver*night", adv. 1. In the fore part of the night last past; in the evening before.

overnoise.c: Overnoise O`ver*noise" (?), v. t. To overpower by noise.

overnumerous.c: Overnumerous O"ver*nu"mer*ous (?), a. Excessively numerous; too many.

overoffice.c: Overoffice O`ver*of"fice (?), v. t. To domineer over by virtue of office. [Obs.] Shak.

overofficious.c: Overofficious O"ver*of*fi"cious (?), a. Too busy; too ready to intermeddle; too officious. Collier.

overpaint.c: Overpaint O`ver*paint" (?), v. t. To color or describe too strongly. Sir W. Raleigh.

overpamper.c: Overpamper O`ver*pam"per (?), v. t. To pamper excessively; to feed or dress too much. Dryton.

overpart.c: Overpart O`ver*part" (?), v. t. To give too important or difficult a part to. [Obs.] B. Jonson.

overpass.c: Overpass O`ver*pass" (?), v. t. [imp. & p. p. Overpassed (?); p. pr. & vb. n. Overpassing.] [Cf. Surpass.]
Overpass O`ver*pass", v. i. To pass over, away, or off.

overpassionate.c: Overpassionate O"ver*pas"sion*ate (?), a. Passionate to excess. -- O"ver*pas"sion*ate*ly, adv.

overpay.c: Overpay O`ver*pay" (?), v. t. [imp. & p. p. Overpaid (?); p. pr. & vb. n. Overpaying.] 1. To pay too much to; to reward too highly.

overpeer.c: Overpeer O`ver*peer" (?), v. t. To peer over; to rise above.

overpeople.c: Overpeople O`ver*peo"ple (?), v. t. To people too densely.

overperch.c: Overperch O`ver*perch" (?), v. t. To perch upon; to fly over. [Obs.] Shak.

overpersuade.c: Overpersuade O`ver*per*suade" (?), v. t. To persuade or influence against one's inclination or judgment. Pope.

overpester.c: Overpester O`ver*pes"ter (?), v. t. To pester exceedingly or excessively. Sir W. Raleigh.

overpicture.c: Overpicture O`ver*pic"ture (?), v. t. To surpass nature in the picture or representation of. [Obs.] “O'erpicturing that Venus.” Shak.

overplease.c: Overplease O`ver*please" (?), v. t. To please excessively.

overplus.c: Overplus O"ver*plus (?), n. [Over + L. plus more. See Plus, and cf. Surplus.] That which remains after a supply, or beyond a quantity proposed; surplus. Shak.

overply.c: Overply O`ver*ply" (?), v. t. To ply to excess; to exert with too much vigor; to overwork. Milton.

overpoise.c: Overpoise O`ver*poise" (?), v. t. To outweigh; to overbalance. [R.] Sir T. Browne.
Overpoise O"ver*poise`, n. Preponderant weight; a counterbalance. [R.] Mrs. Browning.

overpolish.c: Overpolish O`ver*pol"ish (?), v. t. To polish too much.

overpost.c: Overpost O`ver*post" (?), v. t. To post over; to pass over swiftly, as by post. Shak.

overpotent.c: Overpotent O"ver*po"tent (?), a. Too potent or powerful.

overpower.c: Overpower O`ver*pow"er (?), v. t. [imp. & p. p. Overpowered (?); p. pr. & vb. n. Overpowering.] To excel or exceed in power; to cause to yield by superior power; to vanquish; to subdue; as, the light overpowers the eyes. “And overpower'd that gallant few.” Wordsworth.
Overpower O"ver*pow`er, n. A dominating power. Bacon.

overpowering.c: Overpowering O`ver*pow"er*ing, a. Excelling in power; too powerful; irresistible. -- O`ver*pow"er*ing*ly, adv.

overpraise.c: Overpraise O`ver*praise" (?), v. t. [Cf. Overprize, Superpraise.] To praise excessively or unduly.

overpraising.c: Overpraising O`ver*prais"ing, n. The act of praising unduly; excessive praise. Milton.

overpress.c: Overpress O`ver*press" (?), v. t. 1. To bear upon with irresistible force; to crush; to overwhelm. Shak.

overpressure.c: Overpressure O"ver*pres"sure (?), n. Excessive pressure or urging. London Athenaeum.

overprize.c: Overprize O`ver*prize" (?), v. t. [Cf. Overpraise.] To prize excessively; to overvalue. Sir H. Wotton.

overproduction.c: Overproduction O"ver*pro*duc"tion (?), n. Excessive production; supply beyond the demand. J. S. Mill.

overprompt.c: Overprompt O"ver*prompt" (?), a. Too prompt; too ready or eager; precipitate. -- O`ver*prompt"ness, n.

overproof.c: Overproof O"ver*proof" (?), a. Containing more alcohol than proof spirit; stronger than proof spirit; that is, containing more than 49.3 per cent by weight of alcohol.

overproportion.c: Overproportion O`ver*pro*por"tion (?), v. t. To make of too great proportion.

overproud.c: Overproud O"ver*proud" (?), a. Exceedingly or unduly proud. “Overproud of his victory.” Milton.

overprovoke.c: Overprovoke O`ver*pro*voke" (?), v. t. To provoke excessively. Bp. Hall.

overquell.c: Overquell O`ver*quell" (?), v. t. To quell or subdue completely. [R.] Bp. Hall.

overquietness.c: Overquietness O"ver*qui"et*ness (?), n. Too much quietness. Sir. T. Browne.

overrake.c: Overrake O`ver*rake" (?), v. t. [imp. & p. p. Overraked (?); p. pr. & vb. n. Overraking.] (Naut.) To rake over, or sweep across, from end to end, as waves that break over a vessel anchored with head to the sea.

overrank.c: Overrank O"ver*rank" (?), a. Too rank or luxuriant.

overrate.c: Overrate O`ver*rate" (?), v. t. [imp. & p. p. Overrated; p. pr. & vb. n. Overrating.] To rate or value too highly; to overestimate.
Overrate O"ver*rate`, n. An excessive rate. [R.] Massinger.

overreach.c: Overreach O`ver*reach" (ō`vẽr*rēch"), v. t. [imp. & p. p. Overreached (?), (Overraught (?), obs.); p. pr. & vb. n. Overreaching.]

Overreach O`ver*reach", v. i. 1. To reach too far; as: (a) To strike the toe of the hind foot against the heel or shoe of the forefoot; -- said of horses. (b) (Naut.) To sail on one tack farther than is necessary. Shak.
Overreach O"ver*reach` (ō"vẽr*rēch`), n. The act of striking the heel of the fore foot with the toe of the hind foot; -- said of horses.

overreacher.c: Overreacher O`ver*reach"er (?), n. One who overreaches; one who cheats; a cheat.

overread.c: Overread O`ver*read" (?), v. t. To read over, or peruse. Shak.

overready.c: Overready O"ver*read"y (?), a. Too ready. -- O"ver*read"*i*ly (#), adv. -- O"ver*read"i*ness, n.

overreckon.c: Overreckon O`ver*reck"on (?), v. t. To reckon too highly.

overred.c: Overred O`ver*red" (?), v. t. To smear with red. [Obs.]

overrefine.c: Overrefine O`ver*re*fine" (?), v. t. To refine too much.

overrent.c: Overrent O`ver*rent" (?), v. t. To rent for too much.

override.c: Override O`ver*ride" (?), v. t. [imp. Overrode (?); p. p. Overridden (?), Overrode, Overrid (?); p. pr. & vb. n. Overriding.] [AS. offerīdan.] 1. To ride over or across; to ride upon; to trample down.

overrigged.c: Overrigged O"ver*rigged" (?), a. Having too much rigging.

overrighteous.c: Overrighteous O"ver*right"eous (?), a. Excessively righteous; -- usually implying hypocrisy.

overrigid.c: Overrigid O"ver*rig"id (?), a. Too rigid; too severe.

overripe.c: Overripe O"ver*ripe" (?), a. Matured to excess. Milton.

overripen.c: Overripen O`ver*rip"en (?), v. t. To make too ripe. Shak.

overroast.c: Overroast O`ver*roast" (?), v. t. To roast too much. Shak.

overrule.c: Overrule O`ver*rule" (?), v. t. [imp. & p. p. Overruled (?); p. pr. & vb. n. Overruling.] 1. To rule over; to govern or determine by superior authority.
Overrule O`ver*rule", v. i. To be superior or supreme in rulling or controlling; as, God rules and overrules. Shak.

overruler.c: Overruler O`ver*rul"er (?), n. One who, or that which, controls, governs, or determines. Sir P. Sidney.

overruling.c: Overruling O`ver*rul"ing, a. Exerting controlling power; as, an overruling Providence. -- O`ver*rul"ing*ly, adv.

overrun.c: Overrun O`ver*run" (?), v. t. [imp. Overran (?); p. p. Overrun; p. pr. & vb. n. Overrunning. ] 1. To run over; to grow or spread over in excess; to invade and occupy; to take possession of; as, the vine overran its trellis; the farm is overrun with witch grass.
Overrun O`ver*run", v. i. 1. To run, pass, spread, or flow over or by something; to be beyond, or in excess.

overrunner.c: Overrunner O`ver*run"ner (?), n. One that overruns. Lovelace.

oversaturate.c: Oversaturate O`ver*sat"u*rate (?), v. t. [Cf. Supersaturate.] To saturate to excess.

oversay.c: Oversay O`ver*say" (?), v. t. To say over; to repeat. Ford.

overscrupulousness.c: Overscrupulousness O`ver*scru"pu*lous*ness, n. The quality or state of being overscrupulous; excess of scrupulousness.

oversea.c: Oversea O"ver*sea" (?), a. Beyond the sea; foreign.

overseas.c: Overseas Oversea { O"ver*sea" (?), O"ver*seas" (?), } adv. Over the sea; abroad. Milton. Tennyson.

oversearch.c: Oversearch O`ver*search" (?), v. t. To search all over.

overseason.c: Overseason O`ver*sea"son (?), v. t. To season too highly.

oversee.c: Oversee O`ver*see" (?), v. t. [imp. Oversaw (?); p. p. Overseen (?); p. pr. & vb. n. Overseeing.] [AS. oferséon to survey, to despise. See Over, and See.]
Oversee O`ver*see", v. i. To see too or too much; hence, to be deceived. [Obs.]

overseer.c: Overseer O`ver*seer" (?), n. One who oversees; a superintendent; a supervisor; as, an overseer of a mill; specifically, one or certain public officers; as, an overseer of the poor; an overseer of highways.

overseership.c: Overseership O`ver*seer"ship, n. The office of an overseer.

oversell.c: Oversell O`ver*sell` (?), v. t. [imp. & p. p. Oversold (?); p. pr. & vb. n. Overselling. ] 1. To sell for a higher price than; to exceed in selling price.

overset.c: Overset O`ver*set" (?), v. t. [imp. & p. p. Overset; p. pr. & vb. n. Oversetting. ] 1. To turn or tip (anything) over from an upright, or a proper, position so that it lies upon its side or bottom upwards; to upset; as, to overset a chair, a coach, a ship, or a building. Dryden.
Overset O`ver*set", v. i. To turn, or to be turned, over; to be upset. Mortimer.
Overset O"ver*set` (?), n. 1. An upsetting; overturn; overthrow; as, the overset of a carriage.

overshade.c: Overshade O`ver*shade` (?), v. t. [AS. ofersceadwian. See Over, and Shade, and cf. Overshadow.] To cover with shade; to render dark or gloomy; to overshadow. Shak.

overshadow.c: Overshadow O`ver*shad"ow (?), v. t. [imp. & p. p. Overshadowed(?); p. pr. & vb. n. Overshadowing. ] [Cf. Overshade. ] 1. To throw a shadow, or shade, over; to darken; to obscure.

overshadower.c: Overshadower O"ver*shad"ow*er (?), n. One that throws a shade, or shadow, over anything. Bacon.

overshake.c: Overshake O`ver*shake" (?), v. t. To shake over or away; to drive away; to disperse. [Obs.] Chaucer.

overshine.c: Overshine O`ver*shine" (?), v. t. 1. To shine over or upon; to illumine. Shak.

overshoe.c: Overshoe O"ver*shoe` (?), n. A shoe that is worn over another for protection from wet or for extra warmth; esp., an India-rubber shoe; a galosh.

overshoot.c: Overshoot O`ver*shoot" (?), v. t. [imp. & p. p. Overshot (?); p. pr. & vb. n. Overshooting.] 1. To shoot over or beyond; to miss; as, to overshoot a mark; to overshoot the green in golf. “Not to overshoot his game.” South.
Overshoot O`ver*shoot", v. i. To fly beyond the mark. Collier.

overshot.c: Overshot O"ver*shot` (?), a. From Overshoot, v. t.
Overshot O"ver*shot`, a. (Zool.) Having the upper teeth projecting beyond the lower; -- said of the jaws of some dogs.

oversight.c: Oversight O"ver*sight` (?), n. 1. Watchful care; superintendence; general supervision.

oversize.c: Oversize O`ver*size" (?), v. t. To surpass in size.
Oversize O`ver*size", v. t. To cover with viscid matter. [R.]

overskip.c: Overskip O`ver*skip" (?), v. t. To skip or leap over; to treat with indifference. Shak.

overskirt.c: Overskirt O"ver*skirt` (?), n. An upper skirt, shorter than the dress, and usually draped.

overslaugh.c: Overslaugh O"ver*slaugh` (?), n. [D. overslag.] A bar in a river; as, the overslaugh in the Hudson River. [Local, U. S.] Bartlett.

Overslaugh O`ver*slaugh", v. t. [D. overslaan.] To hinder or stop, as by an overslaugh or an impediment; as, to overslaugh a bill in a legislative body; to overslaugh a military officer, that is, to hinder his promotion or employment. [Local Cant, U. S.]

oversleep.c: Oversleep O`ver*sleep" (?), v. t. To sleep beyond; as, to oversleep one's self or one's usual hour of rising.
Oversleep O`ver*sleep", v. i. To sleep too long.

overslide.c: Overslide O`ver*slide" (?), v. t. To slide over or by.

overslip.c: Overslip O`ver*slip" (?), v. t. To slip or slide over; to pass easily or carelessly beyond; to omit; to neglect; as, to overslip time or opportunity.

overslop.c: Overslop O"ver*slop` (?), n. [AS. oferslop.] An outer garment, or slop. [Obs.] Chaucer.

overslow.c: Overslow O`ver*slow" (?), v. t. To render slow; to check; to curb. [Obs.] Hammond.

oversman.c: Oversman O"vers*man (?), n.; pl. Oversmen (?). 1. An overseer; a superintendent.

oversnow.c: Oversnow O`ver*snow" (?), v. t. To cover with snow, or as with snow. [Poetic] Shak. Dryden.

oversoon.c: Oversoon O"ver*soon" (?), adv. Too soon. Sir P. Sidney.

oversorrow.c: Oversorrow O`ver*sor"row (?), v. t. To grieve or afflict to excess. [Obs.] Milton.

oversow.c: Oversow O`ver*sow" (?), v. t. [AS. ofersawan.] To sow where something has already been sown. [R.]

overspan.c: Overspan O`ver*span" (?), v. t. To reach or extend over.

overspeak.c: Overspeak O`ver*speak" (?), v. t. & i. [AS. ofersprecan.] To exceed in speaking; to speak too much; to use too many words.

overspin.c: Overspin O`ver*spin" (?), v. t. To spin out to too great length; to protract unduly. W. Cartwright.

overspread.c: Overspread O`ver*spread" (?), v. t. [imp. & p. p. Overspread; p. pr. & vb. n. Overspreading.] [AS. ofersprǣdan.] To spread over; to cover; as, the deluge overspread the earth. Chaucer.
Overspread O`ver*spread", v. i. To be spread or scattered over.

overspring.c: Overspring O`ver*spring" (?), v. t. To spring or leap over.

overstand.c: Overstand O`ver*stand" (?), v. t. To stand on the price or conditions of, so as to lose a sale; to lose by an extravagant price or hard conditions. [Obs.]

overstare.c: Overstare O`ver*stare" (?), v. t. To outstare. [Obs.] Shak.
Overstare O`ver*stare", v. i. To stare wildly. [Obs.] Ascham.

overstate.c: Overstate O`ver*state" (?), v. t. [imp. & p. p. Overstated; p. pr. & vb. n. Overstating.] To state in too strong terms; to exaggerate. Fuller.

overstatement.c: Overstatement O"ver*state"ment (?), n. An exaggerated statement or account.

overstay.c: Overstay O`ver*stay" (?), v. t. [imp. & p. p. Overstayed (?) or Overstaid (?); p. pr. & vb. n. Overstaying.] To stay beyond the time or the limits of; as, to overstay the appointed time; to overstay one's welcome. Bp. Hall.

overstep.c: Overstep O`ver*step" (?), v. t. [imp. & p. p. Overstepped (?); p. pr. & vb. n. Overstepping.] [AS. ofersteppan.] To step over or beyond; to transgress; as, to overstep the bounds of propriety. Shak.

overstock.c: Overstock O"ver*stock` (?), n. Stock in excess. Tatler.
Overstock O`ver*stock", v. t. [imp. & p. p. Overstocked (?); p. pr. & vb. n. Overstocking.] To fill too full; to supply in excess; as, to overstock a market with goods, or a farm with cattle.

overstore.c: Overstore O`ver*store" (?), v. t. To overstock. Sir. M. Hale.

overstory.c: Over-story O`ver-sto`ry (?), n. (Arch.) The clearstory, or upper story, of a building.

overstrain.c: Overstrain O`ver*strain" (?), v. i. [imp. & p. p. Overstrained (?); p. pr. & vb. n. Overstraining.] To strain one's self to excess. Dryden.
Overstrain O`ver*strain", v. t. To stretch or strain too much; as, to overstrain one's nerves. Ayliffe.

overstraitly.c: Overstraitly O`ver*strait"ly (?), adv. Too straitly or strictly. [Obs.] Sir W. Raleigh.

overstraw.c: Overstraw O`ver*straw" (?), v. t. To overstrew. [Obs.] Shak.

overstrew.c: Overstrew O`ver*strew" (?), v. t. To strew or scatter over.

overstride.c: Overstride O`ver*stride" (?), v. t. To stride over or beyond.

overstrike.c: Overstrike O`ver*strike" (?), v. t. To strike beyond. [Obs.]

oversubtle.c: Oversubtle Oversubtile O"ver*sub"tile, O"ver*sub"tle (?), a. Excessively subtle.

oversum.c: Oversum O"ver*sum` (?), n. A sum or quantity over; surplus. [Obs.] Holinshed.

oversupply.c: Oversupply O`ver*sup*ply" (?), v. t. To supply in excess.
Oversupply O"ver*sup*ply`, n. An excessive supply; a supply in excess of demand.

oversway.c: Oversway O`ver*sway" (?), v. t. To bear sway over.

overswell.c: Overswell O`ver*swell" (?), v. t. & i. To swell or rise above; to overflow. [R.] Shak.

overt.c: overt o"vert (ō*vẽrt" or ō"vẽrt), a. [OF. overt, F. ouvert, p. p. of OF. ovrir, F. ouvrir, to open, of uncertain origin; cf. It. aprire, OIt. also oprire, L. aperire to open, operire to cover, deoperire to uncover. Perh. from L. aperire influenced by F. couvrir to cover. Cf. Aperient, Cover.]

overtake.c: Overtake O`ver*take" (?), v. t. [imp. Overtook (?); p. p. Overtaken (?); p. pr. & vb. n. Overtaking.]

overtalk.c: Overtalk O`ver*talk" (?), v. i. To talk to excess. Milton.

overtask.c: Overtask O`ver*task" (?), v. t. To task too heavily.

overtax.c: Overtax O`ver*tax" (?), v. t. To tax or to task too heavily; as, a job that overtaxed his physical energies.

overtempt.c: Overtempt O`ver*tempt" (?), v. t. To tempt exceedingly, or beyond the power of resistance. Milton.

overthrow.c: Overthrow O`ver*throw" (?), v. t. [imp. Overthrew (?); p. p. Overthrown (?); p. pr. & vb. n. Overthrowing.] 1. To throw over; to overturn; to upset; to turn upside down.
Overthrow O"ver*throw` (?), n. 1. The act of overthrowing; the state of being overthrown; ruin.

overthwart.c: Overthwart O"ver*thwart" (ō"vẽr*thwärt"), a. 1. Having a transverse position; placed or situated across; hence, opposite. “Our overthwart neighbors.” Dryden.
Overthwart O"ver*thwart", adv. Across; crosswise; transversely. “Y'clenched overthwart and endelong.” Chaucer.
Overthwart O"ver*thwart", prep. Across; from alde to side of. “Huge trees overthwart one another.” Milton.
Overthwart O"ver*thwart`, n. That which is overthwart; an adverse circumstance; opposition. [Obs.] Surrey.
Overthwart O`ver*thwart", v. t. To cross; to oppose. [Obs.]

overthwartly.c: Overthwartly O"ver*thwart"ly, adv. In an overthwart manner; across; also, perversely. [Obs.] Peacham.

overthwartness.c: Overthwartness O"ver*thwart"ness, n. The state of being overthwart; perverseness. [Obs.] Lord Herbert.

overtilt.c: Overtilt O`ver*tilt" (ō`vẽr*tĭlt"), v. t. To tilt over; to overturn.

overtime.c: Overtime O"ver*time` (?), n. 1. Time beyond, or in excess of, a limit; esp., extra working time.

overtire.c: Overtire O`ver*tire" (?), v. t. To tire to excess; to exhaust.
Overtire O`ver*tire", v. t. To become too tired. Br. Hall.

overtitle.c: Overtitle O`ver*ti"tle (?), v. t. To give too high a title to.

overtoil.c: Overtoil O`ver*toil", v. t. To weary excessively; to exhaust.

overtone.c: Overtone O"ver*tone` (?), n. [A translation of G. oberton. See Over, Tone.] (Mus.) One of the harmonics faintly heard with and at a higher frequency than a fundamental tone as it dies away, produced by some aliquot portion of the vibrating sting or column of air which yields the fundamental tone; one of the natural harmonic scale of tones, as the octave, twelfth, fifteenth, etc.; an aliquot or “partial” tone; a harmonic. See Harmonic, and Tone. Tyndall.

overtop.c: Overtop O`ver*top" (?), v. t. [imp. & p. p. Overtopped (?); p. pr. & vb. n. Overtopping.] 1. To rise above the top of; to exceed in height; to tower above. “To o'ertop old Pelion.” Shak.

overtower.c: Overtower O`ver*tow"er (?), v. t. To tower over or above.
Overtower O`ver*tow"er, v. i. To soar too high. [R.] Fuller.

overtrade.c: Overtrade O`ver*trade" (?), v. i. To trade beyond one's capital; to buy goods beyond the means of paying for or selling them; to overstock the market.

overtrading.c: Overtrading O`ver*trad"ing (?), n. The act or practice of buying goods beyond the means of payment; a glutting of the market.

overtread.c: Overtread O`ver*tread" (?), v. t. [AS. oferiredan.] To tread over or upon.

overtrip.c: Overtrip O`ver*trip" (?), v. t. To trip over nimbly.

overtrow.c: Overtrow O`ver*trow" (?), v. i. To be too trustful or confident; to trust too much. [Obs.] Wyclif (1 Cor. iv. 4).

overtrust.c: Overtrust O`ver*trust", v. t. & i. To trust too much. Bp. Hall.

overture.c: Overture O"ver*ture (?), [OF. overture, F. ouverture, fr. OF. ovrir, F. ouvrir. See Overt.] 1. An opening or aperture; a recess; a chamber. [Obs.] Spenser. “The cave's inmost overture.” Chapman.
Overture O"ver*ture, v. t. To make an overture to; as, to overture a religious body on some subject.

overturn.c: Overturn O`ver*turn" (?), v. t. [imp. & p. p. Overturned (?); p. pr. & vb. n. Overturning.] 1. To turn or throw from a basis, foundation, or position; to overset; as, to overturn a carriage or a building.
Overturn O"ver*turn`, n. The act off overturning, or the state of being overturned or subverted; overthrow; as, an overturn of parties.

overturnable.c: Overturnable O`ver*turn"a*ble (?), a. Capable of being, or liable to be, overturned or subverted.

overturner.c: Overturner O`ver*turn"er (?), n. One who overturns. South.

overvalue.c: Overvalue O`ver*val"ue (?), v. t. [imp. & p. p. Overvalued (?); p. pr. & vb. n. Overvaluing.] 1. To value excessively; to rate at too high a price. “To overvalue human power.” Holyday.

overveil.c: Overveil O`ver*veil" (?), v. t. To veil or cover. Shak.

overview.c: Overview O"ver*view` (?), n. [Cf. Survey.] 1. An inspection or overlooking. [Obs.] Shak.

overvote.c: Overvote O`ver*vote" (?), v. t. To outvote; to outnumber in votes given. [R.] Eikon Basilike.

overwalk.c: Overwalk O`ver*walk" (?), v. t. To walk over or upon.

overwar.c: Overwar O`ver*war" (?), v. t. To defeat. [Obs.] Warner.

overwary.c: Overwary O"ver*wa"ry (?), a. Too wary; too cautious.

overwash.c: Overwash O`ver*wash" (?), v. t. To overflow. Holinshed.

overwasted.c: Overwasted O`ver*wast"ed (?), a. Wasted or worn out; consumed; spent [Obs.] Drayton.

overwatch.c: Overwatch O"ver*watch" (?), v. t. 1. To watch too much.

overwax.c: Overwax O`ver*wax" (?), v. i. To wax or grow too rapidly or too much. [Obs.] R. of Gloucester.

overweak.c: Overweak O"ver*weak" (?), a. Too weak; too feeble.

overwear.c: Overwear O`ver*wear" (-wâr"), v. t. To wear too much; to wear out. Drayton.
Overwear O"ver*wear` (-wâr`), n. Clothing worn over the ordinary indoor clothing, as overcoats, wraps, etc.

overweary.c: Overweary O"ver*wea"ry (?), v. t. To weary too much; to tire out. Dryden.

overweather.c: Overweather O`ver*weath"er (?), v. t. To expose too long to the influence of the weather. [Obs.] Shak.

overween.c: Overween O`ver*ween" (?), v. t. [AS. oferwēnian. See Over, and Ween.] To think too highly or arrogantly; to regard one's own thinking or conclusions too highly; hence, to be egotistic, arrogant, or rash, in opinion; to think conceitedly; to presume.

overweening.c: Overweening O`ver*ween"ing, a. Unduly confident; arrogant; presumptuous; conceited. -- O`ver*ween"ingly, adv. Milton. -- O`ver*ween"ing*ness, n.

overweigh.c: Overweigh O`ver*weigh" (?), v. t. To exceed in weight; to overbalance; to weigh down. Drayton. Hooker.

overweight.c: Overweight O"ver*weight` (?), n. 1. Weight over and above what is required by law or custom.
Overweight O"ver*weight", a. 1. Overweighing; excessive. [Obs.] “Of no overweight worth.” Fuller.

overwell.c: Overwell O`ver*well" (?), v. t. To overflow. R. D. Blackmore.

overwhelm.c: Overwhelm O`ver*whelm" (?), v. t. [imp. & p. p. Overwhelmed (?); p. pr. & vb. n. Overwhelming.]
Overwhelm O"ver*whelm`, n. The act of overwhelming. [R.]

overwhelming.c: Overwhelming O`ver*whelm"ing, a. Overpowering; irresistible. -- O`ver*whelm"ing*ly, adv.

overwind.c: Overwind O`ver*wind" (?), v. t. To wind too tightly, as a spring, or too far, as a hoisting rope on a drum.

overwing.c: Overwing O`ver*wing" (?), v. t. To outflank. [Obs.] Milton.

overwise.c: Overwise O"ver*wise" (?), a. Too wise; affectedly wise. -- O`ver*wise"ly, adv. -- O`ver*wise"ness, n.

overwit.c: Overwit O`ver*wit" (?), v. t. To outwit. Swift.

overword.c: Overword O`ver*word" (?), v. t. To say in too many words; to express verbosely. Hales.

overwork.c: Overwork O`ver*work" (?), v. t. [imp. & p. p. Overworked (?) or Overwrought (?); p. pr. & vb. n. Overworking.] 1. To work beyond the strength; to cause to labor too much or too long; to tire excessively; as, to overwork a horse.
Overwork O`ver*work", v. i. To work too much, or beyond one's strength.
Overwork O"ver*work`, n. Work in excess of the usual or stipulated time or quantity; extra work; also, excessive labor.

overworn.c: Overworn O`ver*worn" (?), p. p. & a. from Overwear, v. t. Worn out or subdued by toil; worn out so as to be trite.

overwrest.c: Overwrest O`ver*wrest" (?), v. t. To wrest or force from the natural or proper position. Shak.

overwrestle.c: Overwrestle O`ver*wres"tle (?), v. t. To subdue by wrestling. [Obs.] Spenser.

overwrought.c: Overwrought O`ver*wrought (?), p. p. & a. from Overwork. 1. Wrought upon excessively; overworked.

overzeal.c: Overzeal O"ver*zeal (?), n. Excess of zeal. Fairfax.

ovicapsule.c: Ovicapsule O`vi*cap"sule (?), n. [Ovum + capsule.] 1. (Anat.) The outer layer of a Graafian follicle.

ovicell.c: Ovicell O"vi*cell` (?), n. [Ovum + cell.] (Zool.) One of the dilatations of the body wall of Bryozoa in which the ova sometimes undergo the first stages of their development. See Illust. of Chilostoma.

ovicular.c: Ovicular O*vic"u*lar (?), a. [L. ovum an egg.] (Biol.) Of or pertaining to an egg.

ovicyst.c: Ovicyst O"vi*cyst (?), n. [Ovum + cyst.] (Zool.) The pouch in which incubation takes place in some Tunicata.

ovidian.c: Ovidian O*vid"i*an (?), a. Of or pertaining to the Latin poet Ovid; resembling the style of Ovid.

oviducal.c: Oviducal O`vi*du"cal (?), a. (Anat.) Of or pertaining to oviducts; as, oviducal glands.

oviduct.c: Oviduct O"vi*duct (?), n. [Ovum + duct: cf. F. oviducte.] (Anat.) A tube, or duct, for the passage of ova from the ovary to the exterior of the animal or to the part where further development takes place. In mammals the oviducts are also called Fallopian tubes.

oviferous.c: Oviferous O*vif"er*ous (?), a. [Ovum + -ferous: cf. F. ovifère.] (Biol.) Egg-bearing; -- applied particularly to certain receptacles, as in Crustacea, that retain the eggs after they have been excluded from the formative organs, until they are hatched.

oviform.c: Oviform O"vi*form (ō"vĭ*fôrm), a. [Ovum + -form: cf. F. oviforme.] (Biol.) Having the form or figure of an egg; egg-shaped; as, an oviform leaf.

ovigerous.c: Ovigerous O*vig"er*ous (?), a. [Ovum + -gerous: cf. F. ovigere.] (Biol.) Bearing eggs; oviferous.

ovine.c: Ovine O"vine (ō"vīn), a. [L. ovinus, fr. ovis sheep: cf. F. ovine.] Of or pertaining to sheep; consisting of sheep.

ovipara.c: Ovipara ‖O*vip"a*ra (?), n. pl. [NL. See Oviparous.] (Zool.) An artificial division of vertebrates, including those that lay eggs; -- opposed to Vivipara.
