oviparity.c: Oviparity O`vi*par"i*ty (?), n. [See Oviparous.] (Biol.) Generation by means of ova. See Generation.

oviparous.c: Oviparous O*vip"a*rous (?), a. [L. oviparus; ovum egg + parere to bring forth: cf. F. ovipare.] (Physiol.) Producing young from eggs; as, an oviparous animal, in which the egg is generally separated from the animal, and hatched after exclusion; -- opposed to viviparous.

oviposit.c: Oviposit O`vi*pos"it (?), v. i. [imp. & p. p. Oviposited; p. pr. & vb. n. Ovipositing.] [See Ovum, and Posit.] To lay or deposit eggs; -- said esp. of insects.
Oviposit O`vi*pos"it, v. t. To deposit or lay (an egg).

oviposition.c: Oviposition Ovipositing { O`vi*pos"it*ing (?), O`vi*po*si"tion (?), } n. The depositing of eggs, esp. by insects.

ovipositor.c: Ovipositor O`vi*pos"i*tor (?), n. [L. ovum an egg + positor a placer, fr. ponere to place.] (Zool.) The organ with which many insects and some other animals deposit their eggs. Some ichneumon files have a long ovipositor fitted to pierce the eggs or larvae of other insects, in order to lay their own eggs within the same.

ovisac.c: Ovisac O"vi*sac (?), n. [Ovum + sac.] (Anat.) (a) A Graafian follicle; any sac containing an ovum or ova. (b) The inner layer of the fibrous wall of a Graafian follicle.

ovism.c: Ovism O"vism (?), n. [Ovum + -ism.] (Zool.) The old theory that the egg contains the whole embryo of the future organism and the germs of all subsequent offsprings and is merely awakened to activity by the spermatozoon; -- opposed to spermism or animalculism.

ovist.c: Ovist O"vist (?), n. (Zool.) A believer in ovism. Same as Ovulist.

ovococcus.c: Ovococcus ‖O`vo*coc"cus (?), n.; pl. Ovococci (#). [Ovum + Gr.? grain, seed.] (Biol.) A germinal vesicle.

ovoidal.c: Ovoidal Ovoid { O"void (?), O*void"al (?), } a. [Ovum + -oid: cf. F. ovoïde.] Resembling an egg in shape; egg-shaped; ovate; as, an ovoidal apple.

ovoid.c: Ovoid O"void (?), n. A solid resembling an egg in shape.

ovolo.c: Ovolo O"vo*lo (?), n. [It. ovolo, uovolo, fr. L. ovum an egg. Cf. Ovule.] (Arch.) A round, convex molding. See Illust. of Column.

ovology.c: Ovology O*vol"o*gy (?), n. [Ovum + -logy. Cf. F. ovologie.] That branch of natural history which treats of the origin and functions of eggs.

ovoplasma.c: Ovoplasma O`vo*plas"ma (?), n. [Ovum + plasma.] (Boil.) Yolk; egg yolk. Haeckel.

ovotesttis.c: Ovotesttis O`vo*test"tis (?), n. [NL. See Ovum, and Testis.] (Zool.) An organ which produces both ova and spermatozoids; an hermaphrodite gland.

ovoviviparous.c: Ovoviviparous O*vo*vi*vip"a*rous (?), a. [Ovum + viviparous: cf. F. ovovivipare.] (Biol.) Oviparous, but hatching the egg while it is within the body, as some fishes and reptiles.

ovular.c: Ovular O"vu*lar (?), a. (Biol.) Relating or belonging to an ovule; as, an ovular growth.

ovulate.c: Ovulate O"vu*late (?), a. (Biol.) Containing an ovule or ovules.

ovulation.c: ovulation o`vu*la"tion (?), n. (Physiol.) The formation of ova or eggs in the ovary, and the discharge of the same. In the human female the discharge occurs about halfway between menstruation times.

ovule.c: Ovule O"vule (?), n. [Dim. of L. ovum an egg: cf. F. ovule. Cf. Ovolo, Ovulum.] (Biol.) (a) The rudiment of a seed. It grows from a placenta, and consists of a soft nucleus within two delicate coatings. The attached base of the ovule is the hilum, the coatings are united with the nucleus at the chalaza, and their minute orifice is the foramen. (b) An ovum.

ovulist.c: Ovulist O"vu*list (?), n. (Biol.) A believer in the theory (called encasement theory), current during the last century, that the egg was the real animal germ, and that at the time of fecundation the spermatozoa simply gave the impetus which caused the unfolding of the egg, in which all generations were inclosed one within the other. Also called ovist.

ovulum.c: Ovulum ‖O"vu*lum (?), n.; pl. Ovula (#). [NL. See Ovule.] (Biol.) An ovule.

ovum.c: Ovum ‖O"vum (ō"vŭm), n.; pl. L. Ova (ō"vȧ), E. Ovums (ō"vŭmz). [L., an egg. See Oval.] 1. (Biol.) A more or less spherical and transparent cell, which by a process of multiplication and growth develops into a mass of cells, constituting a new individual like the parent; an egg, spore, germ, or germ cell. See Illust. of Mycropyle.

owe.c: Owe Owe (ō), v. t. [imp. & p. p. Owed (ōd), (Ought (ät) obs.); p. pr. & vb. n. Owing (ō"ĭng).] [OE. owen, awen, aghen, to have, own, have (to do), hence, owe, AS. āgan to have; akin to G. eigen, a., own, Icel. eiga to have, Dan. eie, Sw. äga, Goth. áigan, Skr. īç. √110. Cf. Ought, v., 2d Own, Fraught.] 1. To possess; to have, as the rightful owner; to own. [Obs.]

owel.c: Owel Ow"el (?), a. [OF. oel, owel, iwel, ivel, F. égal, fr. L. aequalis.] (Law) Equal. [Obs.] Burrill.

owelty.c: Owelty Ow"el*ty (?), n. [OF. oelté, ivelté.] (Law) Equality; -- sometimes written ovelty and ovealty. Burrill.

owenite.c: Owenite Ow"en*ite (?), n. A follower of Robert Owen, who tried to reorganize society on a socialistic basis, and established an industrial community on the Clyde, Scotland, and, later, a similar one in Indiana.

owher.c: Owher O"wher (?), adv. [AS. āhwaer.] Anywhere. [Obs.] “If he found owher a good fellow.” Chaucer.

owing.c: Owing Ow`ing (?), p. p. & a. [Used in a passive sense for owed (AS. āgen. See Own).] 1. Had or held under obligation of paying; due.

owl.c: Owl Owl (oul), n. [AS. ūle; akin to D. uil, OHG. ūwila, G. eule, Icel. ugla, Sw. ugla, Dan. ugle.]
Owl Owl, v. i. [imp. & p. p. Owled (?); p. pr. & vb. n. Owling.] 1. To pry about; to prowl. [Prov. Eng.]

owler.c: Owler Owl"er (?), n. [From Owl, v. i.] One who owls; esp., one who conveys contraband goods. See Owling, n. [Obs. or Prov. Eng.] T. Brown.

owlery.c: Owlery Owl"er*y (?), n.; pl. Owleries (?). An abode or a haunt of owls.

owlet.c: Owlet Owl"et (?), n. [Dim. of owl. Cf. Howlet.] (Zool.) A small owl; especially, the European species (Athene noctua), and the California flammulated owlet (Megascops flammeolus).

owleyed.c: Owl-eyed Owl"-eyed` (?), a. Having eyes like an owl's.

owling.c: Owling Owl"ing, n. [From Owl, v. i.] (O. Eng. Law) The offense of transporting wool or sheep out of England contrary to the statute formerly existing. Blackstone.

owlish.c: Owlish Owl"ish, a. Resembling, or characteristic of, an owl.

owlism.c: Owlism Owl"ism (?), n. Affected wisdom; pompous dullness. [R.]

owllight.c: Owllight Owl"light` (?), n. Glimmering or imperfect light. [R.] Bp. Warburton.

own.c: Own Own (ōn), v. t. [OE. unnen to grant, permit, be pleased with, AS. unnan to grant; akin to OS. giunnan, G. gönnen, Icel. unna; of uncertain origin. This word has been confused with own to possess.] To grant; to acknowledge; to admit to be true; to confess; to recognize in a particular character; as, we own that we have forfeited your love.

Own Own, a. [OE. owen, awen, auen, aughen, AS. āgen, p. p. of āgan to possess; akin to OS. ēgan, G. & D. eigen, Icel. eiginn, Sw. & Dan. egen. √110. See Owe.] Belonging to; belonging exclusively or especially to; peculiar; -- most frequently following a possessive pronoun, as my, our, thy, your, his, her, its, their, in order to emphasize or intensify the idea of property, peculiar interest, or exclusive ownership; as, my own father; my own composition; my own idea; at my own price. “No man was his own [i. e., no man was master of himself, or in possession of his senses].” Shak.

Own Own, v. t. [imp. & p. p. Owned (?); p. pr. & vb. n. Owning.] [OE. ohnien, ahnien, AS. āgnian, fr. āgen own, a. See Own, a.] To hold as property; to have a legal or rightful title to; to be the proprietor or possessor of; to possess; as, to own a house.

owner.c: Owner Own"er (?), n. One who owns; a rightful proprietor; one who has the legal or rightful title, whether he is the possessor or not. Shak.

ownership.c: Ownership Own"er*ship, n. The state of being an owner; the right to own; exclusive right of possession; legal or just claim or title; proprietorship.

owre.c: Owre Owre (?), n. [AS. ūr; akin to G. auerochs, OHG. ūr, ūrohso, Icel. ūrr.] (Zool.) The aurochs. [Obs.]

owser.c: Owser Owse { Owse (ouz), Ow"ser (ou"zẽr), } n. Tanner's ooze. See Ooze, 3.

ox.c: Ox Ox (ŏks), n.; pl. Oxen (#). [AS. oxa; akin to D. os. G. ochs, ochse, OHG. ohso, Icel. oxi, Sw. & Dan. oxe, Goth. aúhsa, Skr. ukshan ox, bull; cf. Skr. uksh to sprinkle. √214. Cf. Humid, Aurochs.] (Zool.) The male of bovine quadrupeds, especially the domestic animal when castrated and grown to its full size, or nearly so. The word is also applied, as a general name, to any species of bovine animals, male and female.

oxalan.c: Oxalan Ox"a*lan (?), n. [From Alloxan, by transposition of letters.] (Chem.) A complex nitrogenous substance C3N3H5O3 obtained from alloxan (or when urea is fused with ethyl oxamate), as a stable white crystalline powder; -- called also oxaluramide.

oxalantin.c: Oxalantin Ox`a*lan"tin (?), n. [From Alloxantin, by transposition of letters.] (Chem.) A white crystalline nitrogenous substance (C6H4N4O5) obtained by the reduction of parabanic acid; -- called also leucoturic acid.

oxalate.c: Oxalate Ox"a*late (?), n. [Cf. F. oxalate. See Oxalic.] (Chem.) A salt of oxalic acid.

oxaldehyde.c: Oxaldehyde Ox*al"de*hyde (?), n. [Oxalic + aldehyde.] (Chem.) Same as Glyoxal.

oxalethyline.c: Oxalethyline Ox`al*eth"yl*ine (?), n. [Oxalic + ethyl + -ine.] A poisonous nitrogenous base (C6H10N2) obtained indirectly from oxamide as a thick transparent oil which has a strong narcotic odor, and a physiological action resembling that of atropine. It is probably related to pyridine.

oxalic.c: Oxalic Ox*al"ic (?), a. [From Oxalis: cf. F. oxalique.] (Chem.) Pertaining to, derived from, or contained in, sorrel, or oxalis; specifically, designating an acid found in, and characteristic of, oxalis, and also certain plant of the Buckwheat family.

oxalis.c: Oxalis Ox"a*lis (?), n. [L., a kind of sorrel, Gr. 'oxali`s, fr. 'oxy`s sharp, pungent, acid.] (Bot.) A genus of plants, mostly herbs, with acid-tasting trifoliolate or multifoliolate leaves; -- called also wood sorrel.

oxalite.c: Oxalite Ox"a*lite (?), n. (Min.) A yellow mineral consisting of oxalate of iron.

oxaluramide.c: Oxaluramide Ox`a*lur*am"ide (?), n. [Oxaluric + amide.] (Chem.) Same as Oxalan.

oxalurate.c: Oxalurate Ox`a*lur"ate (?), n. (Chem.) A salt of oxaluric acid.

oxaluric.c: Oxaluric Ox`a*lur"ic (?), a. [Oxalyl + urea.] (Chem.) Pertaining to, or designating, a complex nitrogenous acid related to the ureids, and obtained from parabanic acid as a white silky crystalline substance.

oxalyl.c: Oxalyl Ox"a*lyl (?), n. [Oxalic + -yl.] (Chem.) (a) A hydrocarbon radical (C2O2) regarded as a residue of oxalic acid and occurring in derivatives of it. (b) An old name for carbonyl. (c) An old name for carboxyl.

oxamate.c: Oxamate Ox*am"ate (?), n. (Chem.) A salt of oxamic acid.

oxamethane.c: Oxamethane Ox`a*meth"ane (?), n. [Oxamic + ethyl.] (Chem.) Ethyl oxamate, obtained as a white scaly crystalline powder.

oxamethylane.c: Oxamethylane Ox`a*meth"yl*ane (?), n. [Oxamic + methyl.] (Chem.) Methyl oxamate, obtained as a pearly white crystalline substance.

oxamic.c: Oxamic Ox*am"ic (?), a. [Oxalic + amido] (Chem.) Pertaining to, or designating, an acid NH2.CO.CO.HO obtained as a fine crystalline powder, intermediate between oxalic acid and oxamide. Its ammonium salt is obtained by boiling oxamide with ammonia.

oxamide.c: Oxamide Ox*am"ide (?), n, [Oxalic + amide.] (Chem.) A white crystalline neutral substance (C2O2(NH2)2) obtained by treating ethyl oxalate with ammonia. It is the acid amide of oxalic acid. Formerly called also oxalamide.

oxamidine.c: Oxamidine Ox*am"i*dine (?), n. [Oxygen + amido + -ine.] (Chem.) One of a series of bases containing the amido and the isonitroso groups united to the same carbon atom.

oxanilamide.c: Oxanilamide Ox`a*nil*am"ide (?), n. [Oxanilic + amide.] (Chem.) A white crystalline nitrogenous substance, obtained indirectly by the action of cyanogen on aniline, and regarded as an anilide of oxamic acid; -- called also phenyl oxamide.

oxanilate.c: Oxanilate Ox*an"i*late (?), n. (Chem.) A salt of oxanilic acid.

oxanilic.c: Oxanilic Ox`an*il"ic (?), a. [Oxalic + aniline.] (Chem.) Pertaining to, or derived from, oxalic acid and aniline; -- used to designate an acid obtained in white crystalline scales by heating these substances together.

oxanilide.c: Oxanilide Ox*an"i*lide (?), n. [Oxalic + aniline + amide.] (Chem.) A white crystalline substance, resembling oxanilamide, obtained by heating aniline oxalate, and regarded as a double anilide of oxalic acid; -- called also diphenyl oxamide.

oxbane.c: Oxbane Ox"bane` (?), n. (Bot.) A poisonous bulbous plant (Buphane toxicaria) of the Cape of Good Hope.

oxbird.c: Oxbird Ox"bird` (?), n. (Zool.) (a) The dunlin. (b) The sanderling. (c) An African weaver bird (Textor alector).

oxbiter.c: Oxbiter Ox"bit`er (?), n. (Zool.) The cow blackbird. [Local, U. S.]

oxbow.c: Oxbow Ox"bow` (?), n. A frame of wood, bent into the shape of the letter U, and embracing an ox's neck as a kind of collar, the upper ends passing through the bar of the yoke; also, anything so shaped, as a bend in a river.

oxeye.c: Oxeye Ox"eye` (?), n. [Ox + eye.] 1. (Bot.) (a) The oxeye daisy. See under Daisy. (b) The corn camomile (Anthemis arvensis). (c) A genus of composite plants (Buphthalmum) with large yellow flowers.

oxeyed.c: Oxeyed Ox"*eyed` (?), a. Having large, full eyes, like those of an ox. Burton.

oxfly.c: Oxfly Ox"fly` (?), n. (Zool.) The gadfly of cattle.

oxford.c: Oxford Ox"ford (?), prop. a. Of or pertaining to the city or university of Oxford, England.

oxgang.c: Oxgang Ox"gang` (?), n. [Ox + gang, n., 1.] (O. Eng. Law) See Bovate.

oxgoad.c: Oxgoad Ox"goad` (?), n. A goad for driving oxen.

oxhead.c: Oxhead Ox"head` (?), n. [Cf. Hogshead.] Literally, the head of an ox (emblem of cuckoldom); hence, a dolt; a blockhead.

oxheart.c: Oxheart Ox"heart` (?), n. A large heart-shaped cherry, either black, red, or white.

oxhide.c: Oxhide Ox"hide` (?), n. 1. The skin of an ox, or leather made from it.

oxidability.c: Oxidability Ox`i*da*bil"i*ty (?), n. [Cf. F. oxydabilité.] Capability of being converted into an oxide.

oxidable.c: Oxidable Ox"i*da*ble (?), a. [Cf. F. oxydable.] Capable of being converted into an oxide.

oxidate.c: Oxidate Ox"i*date (?), v. t. [imp. & p. p. Oxidated (?); p. pr. & vb. n. Oxidating.] [Cf. f. oxyder. See Oxide.] (Chem.) To oxidize. [Obs.]

oxidation.c: Oxidation Ox`i*da"tion (?), n. [Cf. F. oxidation.] (Chem.) The act or process of oxidizing, or the state or result of being oxidized.

oxide.c: Oxide Ox"ide (ŏks"ĭd or ŏks"īd), n. [F. oxygène oxygen + acide acid: cf. F. oxyde. The French word was correctly spelt oxide, till about the year 1840, when, in ignorance or forgetfulness of the true history and composition of the word, the orthography was change to make it represent the υ of Gr. 'oxy`s, from which it was supposed to be directly derived.] (Chem.) A binary compound of oxygen with an atom or radical, or a compound which is regarded as binary; as, iron oxide, ethyl oxide, nitrogen oxide, etc.

oxidizable.c: Oxidizable Ox"i*di`za*ble (?), a. Capable of being oxidized.

oxidize.c: Oxidize Ox"i*dize (ŏks"ĭ*dīz), v. t. [imp. & p. p. Oxidized (ŏks"ĭ*dīzd); p. pr. & vb. n. Oxidizing.] (Chem.) To combine with oxygen, or subject to the action of oxygen, or of an oxidizing agent. Specifically: (a) To combine with oxygen or with more oxygen; to add oxygen to; as, to oxidize nitrous acid so as to form nitric acid. (b) To remove hydrogen from (anything), as by the action of oxygen; as, to oxidize alcohol so as to form aldehyde. (c) To subject to the action of oxygen or of an oxidizing agent, so as to bring to a higher grade, as an -ous compound to an -ic compound; as, to oxidize mercurous chloride to mercuric chloride.

oxidizer.c: Oxidizer Ox"i*di`zer (?), n. (Chem.) An agent employed in oxidation, or which facilitates or brings about combination with oxygen; as, nitric acid, chlorine, bromine, etc., are strong oxidizers.

oxidulated.c: Oxidulated Ox*id"u*la`ted (?), a. (Chem.) Existing in the state of a protoxide; -- said of an oxide. [R.]

oxime.c: Oxime Ox"ime (?), n. (Chem.) One of a series of isonitroso derivatives obtained by the action of hydroxylamine on aldehydes or ketones.

oxindol.c: Oxindol Ox*in"dol (?), n. [Oxygen + indol.] (Chem.) A white crystalline nitrogenous substance (C8H7NO) of the indol group, obtained by the reduction of dioxindol. It is a so-called lactam compound.

oxiodic.c: Oxiodic Ox`i*od"ic (?), a. [Oxy- (a) + iodic.] (Chem.) Pertaining to, or designating, certain compounds of iodine and oxygen.

oxlike.c: Oxlike Ox"like (?), a. Characteristic of, or like, an ox.

oxlip.c: Oxlip Ox"lip` (?), n. [AS. oxanslyppe. See Ox, and Cowslip.] (Bot.) The great cowslip (Primula veris, var. elatior).

oxonate.c: Oxonate Ox"o*nate (?), n. (Chem.) A salt of oxonic acid.

oxonian.c: Oxonian Ox*o"ni*an (?), prop. a. Of or relating to the city or the university of Oxford, England. Macaulay.
Oxonian Ox*o"ni*an, prop. n. A student or graduate of Oxford University, in England.

oxonic.c: Oxonic Ox*on"ic (?), a. [Prob. glyoxalic + carbonic.] (Chem.) Pertaining to, or designating, a complex nitrogenous acid (C4H5N3O4) not known in the free state, but obtained, in combination with its salts, by a slow oxidation of uric acid, to which it is related.

oxpecker.c: Oxpecker Ox"peck`er (?), n. (Zool.) An African bird of the genus Buphaga; the beefeater.

oxshoe.c: Oxshoe Ox"shoe` (?), n. A shoe for oxen, consisting of a flat piece of iron nailed to the hoof.

oxter.c: Oxter Ox"ter (?), n. [AS. ōhsta.] The armpit; also, the arm. [Prov. Eng. & Scot.]

oxtongue.c: ox-tongue oxtongue ox"tongue`, ox"-tongue` (?), n. (Bot.) A widespread European weed (Picris echioides formerly Helminthia echioides) with spiny tongue-shaped leaves and yellow flowers. The name is applied to several plants, from the shape and roughness of their leaves; as, Anchusa officinalis, a kind of bugloss, and Helminthia echioides, both European herbs. It has been naturalized in the U. S.

oxy.c: Oxy- Ox"y- (?). (Chem.) A prefix, also used adjectively, designating: (a) A compound containing oxygen. (b) A compound containing the hydroxyl group, more properly designated by hydroxy-. See Hydroxy-.

oxyacetic.c: oxyacetic ox`y*a*ce"tic (?), a. [Oxy- (b) + acetic.] Hydroxyacetic; designating an acid called also glycolic acid.

oxyacid.c: Oxyacid Ox`y*ac"id (?), n. [Oxy- (a) + acid.] (Chem.) An acid containing oxygen, as chloric acid or sulphuric acid; -- contrasted with the hydracids, which contain no oxygen, as hydrochloric acid. See Acid, and Hydroxy-.

oxyammonia.c: Oxyammonia Ox`y*am*mo"ni*a (?), n. [Oxy- (b) + ammonia.] (Chem.) Same as Hydroxylamine.

oxybenzene.c: Oxybenzene Ox`y*ben"zene (?), n. [Oxy- (b) + benzene.] (Chem.) Hydroxy benzene. Same as Phenol.

oxybenzoic.c: Oxybenzoic Ox`y*ben*zo"ic (?), a. [Oxy- (b) + benzoic.] (Chem.) Hydroxybenzoic; pertaining to, or designating, any one of several hydroxyl derivatives of benzonic acid, of which the commonest is salicylic acid.

oxybromic.c: Oxybromic Ox`y*bro"mic (?), a. [Oxy- (a) + bromic.] (Chem.) Pertaining to, or designating, certain compounds of oxygen and bromine.

oxybutyric.c: Oxybutyric Ox`y*bu*tyr"ic (?), a. [Oxy- (b) + butyric.] (Chem.) Hydroxybutyric; designating any one of a group of metameric acids ((C3H6.OH).CO2H).

oxycalcium.c: Oxycalcium Ox`y*cal"ci*um (?), a. [Oxy- (a) + calcium.] Of or pertaining to oxygen and calcium; as, the oxycalcium light. See Drummond light.

oxychloric.c: Oxychloric Ox`y*chlo"ric (?), a. [Oxy- (a) + chloric.] (Chem.) (a) Of, pertaining to, or designating in general, certain compounds containing oxygen and chlorine. (b) Formerly designating an acid now called perchloric acid. See Perchloric.

oxychloride.c: Oxychloride Ox`y*chlo"ride (?), n. [Oxy- (a) + chloride.] (Chem.) A ternary compound of oxygen and chlorine; as, plumbic oxychloride.

oxycrate.c: Oxycrate Ox"y*crate (?), n. [Gr.?????;???? acid +???? to mix: cf. F. oxycrat.] (med.) A Mixture of water and vinegar. Wiseman.

oxycymene.c: Oxycymene Ox`y*cy"mene (?), n. [Oxy- (b) + cymene.] (Chem.) Hydroxy cymene. Same as Carvacrol.

oxygen.c: Oxygen Ox"y*gen (?), n. [F. oxygène, from Gr. 'oxy`s sharp, acid + root of gi`gnesqai to be born. So called because originally supposed to be an essential part of every acid.]

oxygenate.c: Oxygenate Ox"y*gen*ate (?), v. t. [imp. & p. p. Oxygenated (?); p. pr. & vb. n. Oxygenating (?).] [Cf. F. oxygéner.] (Chem.) To unite, or cause to combine, with oxygen; to treat with oxygen; to oxidize; as, oxygenated water (hydrogen dioxide).

oxygenation.c: Oxygenation Ox`y*gen*a"tion (?), n. [Cf. F. oxygénation.] (Chem.) The act or process of combining or of treating with oxygen; oxidation.

oxygenic.c: Oxygenic Ox`y*gen"ic (?), a. (Chem.) Pertaining to, containing, or resembling, oxygen; producing oxygen.

oxygenium.c: Oxygenium ‖Ox`y*ge"ni*um (?), n. [NL.] (Chem.) The technical name of oxygen. [R. and archaic]

oxygenize.c: Oxygenize Ox"y*gen*ize (?), v. t. [imp. & p. p. Oxygenized (?); p. pr. & vb. n. Oxygenizing (?).] (Chem.) To oxidize.

oxygon.c: Oxygon Ox"y*gon (?), n. [Gr. 'oxy`s sharp + gwni`a an angle: cf. F. oxygone.] (Geom.) A triangle having three acute angles.

oxygonial.c: Oxygonial Oxygonal { Ox*yg"o*nal (?), Ox`y*go"ni*al (?), } a. Having acute angles. Barlow.

oxyhaemocyanin.c: Oxyhaemocyanin Oxyhaemacyanin { Ox`y*haem`a*cy"a*nin (?), Ox`y*haem`o*cy"a*nin (?), } n. [Oxy- (a) + haemacyanin, haemocyanin.] (Physiol. Chem.) See Haemacyanin.

oxyhemoglobin.c: Oxyhemoglobin Oxyhaemoglobin { Ox`y*haem`o*glo"bin, Ox`y*hem`o*glo"bin } (?), n. [Oxy- (a) + haemoglobin, hemoglobin.] (Physiol. Chem.) See Hemoglobin.

oxyhydrogen.c: Oxyhydrogen Ox`y*hy"dro*gen (?), a. [Oxy- (a) + hydrogen.] (Chem.) Of, pertaining to, or consisting of, a mixture of oxygen and hydrogen at over 5000° F.

Oxyhydrogen light Oxyhydrogen light. A light produced by the incandescence of some substances, esp. lime, in the oxyhydrogen flame. Coal gas (producing the oxygas light), or the vapor of ether (oxyether light) or methylated spirit (oxyspirit light), may be substituted for hydrogen.

oxymel.c: Oxymel Ox"y*mel (?), n. [L. oxymeli, Gr.???; 'oxy`s acid +??? honey.] (Med.) A mixture of honey, water, vinegar, and spice, boiled to a sirup. Sir T. Elyot.

oxymethylene.c: Oxymethylene Ox`y*meth"yl*ene, n. [Oxy- (a) + methylene.] (Chem.) Formic aldehyde, regarded as a methylene derivative.

oxymoron.c: Oxymoron ‖Ox`y*mo"ron (?), n. [NL., fr. Gr.???, fr.??? pointedly foolish; 'oxy`s sharp + mwro`s foolish.] (Rhet.) A figure in which an epithet of a contrary signification is added to a word; e. g., cruel kindness; laborious idleness.

oxymuriate.c: Oxymuriate Ox`y*mu"ri*ate (?), n. (Old Chem.) A salt of the supposed oxymuriatic acid; a chloride.

oxymuriatic.c: Oxymuriatic Ox`y*mu`ri*at"ic (?), a. [Oxy- (a) + muriatic: cf. F. oxymuriatique.] (Chem.) Pertaining to, or consisting of, oxygen and muriatic acid, that is, hydrochloric acid. [Archaic.]

oxyntic.c: Oxyntic Ox*yn"tic (?), a. [Gr.???? to make acid.] (Physiol.) Acid; producing acid; -- applied especially to certain glands and cells in the stomach.

oxyopy.c: Oxyopy Oxyopia { ‖Ox`y*o"pi*a (?), Ox"y*o`py (?), } n. [NL. oxyopia, from Gr. 'oxy`s sharp +??? sight.] (Med.) Excessive acuteness of sight.

oxyphenic.c: Oxyphenic Ox`y*phe"nic (?), a. [Oxy- (b) + phenol.] (Chem.) Pertaining to, or designating, the phenol formerly called oxyphenic acid, and now oxyphenol and pyrocatechin. See Pyrocatechin.

oxyphenol.c: Oxyphenol Ox`y*phe"nol (?), n. (Chem.) A phenol, C6H4(OH)2, produced by the distillation of catechin; called also oxyphenic acid, and now pyrocatechin.

oxyphony.c: Oxyphony Ox*yph"o*ny (?), n. [Gr. 'oxy`s sharp + fwnh` voice.] Acuteness or shrillness of voice.

oxyquinoline.c: Oxyquinoline Ox`y*quin"o*line (?), n. [Oxy- (b) + quinoline.] (Chem.) Hydroxy quinoline; a phenol derivative of quinoline, -- called also carbostyril.

oxyrhyncha.c: Oxyrhyncha ‖Ox`y*rhyn"cha (?), n. pl. [NL., fr. Gr. 'oxy`s sharp +?????? snout.] (Zool.) The maioid crabs.

oxyrrhodine.c: Oxyrrhodine Ox*yr"rho*dine (?), n. [Gr.??? (sc.???); 'oxy`s acid +???? made of roses, "ro`don rose.] (Med.) A mixture of two parts of the oil of roses with one of the vinegar of roses. Floyer.

oxysalt.c: Oxysalt Ox"y*salt (?), n. [Oxy- (a) + salt.] (Chem.) A salt of an oxyacid, as a sulphate.

oxysulphide.c: Oxysulphide Ox`y*sul"phide (?), n. (Chem.) A ternary compound of oxygen and sulphur.

oxytocic.c: Oxytocic Ox`y*toc"ic (?), a. [Gr. 'oxy`s sharp, quick +???? birth.] (Med.) Promoting uterine contractions, or parturition. -- n. An oxytocic medicine or agent.

oxytoluene.c: Oxytoluene Ox`y*tol"u*ene (?), n. [Oxy- (a) + toluene.] One of three hydroxy derivatives of toluene, called the cresols. See Cresol.

oxytone.c: Oxytone Ox"y*tone (?), a. [Gr.???; 'oxy`s sharp +??? tone.] Having an acute sound; (Gr. Gram.), having an acute accent on the last syllable.

oyer.c: Oyer O"yer (?), n. [Anglo F., a hearing, from OF. oïr, F. ouïr, to hear, L. audire. See Audible.] (Law) A hearing or an inspection, as of a deed, bond, etc., as when a defendant in court prays oyer of a writing. Blackstone.

oyez.c: Oyez O"yez` (ō"yĕs`; 277), interj. [Anglo-F. oyez hear ye. See Oyer.] Hear; attend; -- a term used by criers of courts to secure silence before making a proclamation. It is repeated three times. [Written also oyes.]

oyster.c: Oyster Oys"ter (ois"tẽr), n. [OF. oistre, F. huître, L. ostrea, ostreum, Gr. 'o`streon; prob. akin to 'ostre`on bone, the oyster being so named from its shell. Cf. Osseous, Ostracize.] 1. (Zool.) Any marine bivalve mollusk of the genus Ostrea. They are usually found adhering to rocks or other fixed objects in shallow water along the seacoasts, or in brackish water in the mouth of rivers. The common European oyster (Ostrea edulis), and the American oyster (Ostrea Virginiana), are the most important species.

oyster catcher oystercatcher oystercatcher, oyster catcher n. (Zool.), Any one of several species of wading birds of the genus Haematopus having stout legs and bill and mostly black-and-white plumage, which frequent seashores and feed upon oysters and other shellfish. The European species (Haematopus ostralegus), the common American species (Haematopus palliatus), and the California, or black, oyster catcher (Haematopus Bachmani) are the best known.

oystergreen.c: Oyster-green Oys"ter-green` (?), n. (Bot.) A green membranous seaweed (Ulva) often found growing on oysters but common on stones, piles, etc.

oystering.c: Oystering Oys"ter*ing, n. Gathering, or dredging for, oysters.

ozena.c: ozena o*ze"na (o*zē"nȧ), n. [NL., fr. L. ozaena, Gr. 'o`zaina, fr. 'o`zein to smell.] (Med.) A discharge of fetid matter from the nostril, particularly if associated with ulceration of the soft parts and disease of the bones of the nose.

ozocerite.c: ozocerite o`zo*ce"rite (ō`zo*sē"rīt), n. [Gr. 'o`zein to smell + khro`s wax.] (Min.) A waxlike mineral resin; -- sometimes called native paraffin, and mineral wax.

ozonation.c: Ozonation O`zo*na"tion (ō`zo*nā"shŭn), n. (Chem.) The act of treating with ozone; also, the act of converting into, or producing, ozone; ozonization.

ozone.c: ozone o"zone (ō"zōn or o*zōn"), n. [Gr. 'o`zwn smelling, p. pr. of 'o`zein to smell. See Odor.] (Chem.) A colorless gaseous substance (O3) obtained (as by the silent discharge of electricity in oxygen) as an allotropic form of oxygen, containing three atoms in the molecule. It is a strong oxidizer, and probably exists in the air, though by the ordinary tests it is liable to be confused with certain other substances, as hydrogen dioxide, or certain oxides of nitrogen. It derives its name from its peculiar odor, which resembles that of weak chlorine.
ozone paper o"zone pa"per. (Chem.) Paper coated with starch and potassium iodine, also called starch-iodide paper. It turns blue when exposed to ozone.

ozonic.c: ozonic o*zon"ic (o*zŏn"ĭk), a. (Chem.) Pertaining to, resembling, or containing, ozone.

ozonification.c: ozonification o*zo`ni*fi*ca"tion (o*zō`nĭ*fĭ*kā"shŭn), n. [Ozone + L. -ficare to make. See -fy. ] (Chem.) The act or process of producing, or of subjecting to the action of, ozone.

ozonize.c: Ozonize O"zo*nize (?), v. t. [imp. & p. p. Ozonized (?); p. pr. & vb. n. Ozonizing.] (Chem.) (a) To convert into ozone, as oxygen. (b) To treat with ozone.

ozonizer.c: Ozonizer O"zo*ni`zer (?), n. (Chem.) An apparatus or agent for the production or application of ozone.

ozonometer.c: Ozonometer O`zo*nom"e*ter (?), n. [Ozone + -meter.] An instrument for ascertaining the amount of ozone in the atmosphere, or in any gaseous mixture. Faraday.

ozonometric.c: Ozonometric O`zo*no*met"ric (?), a. (Chem.) Pertaining to, or used for, the determination of the amount of ozone; of or relating to ozonometry.

ozonometry.c: Ozonometry O`zo*nom"e*try (?), n. (Chem.) The measurement or determination of the quantity of ozone.

ozonoscope.c: Ozonoscope O*zo"no*scope (?), n. [Ozone + -scope.] (Chem.) An apparatus employed to indicate the presence, or the amount, of ozone.

ozonoscopic.c: Ozonoscopic O*zo`no*scop"ic (?), a. [Ozone + Gr. skopei^n to view.] (Chem.) Serving to indicate the presence or the amount of ozone.

ozonous.c: ozonous o"zo*nous (ō"zo*nŭs or o*zō"nŭs), a. Pertaining to or containing, ozone.
